teile.einleitung: The Amazon is a huge river in South America. No other river in the world carries so much water. Around it grows the largest rainforest on Earth.
wichtigste: The Amazon flows through **South America**, mainly through Peru and Brazil.
It flows into the **Atlantic Ocean**.
It is the river with the **most water** in the world.
About 60 per cent of the Amazon rainforest lies in **Brazil**.
The pink **Amazon river dolphin** lives in the river.
The **giant water lily** has leaves that grow up to about three metres wide.

abschnitte.text: The Amazon rises in the **Andes** in Peru. From there it flows right across South America to the east. On the coast of Brazil it flows into the **Atlantic Ocean**. It is over 6,000 kilometres long. No other river carries as much **water** into the sea as the Amazon. Many large tributaries feed it.

Around the Amazon grows the largest **rainforest** on Earth. About **60 per cent** of it lies in **Brazil**. The rest is spread across several neighbouring countries such as Peru and Colombia. In the rainforest it is warm and damp all year round. An incredible number of different animals and plants live here.

**River dolphins** live in the Amazon. The **Amazon river dolphin** often turns **pink** with age. That is why it is also called the pink river dolphin. It finds its prey in the murky water with the help of clicking sounds. Many fish also live in the river, for example piranhas.

A special plant in the Amazon region is the **giant water lily**. Its round leaves float on the water. They can grow up to about **three metres** wide. The edge of the leaves is bent upwards like a baking tin. The leaves are so strong that they can carry a small child.

gewusst: When the water is high, the Amazon floods huge areas of forest every year.
Experts do not agree on whether the Amazon or the Nile is the longest river in the world.

teile.einleitung: Anyone hiking in the Alps will at some point see no more trees. The line above which no more trees grow is called the treeline. It depends mainly on the warmth in summer.
wichtigste: The treeline arises mainly from a lack of warmth in the growing season.
There the soil temperature in summer is around 6 to 7 °C.
In the Central Alps, the Swiss stone pine and larch form the treeline.
In Valais and Graubünden it lies at around 2200 to 2400 m.
The reason for the high position is the mass elevation effect.
Because of alpine farming, the forest line is lower in many places.
Today young trees are growing higher up in many places.

abschnitte.text: According to current knowledge, it is above all the **lack of warmth** in the growing season that decides where the **treeline** lies. If the summer is too cool, trees cannot form enough new tissue. Measurements at treelines in all climate zones gave remarkably similar values. In the root zone the **soil temperature** during the growing season is around 6 to 7 °C. Other factors such as wind or avalanches shift the line only locally.

abschnitte.titel: Swiss stone pine, larch and mountain pine
abschnitte.text: In the Central Alps, for example in the **Engadine**, the **Swiss stone pine** and **larch** form the treeline. They tolerate cold and short summers especially well. Especially on limestone, the **dwarf mountain pine** often grows above the forest. It is a prostrate form of the mountain pine and forms a dense **belt of krummholz**. Its flexible branches are pressed down by the snow without breaking.

In the Valais and Graubünden Central Alps, trees grow up to about **2200 to 2400 m**. On the northern edge of the Alps the line lies clearly lower. The reason is the **mass elevation effect**: large, continuous mountain ranges warm up more and have a sunnier, drier climate. As a result the limits of warmth and plant growth rise upwards.

abschnitte.titel: From the tropics to the pole
abschnitte.text: Worldwide, the treeline lies highest in the **subtropics**. The further you go towards the poles, the cooler the summers are. That is why the treeline sinks ever lower. In the **subarctic**, trees finally grow only close to sea level. Further north still, the treeless tundra begins.

In many Alpine valleys the present **forest line** lies lower than the climate would allow. The reason is the centuries of **alpine farming**: for pastures the upper forest was cleared and grazed. Since the 20th century it has been observed in many places that **young trees** are growing higher up. Warmer summers and abandoned alpine pastures make this possible.

gewusst: Swiss stone pines at the treeline can become several hundred years old.
The larch is the only native conifer that loses its needles in autumn.

teile.einleitung: The Val Müstair is a remote valley in the south-east of the canton of Graubünden. It borders Italy and is known for its ancient monastery. Together with the Swiss National Park it forms a UNESCO biosphere reserve.
wichtigste: The Val Müstair lies in Graubünden and borders Italy.
From the Engadine you reach the valley over the Ofen Pass.
The Convent of St John in Müstair is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
According to legend, Charlemagne founded the monastery.
The monastery church is famous for very old wall paintings.
The locals speak mainly Romansh.
The water from the valley flows into the Adriatic.

abschnitte.text: The **Val Müstair** lies in the far south-east of Switzerland, in the canton of **Graubünden**. It borders **Italy**, more precisely the Vinschgau in South Tyrol. From the Engadine you reach the valley over the **Ofen Pass**. The stream of the valley flows into Italy, into the Adige, and with it into the **Adriatic**. So the Val Müstair does not belong to the catchment area of the Rhine or the Inn.

In the village of Müstair stands the **Convent of St John**. Since 1983 it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage site**. According to legend, **Charlemagne** founded it. The monastery church is famous for its very old **wall paintings** from around the year 800. To this day Benedictine nuns live there.

The local population speaks mainly **Romansh**. Romansh is one of the four national languages of Switzerland. In the valley lie small villages with old houses. The people live mainly from agriculture, crafts and tourism.

The **Biosfera Val Müstair** is a regional nature park. Together with the **Swiss National Park** the valley forms a **UNESCO biosphere reserve**. In a biosphere reserve, nature is to be protected while people live and work there sustainably. Support is given, for example, to products from the region and gentle tourism.

gewusst: The wall paintings in Müstair are among the oldest surviving picture cycles of this kind.
The Swiss National Park is the oldest national park in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: The pear is a popular fruit that grows on trees here. It is juicy, sweet and easy to recognise by its typical shape. In Switzerland it is eaten fresh, dried and baked.
wichtigste: A typical pear is thick at the bottom and narrow at the top towards the stalk.
Like the apple, the pear belongs to the rose family.
Because it has a core, it counts as pome fruit.
Pears keep ripening after picking and become soft and sweet.
Small hard stone cells make some pears a little gritty.
Many Williams pears grow in Valais.

abschnitte.text: A pear is **bulbous** at the bottom and becomes narrower towards the stalk at the top. The **light bulb** was even named after this shape, as in German it is called a Glühbirne, a glowing pear. The pear is closely related to the **apple**. Both belong to the **rose family**. Inside, the pear has a **core** with small pips. That is why, like the apple and the quince, it counts as **pome fruit**.

In the flesh of the pear there are tiny, hard cells. They are called **stone cells**. When chewing you feel them as fine grains. In some varieties there are more, in others fewer. The pear is healthy all the same: it contains water, sugar, vitamins and fibre.

Pears are often harvested while they are still hard. They **keep ripening after picking**. If they lie in the kitchen for a few days, they become softer and sweeter. Ripe pears are delicate and quickly get bruises. So you should handle them carefully and eat them soon.

In sunny **Valais** many **Williams pears** grow. They are very juicy and smell strongly. In the past, many high-stem pear trees stood on meadows all over Switzerland. From dried pears people make **Birnbrot**, a pastry with a dark, sweet filling that is eaten mainly in winter.

gewusst: For Birnbrot, pears are dried. Dried pears keep for a long time and used to be an important winter store.
From thickened pear juice comes the spread **Birnel**, which has a long tradition in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Leaves do not sit on the stem by chance. Every plant species arranges them according to a certain pattern. This arrangement is called **leaf arrangement** and helps to capture as much light as possible.
wichtigste: The place where a leaf sits on the shoot is called a node.
Alternate: only one leaf sits at each node, as in the beech.
Opposite: two leaves sit facing each other at the same node, as in the lilac.
Decussate: each pair of leaves is turned by 90 degrees, as in peppermint and nettle.
Whorled: three or more leaves form a ring, as in woodruff.
Staggered leaves shade each other less.

abschnitte.text: The place on the shoot where a leaf attaches is called a **node**. If only a single leaf sits at each node, the arrangement is **alternate**. The leaves then stand alternately on different sides. An example is the **beech**. The **plane tree** also has alternate leaves.

In an **opposite** arrangement, two leaves sit exactly opposite each other at the same node, as in the **lilac** or the **maple**. This way you can tell maple and plane tree apart well, although their leaves look similar. If each pair of leaves is turned by a right angle to the previous one, it is called **decussate**. This is typical of the mint family such as **peppermint** and also of the **stinging nettle**.

If three or more leaves sit at one node, they form a ring around the stem. This arrangement is called **whorled**. A well-known example is **woodruff**. In the **dandelion** all the leaves arise close together at the base of the plant. They lie flat on the ground in a circle. This arrangement is called a **rosette**.

If the leaves are staggered, they do not lie exactly on top of each other. This way **they shade each other less**, and every leaf gets plenty of light. Some plants form a **leaf mosaic**. With stalks of different lengths, the leaves orient themselves so that they fit together like puzzle pieces. You can see this well in **ivy** on a wall.

gewusst: In many plants the leaf arrangement follows fixed number patterns connected with the so-called Fibonacci sequence.
Whether leaves are opposite or alternate can be recognised in winter too, from the buds.

teile.einleitung: The apoplast is a term from plant science. It describes everything in a plant that lies outside the living cell contents: the cell walls, the spaces between the cells and the dead conducting tubes. It plays a big role in the transport of water and substances.
wichtigste: The apoplast includes cell walls, intercellular spaces and dead conducting elements of the xylem.
It lies outside the plasma membranes, that is, outside the living protoplasts.
Water can flow in the apoplast without crossing a membrane.
Because there are no membranes in the way, the flow resistance is low.
The cuticle protects the apoplast of the leaves from evaporation.
The liquid in the apoplast is usually slightly acidic, around pH 5 to 6.

abschnitte.text: Every plant cell has a living part inside, the **protoplast**, which is wrapped in the **plasma membrane**. Everything outside these membranes together forms the **apoplast**. This includes the **cell walls**, the air- or water-filled **intercellular spaces** and the dead cells of the **xylem**. The counterpart is called the **symplast**: this is all the living cell contents together, which are connected with each other by fine channels, the **plasmodesmata**.

Water from the soil has to get through the root cortex to the vascular bundles. On the **apoplastic path** it flows through the network of cell walls and spaces. On the **symplastic path** it travels from cell to cell through the plasmodesmata. On the **transcellular path** it crosses every cell and its membranes, often through water channels called **aquaporins**. Because the apoplast contains no membranes, water flows there particularly easily and quickly.

The **xylem** carries water from the roots up to the leaves. Its conducting elements, the **tracheae** and **tracheids**, die as they mature. All that is left are the woody, firm cell walls, which act like tubes. Since they no longer have any living contents, they belong entirely to the apoplast. This creates a continuous conducting system outside the living cells.

In the leaves, too, the cell walls are soaked with water. So that this water does not simply evaporate, the **cuticle** lies on the outer wall of the **epidermis**. It is a waxy layer that lets almost no water through. The plant regulates gas exchange instead through small openings, the **stomata**.

abschnitte.titel: An acidic space and sugar transport
abschnitte.text: In the plasma membrane sit **proton pumps**, which move hydrogen ions (H+) outwards. That is why the liquid in the apoplast is usually slightly acidic, with a pH of around 5 to 6. The plant uses this gradient as a source of energy. In **apoplastic phloem loading**, sugar (**sucrose**) is first released into the cell wall. A **sucrose-proton symporter** then takes it up together with protons into the cells of the phloem, even against the concentration gradient.

gewusst: In the root there is a barrier: the **Casparian strip** in the endodermis seals the cell walls, so that water has to pass through living cells there.
The terms apoplast and symplast were coined around 1930 by the German forestry scientist Ernst Münch.

teile.einleitung: Agroscope is the federal centre of competence for agricultural research. It researches arable farming, fruit, wine, animals and food at several sites in Switzerland. Among other things, its newly bred grape varieties are well known.
wichtigste: Agroscope is the federal government’s agricultural research.
It belongs to the Federal Office for Agriculture in the EAER department.
Sites include Wädenswil and Changins near Nyon.
Agroscope bred the grape varieties Gamaret and Divico.
An important aim is disease-resistant varieties.
Agroscope supplies bacterial cultures for cheese dairies.

abschnitte.text: **Agroscope** is part of the **Federal Office for Agriculture**. This belongs to the **Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research**, **EAER** for short. Agroscope does research for an agriculture that brings good harvests while protecting the environment and the soil. The results help farming families, authorities and the food industry.

Agroscope has several sites in Switzerland. In **Wädenswil** on Lake Zurich, research is done on **fruit**, vines and **vegetables**, among other things. New apple varieties were also bred there. In **Changins** near Nyon in the canton of Vaud stands a large site for **arable farming** and **viticulture**. There, among other things, new cereal and grape varieties are tested.

Agroscope has been breeding vines for decades. The red variety **Gamaret** arose from a cross between **Gamay** and **Reichensteiner**. It is now grown in several cantons. A more modern red wine variety is **Divico**. It is very robust against **mildew** and other fungal diseases. That is why it needs far less spraying.

An important aim of plant breeding at Agroscope is **disease-resistant varieties**. Such varieties fall ill less often. In this way you can save on **sprays** and still harvest well. That is good for the environment and lowers the costs of farms.

Agroscope breeds and supplies **lactic acid bacteria** for cheese dairies. These **bacterial cultures** are needed for Emmentaler, Gruyère and many other cheeses. They shape the **flavour** and also the **holes** in the cheese. In this way the federal government’s research helps Swiss cheese keep its typical quality.

gewusst: The grape variety Divico is named after a leader of the Helvetii.
The holes in Emmentaler arise from gases that bacteria form as the cheese ripens.

teile.einleitung: Biomagnification means that a pollutant builds up more and more along the food chain. Animals at the top of the chain therefore carry especially much of it in them. Well-known examples are DDT, PCBs and mercury.
wichtigste: In biomagnification the concentration of a pollutant rises along the food chain.
Especially affected are fat-soluble substances that are hard to break down.
DDT led to thin eggshells in birds of prey.
Rachel Carson wrote the book “Silent Spring” in 1962.
Large predatory fish such as tuna often contain a lot of mercury.
Killer whales are especially heavily contaminated with PCBs.
The Stockholm Convention of 2001 bans or restricts such substances.

abschnitte.text: A pollutant gets into the water, for example, and is taken up by plankton. Small fish eat a lot of plankton, large fish many small fish. Because the substance stays in the body, it becomes more **concentrated** at every level. This is called **biomagnification**. **Bioaccumulation**, by contrast, describes the build-up in a single living thing.

Especially susceptible are substances that are **fat-soluble** and **hard to break down**. They are stored in fatty tissue and hardly excreted. These include the insecticide **DDT** and the industrial chemicals **PCBs**. **Mercury** too builds up in food chains. That is why large predatory fish such as **tuna** and **swordfish** often contain especially much of it.

DDT used to be sprayed a lot against insects. Through the food chain it got into birds of prey. Their **eggshells** became thin as a result and broke. The American biologist **Rachel Carson** drew attention to the consequences of pesticides in 1962 with the book **“Silent Spring”**. After that DDT was banned in many countries.

In **Japan** in 1956 a severe mercury poisoning through contaminated fish was officially identified. It is known as **Minamata disease**. **Killer whales** stand at the top of long food chains and are today especially heavily contaminated with PCBs. The **Stockholm Convention** of 2001 bans or restricts long-lived organic pollutants such as DDT and PCBs. Switzerland too has signed it.

gewusst: Many populations of birds of prey have recovered since the DDT ban.
PCBs have long been banned, but because of their long life they stay in the environment for decades.

teile.einleitung: In everyday life we call many small, juicy fruits berries. Botanists, however, mean something specific by it. That is why tomato, banana and kiwi are true berries, but strawberry and raspberry are not.
wichtigste: In a berry the whole fruit wall is fleshy.
A berry has no hard stone.
Tomato, banana, kiwi and pepper are botanically berries.
Strawberry and raspberry are called berries only in everyday speech.
Pumpkin, cucumber and melon form pepos.
The date is a one-seeded berry.
The black berries of deadly nightshade are very poisonous.

abschnitte.text: In botany a **berry** is a fruit whose whole **fruit wall** stays fleshy and juicy. The seeds lie free in the flesh. They are not enclosed by a hard **stone** as in the cherry. A berry usually contains several seeds. Grapes and blueberries are berries, as you would expect.

The **tomato** develops from an ovary with a fleshy fruit wall and many seeds. So it is a berry. The **pepper** too is botanically a berry. The **banana** is also regarded as a berry, and in cultivated bananas the seeds are only tiny dots. The **kiwi**, with its brown, hairy skin, has many small black seeds in the green flesh. Strawberry and raspberry, on the other hand, bear the name berry only in everyday speech.

In **pumpkin**, cucumber and melon, the outer layer of the fruit wall becomes firm and leathery. That is why it is called a **pepo**. The **orange** is also a special berry. Its segments are filled with many small **juice sacs**. These grow from the innermost layer of the fruit wall.

The **date** contains only a single hard stone. Nevertheless it is a berry. Its stone is namely the **seed** itself and not a stone formed from the fruit wall. That is why the date is called a **one-seeded berry**. In a stone fruit such as the plum, by contrast, the innermost layer of the fruit wall has become hard.

Not all berries are edible. The **deadly nightshade** also grows in Swiss forests. It forms cherry-sized, shiny **black berries**. Even a few of them are life-threatening. So the rule is: you never eat unknown berries.

gewusst: The cucumber, which we know as a vegetable, is botanically a berry.
The strawberry is an aggregate accessory fruit: the small yellow dots on the outside are the actual fruits.

teile.einleitung: Upright brome is a grass that grows on poor, dry meadows. It is an important characteristic species of semi-dry grassland. Where it is common, you usually also find many flowers and butterflies.
wichtigste: Upright brome belongs to the grass family.
The genus name of the bromes is Bromus.
It is an important characteristic species of semi-dry grassland.
The plant community Mesobrometum is named after it.
It grows in dense tussocks and reaches about 0.3 to 1 metre in height.
With heavy fertilising, it is pushed out by vigorous fodder grasses.

abschnitte.text: **Upright brome** belongs to the **grass family**, like wheat and barley. The scientific genus name of the bromes is **Bromus**. It grows in dense **tussocks**, that is, in firm clumps. Its stems stand upright and grow **about 0.3 to 1 metre** tall. The leaves at the base are narrow and often slightly hairy.

Upright brome prefers **lime-rich, poor and rather dry soils**. Such soils are found, for example, on sunny slopes in the **Jura** and in the Alpine foothills. It is typical of **semi-dry grassland**, for which it is an important **characteristic species**. A characteristic species shows which plant community you are dealing with. Semi-dry grasslands are traditionally mown only once a year or lightly grazed.

In science, plant communities are given Latin names. Semi-dry grasslands are called **Mesobrometum**. The name is **taken from upright brome**, because “Brometum” comes from Bromus. “Meso” means roughly “middle”, because these meadows are moderately dry. Many rare plants belong to this community, for example orchids and gentians.

If a poor meadow is **heavily fertilised**, its make-up changes. **Vigorous fodder grasses** then grow faster and denser. They **push out** upright brome and many flowers. Even if a meadow is no longer mown at all, it turns to scrub in time. To preserve semi-dry grasslands, suitable management without fertiliser is therefore needed.

gewusst: Semi-dry grasslands with upright brome are among the most species-rich meadows in Central Europe.
On a single square metre of semi-dry grassland, several dozen plant species can grow.

teile.einleitung: Arable weed flora is the name for the wild plants that grow between cereals and other crops. In the past they were often called weeds in a disparaging way. Many of them bloom colourfully and have become rare today.
wichtigste: Arable companion plants grow together with the crop plants.
Typical are the corn poppy, the cornflower and charlock.
Many came to us with arable farming as early as the Neolithic.
Such ancient immigrants are called archaeophytes.
Their seeds often survive for years in the soil.
Some species such as forking larkspur are rare today.

abschnitte.text: At the edge of cereal fields the **corn poppy** often glows with large, red, thin petals. It likes to germinate on open, worked soil. The **cornflower** blooms a strong blue. In the past it was so common that it became a symbol of the cornfield. The yellow-flowered **charlock** belongs to the **crucifers**: its four petals stand like a cross.

**German chamomile** has white flowers with a yellow centre and is traditionally used as **tea**. You recognize it by the fact that its flower base is **hollow** inside. **Forking larkspur** has blue flowers with a long **spur**. It grows on lime-rich soils and is rare today. Many arable wild plants depend on open fields in which enough sun reaches the ground.

Many arable wild plants are not originally native here. They came to us with arable farming from the **Near East** as early as the **Neolithic**. Plants that immigrated with humans before the discovery of America in **1492** are called **archaeophytes**. Plants introduced only later are called **neophytes**.

abschnitte.titel: The seed bank in the soil
abschnitte.text: Through modern agriculture with weedkillers and very dense stands, many species have become rare. But their **seeds** often **stay viable for years** in the soil. This is called a **seed bank**. When conditions are right again, for example on a gently managed field margin, vanished species sometimes reappear after many years. Arable wild plants also offer food for insects and birds.

gewusst: The cornflower was once so widespread that it appears in many songs and poems.
A single corn poppy can produce thousands of tiny seeds.

teile.einleitung: Large cargo ships pump sea water into tanks so that they sail steadily. But with this ballast water, tiny living things also travel around the world. In this way foreign species reach new areas and can do great damage there.
wichtigste: Ballast water gives empty ships stability and the necessary draught.
Plankton, larvae, algae and bacteria are transported with the water.
The IMO Ballast Water Convention came into force on 8 September 2017.
The exchange is supposed to take place at least 200 nautical miles from the coast.
Many ships treat the water with filters and UV light.
The comb jelly Mnemiopsis leidyi harmed fishing in the Black Sea.
The zebra mussel reached the Great Lakes of North America this way.

abschnitte.text: When a cargo ship sails with little cargo, it sits too high in the water and becomes **unstable**. That is why it pumps water into special tanks, the **ballast water**. This gives it the necessary weight and the right **draught**. In the destination port, where new cargo comes on board, the water is let out again. A large ship can move many thousands of tonnes of water in this way.

With the water the ship also sucks in **plankton**, larvae, algae and bacteria. When the water is let out, these living things reach a quite different sea. If they find good conditions there and no enemies, they can multiply strongly. This is called a **biological invasion**. Ballast water is one of the most important ways in which foreign species are spread in the sea.

The **comb jelly Mnemiopsis leidyi** comes from the western Atlantic. In the 1980s it multiplied massively in the Black Sea and ate zooplankton, fish eggs and larvae. This contributed to the collapse of the anchovy fishery. The **zebra mussel** from Europe was discovered in Lake St. Clair in North America in 1988 and clogs water intakes there. The **Chinese mitten crab** probably also reached Europe with ballast water and digs burrows in river banks.

The **International Maritime Organization (IMO)** is a United Nations organisation based in London. It drew up the **Ballast Water Convention**, which was adopted in 2004. It came into force on 8 September 2017. Under the standard **D-1**, the water is to be exchanged if possible at least 200 nautical miles from the coast and in water at least 200 metres deep. Coastal organisms mostly survive badly in the open ocean.

The stricter standard **D-2** requires that only very few living organisms are in the water that is let out. Many ships have installations on board for this. Often the water is first **filtered**, so that larger organisms are caught. Smaller ones are then killed with **UV light** or with chlorine made electrically from salt water.

gewusst: The Chinese mitten crab has dense tufts of hair on its claws, which gave it its name.
The zebra mussel is also common in Swiss lakes today, but it did not get there on ocean-going ships.

teile.einleitung: The alpine snowbell is a delicate mountain flower with little violet bells. It blooms very early in the year, right at the edge of melting snow. Sometimes it even grows up through the snow.
wichtigste: The alpine snowbell blooms **when the snow melts**.
It can grow up through a thin layer of snow.
Its flowers are **blue-violet** and finely **fringed** at the edge.
The little bells hang nodding downwards.
The leaves are round like a coin.
It belongs to the **primrose family**, like the cowslip.

abschnitte.text: The alpine snowbell is one of the first **heralds of spring** in the mountains. It blooms right at the edge of melting snowfields. Sometimes it even grows up through a **thin layer of snow**. In doing so the plant produces a little warmth and so melts a small hole in the snow. The violet flowers then shine beautifully beside the white snow.

The flowers of the alpine snowbell look like small **bells**. They are coloured **blue-violet**. The edge of the bell is deeply cut and looks like fine **fringes**. The little bells hang downwards; they are said to **nod**. In this way the pollen stays dry in rain and snow.

The alpine snowbell has small, **roundish** leaves that recall coins. They are leathery and lie close to the ground. The whole plant is delicate and grows only about 5 to 15 centimetres tall. The alpine snowbell belongs to the **primrose family**. This also includes the cowslip, which many children know from meadows in the valley.

gewusst: In Switzerland several species of snowbell grow, including the common and the small alpine snowbell.
The scientific name of the alpine snowbell is “Soldanella”.

teile.einleitung: The trunk is the thick column of the tree. It carries the crown and conducts water upwards from the roots. From tree trunks we obtain wood for many things.
wichtigste: The trunk carries the branches and the crown.
In the trunk, water with dissolved nutrients rises from the roots to the leaves.
Every year a new layer of wood grows under the bark.
In the middle of the trunk lies the pith.
A felled trunk without branches is called roundwood.
In Switzerland, foresters fell the trees.
A dugout canoe is a boat made from a single tree trunk.

abschnitte.text: The **trunk** is the thick column of the tree. It carries the branches and the **crown**. On the outside the **bark** protects it from cold, dryness and animals. In the trunk, **water** with dissolved nutrients rises from the roots up into the leaves. This way the whole crown gets what it needs.

Right in the middle of the trunk lies the **pith**. Around it the layers of wood grow. Under the bark a new layer of wood forms every year. This way the trunk becomes a little **thicker** every year. On a felled tree you can see these layers as **annual rings**. If you count them, you know roughly how old the tree was.

In Switzerland, **forestry workers** fell the trees and look after the forest. A felled trunk from which the branches have been removed is called **roundwood**. In the sawmill it is made into boards and beams. After felling, a short piece with the roots stays in the ground. It is called a **tree stump**.

Already in the **Stone Age**, people used tree trunks. They hollowed out a single trunk and so built a boat, the **dugout canoe**. Remains of such boats have also been found in Swiss lakes. Today houses, furniture and much more are built from tree trunks.

gewusst: An old tree stump is a habitat for fungi, beetles and mosses.
Wood from the Swiss forest is constantly growing back.

teile.einleitung: In autumn, little propellers sail down from maple trees to the ground. These are the fruits of the maple with their seeds. Their wings help them to fly as far from the tree as possible.
wichtigste: A whole maple fruit has two wings and later splits into two parts.
Each part carries a seed in its thick, round end.
Maple fruits are among the **winged fruits**, like the fruits of ash and elm.
In summer the fruits are green, in autumn they turn brown and dry.
As they fall they spin like a propeller and are carried away by the wind.
In spring the seeds germinate on the ground.

abschnitte.text: On the maple tree the fruits always grow as a pair. Two parts are joined together in the middle, and each has a thin wing. Experts call this a **schizocarp**, because it later splits into two parts. The actual seed sits in the thick knob at the end of the wing. The wing itself is thin and light and serves only for flying.

When one part comes away from the tree, it begins to spin quickly as it falls. The wing acts like the blade of a helicopter. In this way the seed falls more slowly and the wind can carry it far away. Such fruits are also called **helicopter seeds**. The stronger the wind, the farther the seeds travel.

Under a large maple it is shady, and its roots need a lot of water. A young tree would hardly have a chance there. Farther away the seedling finds more **light and space** to grow. That is why it is an advantage for the maple when its seeds fly far.

In Switzerland the main species are the **sycamore**, the **Norway maple** and the **field maple**. You can also tell them apart by their fruits. In the field maple the two wings stand almost horizontally apart, forming nearly a straight line. In the sycamore the wings stand closer together. In the Norway maple they lie in between and form a wide angle.

In summer the fruits are still **green** and soft, sometimes with a reddish tinge. In autumn they ripen, turn **brown** and dry, and fall off. Over the winter the seeds lie on the forest floor. When it gets warmer in **spring**, they germinate. Often you then see many little maple seedlings at once.

gewusst: Many children stick the maple wings on their noses. That is why in some regions they are called “Nasenzwicker”, “nose pinchers”.
Researchers have studied the spinning maple fruits closely in order to gain ideas for small flying devices.

teile.einleitung: The Aare is the longest river that flows entirely within Switzerland. It rises in the Bernese Alps and flows through Bern to the Rhine. Many people know it from swimming in the Aare in Bern.
wichtigste: At 288 kilometres, the Aare is the longest river that runs entirely within Switzerland.
It rises at the Upper and Lower Aar Glaciers in the Bernese Alps.
It flows through Lake Brienz, Lake Thun and Lake Biel.
The cities of Bern, Solothurn and Aarau lie on the Aare.
At Koblenz in the canton of Aargau it flows into the Rhine.
Its catchment area covers almost half of Switzerland.
At the confluence, the Aare carries more water than the Rhine.

abschnitte.text: The **Aare** rises at the **Upper Aar Glacier** and **Lower Aar Glacier** near the Grimsel Pass in the Bernese Alps. First it rushes through the Haslital valley and through the narrow **Aare Gorge** near Meiringen. In places this gorge is over 100 metres deep and can be visited on walkways. After that the Aare flows into Lake Brienz.

After Lake Brienz and Lake Thun, the Aare flows in a great loop around the old town of **Bern**. Since the **Jura Water Correction** in the 19th century, it has been led through a canal into Lake Biel. Then it flows past Solothurn, Olten and Aarau. In all it is 288 kilometres long.

At Brugg the Aare, the **Reuss** and the **Limmat** meet, a spot called the **Wasserschloss**, the “water castle”, of Switzerland. At Koblenz in Aargau the Aare flows into the Rhine opposite Waldshut. There it brings on average even more water than the Rhine itself. Its catchment area is around 17,700 square kilometres, which is almost half of Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: Swimming in the Aare in Bern
abschnitte.text: In summer many people in Bern let the Aare carry them through the city. The **Marzili** open-air pool is popular, where you get out again after swimming. The water is often only about 20 degrees and flows quickly. That is why you should be a good swimmer and heed warnings.

On the Aare there are many **hydroelectric power stations** that generate electricity, and already at the Grimsel there are large reservoirs. In the past, timber and goods were transported on the river by raft and boat. With the Jura Water Correction, floods in the Seeland region were contained and marshland was turned into fertile farmland. Today the banks of the Aare offer space for recreation, cycle paths and nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: The area from which all the water flows into a river.
The place where a river flows into another river, a lake or the sea.
A large, slowly flowing mass of ice in the mountains.
A major building project that reorganized the rivers and lakes in the Seeland region.

gewusst: The canton of Aargau is named after the Aare.
At the Wasserschloss near Brugg, almost all the water from the northern half of Switzerland comes together.
In Bern, swimming in the Aare is as much a matter of course in summer for many people as ice cream.

teile.einleitung: A floodplain is the landscape along a river that is flooded again and again. Gravel banks, pools and woods alternate here. Floodplains are among the habitats richest in species in Switzerland, but have become rare.
wichtigste: A floodplain is the area along a river that is flooded regularly.
The often flooded softwood floodplain is characterised by willows and poplars.
In the less often flooded hardwood floodplain, oaks, ashes and elms grow.
The beaver dams streams and creates new habitats.
Floodplains hold back water during floods like a sponge.
Many floodplains have disappeared because rivers were straightened and embanked.

abschnitte.text: A **floodplain** lies along a river or stream. During a flood the water overflows the banks and floods the land. In the process, gravel, sand and mud are moved around. In this way new **gravel banks**, **pools** and side channels form again and again. A floodplain is constantly changing, and that is just what makes it so valuable.

Close to the water, where flooding is frequent, lies the **softwood floodplain**. Here **willows** and **poplars** grow. They have soft wood, grow fast and withstand long floods. Further away and a little higher lies the **hardwood floodplain**. It is **flooded less often**, and **oaks**, **ashes** and **elms** with hard wood grow there.

The **beaver** is a real master builder of the floodplain. It fells trees and **dams streams**. This creates new ponds and wetlands, from which many other animals benefit. On open **gravel banks** the **little ringed plover** breeds, a small wading bird. Its eggs are so well camouflaged that they look like pebbles.

During floods, floodplains are very useful. They **hold back water like a sponge** and release it only slowly. As a result the flood peak is smaller further downstream. Water also seeps into the ground and tops up the **groundwater**. Floodplains thus also protect villages and towns.

In the past there were many more floodplains in Switzerland. Many have disappeared because **rivers were straightened and embanked** in order to gain land and to protect against floods. A well-known floodplain and forest area is the **Pfynwald** on the **Rhone in the Valais**. Today many rivers are being restored again and given more room. In this way new floodplains can form.

gewusst: Willow twigs that break off in a flood can simply take root in a new place and keep growing.
The eggs of the little ringed plover lie directly on the gravel, with no nest.

teile.einleitung: Aconitine is a very strong plant poison. It is found in monkshood, one of the most poisonous plants in Europe. Monkshood also grows in the Swiss Alps, so you should never touch or pick it.
wichtigste: Aconitine comes from monkshood, scientifically Aconitum.
Most of the poison is in the roots and seeds.
Even about 5 milligrams can be fatal for an adult.
Aconitine keeps sodium channels in nerve cells open.
The first signs are tingling and numbness.
It disturbs above all the heart and breathing.

abschnitte.text: **Blue monkshood** has dark blue flowers that look like a helmet. It likes to grow in damp, nutrient-rich places, for example near mountain huts and on stream banks in the mountains. Monkshoods form the genus **Aconitum**, after which the poison **aconitine** is named. Monkshood belongs to the **buttercup family**. In this family there are many poisonous species. A relative is the pale yellow-flowered **northern wolfsbane**.

Aconitine is found in **all parts** of the plant. The **root tubers** and the **seeds** contain the most. Even around **5 milligrams** of pure aconitine can kill an adult, far less than a gram. The poison can even be absorbed through the skin. That is why you should not touch the plant with bare hands.

Aconitine acts on the **nerve cells**. It keeps certain **sodium channels** open. As a result, nerves and the **heart muscle** no longer work properly. The first signs are **tingling** in the mouth and on the skin, after which the skin in these places becomes **numb**. Later the **heart rhythm** is thrown into disorder, and breathing can be paralysed. If poisoning is suspected, you must get help immediately. In Switzerland, the emergency number **145** of Tox Info Suisse gives advice.

The scientific name of northern wolfsbane is **lycoctonum**. It means “wolf killer”, because in the past it was used against wolves. The name monkshood, too, recalls the shape of the flower, which resembles a knight’s helmet.

gewusst: Blue monkshood is regarded as the most poisonous plant in Europe.
Bumblebees are among the few insects strong enough to crawl into the helmet-shaped flower.

teile.einleitung: Basil is a fragrant kitchen herb. It belongs in Italian cooking like tomatoes and pasta. The plant loves warmth and sun.
wichtigste: Basil is the most important ingredient in green pesto.
You eat mainly the fresh, green leaves.
Basil goes especially well with tomatoes.
The name comes from the Greek word for royal, which is why it is also called the royal herb.
It probably comes from India.
Basil cannot stand frost.
On a pizza Margherita there is classically basil.

abschnitte.text: The name **basil** comes from the Greek word for **royal**. That is why it is also called the **royal herb**. The plant probably comes from **India** and reached Europe through trade. It has soft, green leaves that smell strongly. There are many varieties, some even with purple leaves.

In the cooking of **Italy**, basil is almost impossible to imagine away. It is the most important ingredient in green **pesto**, together with pine nuts, cheese, garlic and olive oil. Basil goes especially well with **tomatoes**, for example with tomatoes and mozzarella. On a **pizza Margherita** there are tomatoes, mozzarella and basil. This way the pizza shows the colours red, white and green.

Of basil you use mainly the fresh **leaves**. You pluck them from the plant and it is best to add them to the food only at the end. With long cooking, basil loses a lot of its scent. If the plant forms flowers, you can pinch them off so that it makes more leaves.

Basil is a plant from **warm** regions. It needs a lot of light and warmth and grows best in a sheltered, sunny place in the garden or on the balcony. It cannot stand **frost** and cold at all, and dies at the first frost. In Switzerland it is therefore put outside only after the Ice Saints in mid-May.

gewusst: Basil belongs to the same plant family as mint and sage.
In India, one kind of basil, tulsi, is regarded as a holy plant.

teile.einleitung: The alpine zone is the part of the mountains above the tree line. Here no trees grow any more, only turf, dwarf shrubs and colourful mountain flowers. Above it follows the zone of rock, snow and ice.
wichtigste: The alpine zone lies **above the tree line**.
Trees no longer grow here because the summer is too short and too cool.
Typical are **alpine meadows** and **dwarf shrubs** such as the alpenrose.
Here **gentian**, **arnica** and many other mountain flowers bloom.
The **marmot** and the **rock ptarmigan** live in this zone.
In Switzerland many areas serve in summer as **Alpine pastures**.

abschnitte.text: When you climb up in the mountains, the plant world changes. First comes forest, then it grows sparser and finally stops. Here lies the **tree line**. In the Swiss Alps it usually lies roughly between 1,800 and 2,300 metres above sea level. Above it begins the **alpine zone**. Higher still follows the **nival zone** with rock, snow and ice.

Trees need enough warmth. Their new shoots have to become **woody**, that is, hard, before winter. Above the tree line the summer is **too short and too cool** for this. That is why only low plants grow there. They stay close to the ground, where it is warmer and less windy.

Typical of the alpine zone are **alpine meadows** of grasses, sedges and flowers. Added to these are **dwarf shrubs** such as the **alpenrose**, which in early summer colours whole slopes red. The **stemless gentian** bears large, deep blue flowers just above the ground. On poor mountain meadows grows the yellow **arnica**. Ointments against bruises are made from its flowers.

The **marmot** digs its burrows in alpine meadows. When in danger it lets out loud **warning whistles**. The **rock ptarmigan** changes its plumage with the seasons. In winter it is **snow-white** and well camouflaged in the snow. Ibex and chamois are also on the move here.

In Switzerland many areas of the alpine zone are used in summer as **Alpine pastures**. Cows, sheep and goats graze there. This **Alpine farming** has a long tradition. In autumn the animals return to the valley before the snow comes.

gewusst: Many alpine plants grow as dense cushions. In this way they protect themselves from wind and cold.
Marmots sleep through the whole winter in their burrow, often for half a year.

teile.einleitung: Pollination is the process in which pollen reaches the stigma of a flower. Only after that can seeds and fruits form. Busy helpers in this are bees, bumblebees, butterflies and the wind.
wichtigste: In pollination, pollen reaches the stigma of a flower.
Pollen is also called flower dust.
Bees carry pollen from flower to flower.
Many flowers attract bees with nectar and striking colours.
The hazel is pollinated mainly by the wind.
If the pollen comes from another plant of the same species, this is called cross-pollination.
After pollination a pollen tube grows through the style to the ovule.

abschnitte.text: Flowers have male parts, the **stamens**, which make the pollen. In the middle sits the female **pistil** with the sticky **stigma** at the top. In **pollination**, pollen reaches this stigma. This is the first step so that a plant can form seeds.

Many plants are pollinated by animals, above all by **insects** such as bees, bumblebees, butterflies and flies. The flowers attract them with sweet **nectar**, scent and bright colours. While the insect drinks, pollen sticks to its fur and is carried to the next flower. In other countries hummingbirds and bats also help with pollination.

Some plants do not need animals, they leave the pollen to the **wind**. These include the hazel, the birch, many conifers and all grasses, including cereals such as wheat and maize. Their flowers are often inconspicuous and have no nectar, but make huge amounts of pollen. It is this pollen that triggers **hay fever** in many people in spring.

If pollen reaches the stigma of a flower of another plant of the same species, this is called **cross-pollination**. If the pollen stays in the same flower or plant, it is called **self-pollination**. Cross-pollination mixes the genes and makes plants more resilient. Many plants, for example most apple varieties, therefore depend on pollen from other plants.

After pollination, a fine **pollen tube** grows from the pollen grain through the style to the **ovule** in the ovary. There male and female cells fuse, which is **fertilisation**. The ovule becomes a seed, and the fruit grows from the ovary. This is how cherries, apples, beans and nuts come about.

A large part of our fruit and vegetable varieties depends on pollinating animals. In Switzerland, besides the honeybee, live around 600 species of **wild bees**, many of which are threatened. Flower meadows, hedges and unsprayed gardens help them. Anyone who plants native flowers on the balcony or hangs up a wild bee hotel supports the pollinators.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine flower dust containing the male cells of the plant.
The sticky tip of the pistil that catches the pollen.
Sweet juice in flowers that attracts animals.
A fine tube that grows from the pollen grain to the ovule.
Pollination with pollen from another plant of the same species.

gewusst: Some orchids, the ophrys orchids, look like female insects and so attract males as pollinators.
In some parts of China fruit trees are pollinated by hand with brushes, because bees are missing there.

teile.einleitung: Algae are living things that live in water and, like plants, make their food with sunlight. Some are so tiny that you can only see them under the microscope, while others grow many metres long.
wichtigste: Algae live mainly in **water**: in ponds, lakes, streams and in the sea.
Many algae are green because they have the pigment **chlorophyll**.
Algae need **light** to grow.
**Filamentous algae** look like long green hair or cotton wool.
In the sea grow the largest algae, the seaweeds.
Too many algae can become dangerous for fish.

abschnitte.text: Algae do it like plants: with sunlight, water and carbon dioxide they make sugar. This is called **photosynthesis**. For it they need the green pigment **chlorophyll**. In the process they give off oxygen into the water. That is why algae grow where enough light reaches, that is, near the surface of the water.

Many algae consist of just a single cell and are tiny. They float in the water in their millions. Others form long green threads, the **filamentous algae**. In the sea grows **kelp**, which can reach many metres in length. There are also red and brown algae.

In summer, when it is warm and a lot of sun is shining, tiny algae multiply very strongly. Then all the pond water turns **green**. Some pond animals like to eat algae. **Water snails** rasp them off stones and plants with their rough tongue. Small crustaceans and tadpoles also eat algae.

abschnitte.titel: When there get to be too many
abschnitte.text: Algae are important, but too many can do harm. When very many algae die, they are broken down by bacteria. In the process a lot of **oxygen** in the water is used up. Then things can get tight for fish. Particularly many algae grow when fertiliser or other nutrients get into the water.

gewusst: A large part of the oxygen on Earth comes from tiny algae in the sea.
In some countries people eat algae. The wrapping of sushi, for example, is made of dried seaweed.

teile.einleitung: If you hold a leaf up to the light, you see fine lines: the **leaf veins**. They are the pipes of the leaf and bring water in and sugar out. At the same time they support the thin leaf blade like a framework.
wichtigste: Leaf veins are vascular bundles in which xylem and phloem run together.
The xylem brings water and minerals from the roots into the leaf.
The phloem transports the sugar from photosynthesis to the rest of the plant.
The strong main vein in the middle is called the midrib.
Broadleaved trees mostly have net venation, grasses and maize have parallel veins.
The veins support the leaf blade like a framework.

abschnitte.text: In many leaves a strong main vein, the **midrib**, runs through the middle. From it **side veins** branch off, which branch ever more finely. This way the pipes reach almost every spot of the leaf. The veins begin at the leaf stalk and link the leaf with the shoot of the plant.

Every leaf vein is a **vascular bundle**. In it two kinds of pipes lie side by side. The **xylem**, also called the wood part, consists of tube-shaped cells. Through them water with minerals rises from the roots to the leaf. The **phloem**, also called the sieve part, carries the **sugar** made in the leaf to the roots, fruits and other parts.

In dicot plants such as **beech** or **lime**, the veins branch into a fine net. This is called **net venation**. In monocot plants such as **maize** and grasses, the veins mostly run **parallel** from the leaf base to the tip. The **ginkgo** has a very old form: its veins fork again and again without forming a net.

The veins do not only transport substances. They also act like a **framework** and keep the thin leaf blade spread out. You can see this especially well in **skeleton leaves**. In them the soft tissue has rotted away, and only the fine net of veins is left.

gewusst: Ginkgo trees are regarded as living fossils: their relatives grew already in the time of the dinosaurs.
With a hand lens you can see countless tiny meshes of the vein net in a foliage leaf.

teile.einleitung: The ear is the part of a cereal plant on which the grains grow. Wheat, barley, rye and spelt carry ears. Oats and maize, by contrast, have other forms of flower cluster.
wichtigste: The ear is the part of the plant with the grains.
The grains are the seeds of the plant.
Some ears have long bristles, the awns.
Barley has especially long awns.
Oats have no ear but a panicle.
Maize carries its grains on a cob.
Ripe ears often hang downwards because the grains are heavy.

abschnitte.text: An **ear** is an **inflorescence**. That is the part of the plant where many small flowers sit together. In an ear the flowers sit directly on a long axis, without little stalks. The flowers later become the **grains**. They are the **seeds** of the plant. A new plant can grow again from every grain. For us humans the grains are important food, and flour is made from them.

On some ears long, thin bristles grow. They are called **awns**. **Barley** has particularly long awns, which is why a field of barley looks soft and shaggy in the wind. Some wheat varieties also have awns, others do not. The awns protect the grains and help the plant, because like small leaves they carry out photosynthesis.

Not all cereals carry ears. In **oats** the grains hang on branching, thin stalks. This inflorescence is called a **panicle**. **Maize** carries its grains on a thick **cob** that is wrapped in leaves. At the top of the maize plant there is in addition a panicle with flowers that supply the pollen.

Young ears are green. In summer they ripen and turn **golden yellow**. The grains become hard and heavy in the process. That is why **ripe ears often hang downwards**. Now the combine harvester drives over the field. It cuts off the stalks and separates the grains from the ears and straw. The straw is pressed into bales and used, for example, as bedding for animals.

gewusst: A single wheat ear carries several dozen grains.
The ear is an ancient sign of the fertility of fields and of harvest and appears on many coats of arms and coins.

teile.einleitung: In a beehive a whole bee colony lives together. Every bee has its task, and together they build combs, collect nectar and make honey. The beekeeper looks after the bees.
wichtigste: The cells of a comb are six-sided.
The bees fly in and out through the entrance.
Normally only one queen lives in a beehive.
In summer, tens of thousands of bees live in a strong colony.
In winter the bees form a cluster and warm each other.
The beekeeper calms the bees with smoke.
A veil protects the beekeeper from stings.

abschnitte.text: A bee colony consists of three kinds of bees. There is normally only one **queen**, who lays eggs. Most of the animals are **workers**: they clean, feed the larvae, build combs, guard the entrance and collect nectar and pollen. In summer male bees also live in the hive, the **drones**. A strong colony numbers tens of thousands of bees in summer.

The bees build their combs from **wax**, which they make themselves. The cells are **six-sided**. This shape saves material and is nevertheless very stable. In the cells the bees store honey and pollen. In other cells the larvae grow up.

The beehive is the dwelling that the beekeeper provides for the colony. In the past these were often woven baskets, today mostly wooden boxes with removable frames. The bees fly in and out through the **entrance**. There guard bees keep strange animals away. This way the beekeeper can inspect the combs and harvest the honey.

In winter the bees hardly fly out. They huddle closely together and form a **winter cluster**. By shivering their flight muscles they produce warmth. The bees swap places as they do so, so that none has to freeze on the outside for too long. As food they use the stores they laid in during summer.

The beekeeper wears a **veil** and often gloves, to protect against stings. With a device that produces smoke, they calm the bees. The **smoke** makes them calmer, so that they sting less. The beekeeper also looks after the health of the colony, for example watching for the varroa mite.

gewusst: For one jar of honey, bees visit a very large number of flowers.
The queen lives for several years, a worker in summer only a few weeks.

teile.einleitung: Aflatoxins are poisons produced by certain moulds. They can form on nuts, maize and spices, above all in warm regions. Because they are harmful even in the tiniest amounts, foods are strictly checked.
wichtigste: Aflatoxins come from Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus.
Aflatoxin B1 can cause liver cancer.
They were discovered in 1960 after a mass die-off of turkeys in England.
Peanuts, pistachios and maize are often affected.
B and G stand for blue and green fluorescent colour under UV light.
Aflatoxin M1 gets into cow’s milk through contaminated feed.

abschnitte.text: Aflatoxins come mainly from the moulds **Aspergillus flavus** and **Aspergillus parasiticus**. In German these fungi are also called **Giesskannenschimmel**, “watering-can mould”. The name aflatoxin is put together from “A. flavus” and “toxin”, that is, poison. The fungi grow well on products rich in oil and starch from warm, damp regions. **Peanuts**, **pistachios**, **maize**, spices and dried figs are especially often affected.

In **1960**, over **100,000 turkeys** died in **England** of a mysterious disease. It was called “Turkey X disease”. The cause was mouldy **peanut meal** in the feed. During the investigation, researchers came across the aflatoxins. There are several kinds of them. Under **UV light** some glow **blue** and the others **green**. That is where the letters in **aflatoxin B1** and **G1** come from. This fluorescent colour is also used to detect the poisons.

**Aflatoxin B1** is among the strongest natural **cancer-causing** substances. It damages above all the **liver**. There it is converted into a particularly reactive substance that binds to **DNA** and causes changes in the genetic material. If you take in aflatoxins over a long time, the risk of **liver cancer** rises. The International Agency for Research on Cancer, the **IARC**, classes aflatoxins in the highest group, group 1.

abschnitte.titel: Through the feed into the milk
abschnitte.text: If **cows** eat contaminated feed, aflatoxin B1 is converted in their liver into **aflatoxin M1**. This gets into the **milk**. That is why checking animal feed is also important.

For cancer-causing substances that damage the genetic material, there is no amount that is certainly harmless. That is why **very low maximum levels** apply to aflatoxins. Exposure is to be kept as low as possible. In Switzerland, the federal authorities and cantonal laboratories monitor that imported nuts, spices and other foods keep to these levels.

gewusst: Aflatoxins are hardly destroyed by cooking or roasting, so the mould has to be prevented in the first place.
Mouldy nuts should always be thrown away, not just the mouldy spot removed.

teile.einleitung: The tree crown is the topmost part of a tree. That is where the branches and leaves sit. In the crown, with the help of sunlight, the food for the whole tree is made.
wichtigste: The crown consists of branches, twigs and leaves or needles.
With light, water and air the leaves make sugar and give off oxygen.
Many crowns together form the canopy.
The tree layer is the highest layer in the forest.
The crowns give shade and cool the air.
Mistletoe grows as a green ball on branches.
Most conifers stay green in winter.

abschnitte.titel: The topmost part of the tree
abschnitte.text: The **tree crown** is the topmost part of the tree. It consists of **branches**, twigs and leaves or needles. Every tree species has a typical crown shape: some are round, others pointed like the spruce. In the **maple** the leaves look like a hand with fingers. They usually have five pointed lobes, and a maple leaf is also on the flag of Canada.

In the leaves of the crown, food is made. With **sunlight**, water and air the leaves make **sugar**. In doing so they give off **oxygen**, which people and animals need for breathing. This process is called **photosynthesis**. The sugar is then distributed throughout the tree.

A forest has several storeys. At the very top lies the **tree layer** with the crowns of the big trees. It gets the most light. When many crowns touch, they form a **canopy** over the forest. Underneath it is shady. On hot days it is cooler in the forest, because the crowns keep out the sun and the leaves evaporate water.

High up in some crowns grows a green ball: the **mistletoe**. It grows on branches and taps into the tree with its roots to fetch water. In winter most broadleaved trees lose their leaves. Most **conifers** such as spruces, firs and pines, on the other hand, keep their needles for several years. That is why their crown stays green in winter too.

gewusst: The larch is an exception: it is a conifer and drops its needles in autumn.
In the crowns of trees live many insects, birds and squirrels.

teile.einleitung: An Alpine pasture is a meadow high up in the mountains. In summer cows, sheep and goats graze there. In winter snow lies on the Alp, and then the animals are back in the valley.
wichtigste: Alpine pastures lie high up in the **mountains** above the villages.
The cows are on the Alp in **summer**.
At the **ascent to the Alp**, the cows climb up in early summer.
At the **descent from the Alp** in autumn they come back to the valley decorated.
On the Alp the **Senn**, the dairyman, makes **Alpine cheese** from the milk.
In summer the Alpine herders live in an **Alpine hut**.

abschnitte.text: In summer fresh, juicy grass with many herbs and flowers grows on the Alpine pastures. In winter **snow** lies up there. That is why the animals are on the Alp only in **summer**. In this time the meadows in the valley can be mown. In this way the farmers have hay for the winter.

In early summer the farmers walk with their cows up to the Alpine pastures. This is called the **Alpaufzug**, the ascent to the Alp. The cows often wear **bells**. Alpine pastures are large and sometimes foggy. From the sound of the bells you can hear where the cows are at the moment.

On the Alp the cows are milked every day. The milk is made into cheese right there on the Alp. This cheese is called **Alpine cheese**. The man who makes cheese on the Alp is called a **Senn**, and a woman is called a Sennerin. In summer the Alpine herders live in a simple **Alpine hut** made of wood or stone.

In autumn it gets cold in the mountains. Then the cows return to the valley. This is the **Alpabzug**, the descent from the Alp. The cows are decorated with **flowers** and ribbons on their heads. This shows that the Alpine summer went well. In many villages the Alpabzug is a big festival with music and markets.

gewusst: The time when the animals are on the Alp is called “Sömmerung”, summering.
In French the descent from the Alp is called “Désalpe”.

teile.einleitung: Bamboo looks like a tree, but it is a gigantic grass. It grows incredibly fast and is very useful. Most species of bamboo grow in Asia.
wichtigste: Bamboo belongs to the grass family, like wheat, maize and rice.
The stem is called a culm, it is usually hollow and divided by nodes.
Some species grow up to about 90 centimetres in one day.
The largest species of bamboo grow over 20 metres tall.
Many species flower only every few decades.
The giant panda eats almost nothing but bamboo.
Young bamboo shoots can be eaten cooked.

abschnitte.text: **Bamboo** belongs to the **grass family**, like wheat, maize and rice. So it is really a grass, only much bigger. As in other grasses, its stem is called a **culm**. The culm is usually **hollow** and divided into separate sections by **nodes**. Most species of bamboo grow in Asia, for example in China. A few species are also found in America and Africa.

Bamboo is one of the fastest plants in the world. Some species grow up to about **90 centimetres** in a single day. That is almost four centimetres every hour. The largest species, the **giant bamboo**, grow over 20 metres tall. That is as high as a building with many storeys.

Many species of bamboo **flower** only very rarely, sometimes only after decades. Often all the plants of a species then flower at the same time, even in places far apart. After flowering, the plants of many species die. This can be a big problem for animals that live on bamboo.

The **giant panda** lives in the mountain forests of China. Almost all its food is bamboo. It eats many kilograms of it every day, because bamboo contains few nutrients. People eat bamboo too: the young **shoots** are popular in Asian cooking. But they must be cooked before eating.

Bamboo is light, hard and grows back quickly. That is why many things are made from it, for example **chopsticks**, baskets, furniture and mats. In Asia, scaffolding for high-rise buildings is even made from bamboo poles. Bamboo sometimes grows in Swiss gardens too, but it can spread strongly there.

gewusst: A bamboo culm does not get any thicker once it has grown out of the ground.
There are well over a thousand different species of bamboo.

teile.einleitung: The apple tree is one of the most important fruit trees in the world and is also very common in Switzerland. In spring it bears white to pink blossoms, and in autumn crisp apples. People make sweet cider, apple purée and much more from its fruit.
wichtigste: The cultivated apple belongs to the rose family.
Its origin lies in Central Asia, mainly in Kazakhstan.
Here the apple tree blossoms in spring.
Apple blossoms are white to pink and are pollinated by bees.
There are thousands of apple varieties worldwide.
In Switzerland, freshly pressed apple juice is called Süssmost (sweet cider).
The core is often called Bütschgi in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The **cultivated apple** is a deciduous tree from the **rose family**. Standing alone, it can grow to about 8 to 15 metres tall, but in orchards it is kept small. Its leaves are egg-shaped with a serrated edge. In spring the white to pink blossoms open, and they smell sweet.

The ancestors of our apples come from the mountain forests of **Central Asia**, especially Kazakhstan. The wild apple Malus sieversii still grows there today. Apples reached Europe along the Silk Road, and the Romans spread their cultivation. The city of Almaty in Kazakhstan used to be called Alma-Ata, which is often translated as father of apples.

For an apple to form, the blossom must be **pollinated**, usually by bees. Most varieties need pollen from another apple variety nearby for this. After pollination, the apple grows from the ovary over the summer. In the middle lies the core with the pips, which in Switzerland is often called the **Bütschgi**.

Worldwide there are many thousands of **apple varieties**; popular ones include Gala, Golden Delicious, Braeburn and Bramley. To keep a variety the same, it is **grafted**: a twig of the desired variety is placed on a rootstock. A pip would grow into a tree with quite different apples. Large apple trees in meadows are called **standard trees** and provide habitat for many birds and insects.

The apple is the most important type of fruit in Switzerland. Particularly many apple trees stand in Thurgau, which is therefore jokingly called **Mostindien**. **Sweet cider** is made from freshly pressed apples, and when fermented it becomes cider, also called sour cider. And in the legend of William Tell, Tell has to shoot an apple off his son’s head.

Apple trees can become ill, for example through fungi such as **apple scab**, which causes dark spots. **Fire blight** is also dangerous, a bacterial disease in which twigs look as if they were burnt. New, resistant varieties help to reduce the use of plant protection products. Old varieties are preserved in Switzerland by organisations such as ProSpecieRara.

begriffe.erklaerung: Attaching a twig of one variety onto another tree.
A large fruit tree with a tall trunk, often in meadows.
The middle part of the apple with the pips, also called Bütschgi in Switzerland.
A plant family that also includes the rose, pear, cherry and strawberry.

gewusst: If you plant an apple pip, almost never do the same apples grow as on the parent tree.
An apple is about 85 per cent water.
The apple variety Granny Smith was named after a woman in Australia who found it in the 19th century.

teile.einleitung: Auxins are plant hormones. They control how plants grow, for example why a seedling bends towards the light. They are also used in horticulture and agriculture.
wichtigste: The most important natural auxin is indole-3-acetic acid (IAA).
The plant makes it mainly from the amino acid tryptophan.
With light from one side, auxin moves to the shaded side, where the cells stretch more.
Charles and Francis Darwin showed in 1880 that the tip of the seedling senses the light.
In the 1920s Frits Went caught the growth substance in small agar blocks.
PIN proteins channel auxin out of the cell in a particular direction.
Synthetic auxins promote root formation in cuttings or serve as weedkillers.

abschnitte.text: **Auxins** are a group of plant hormones. Hormones are messenger substances that work even in the smallest amounts. The most important natural auxin is **indole-3-acetic acid**, IAA for short. The plant makes it mainly from the amino acid **tryptophan**. Other plant hormones such as gibberellins, cytokinins or abscisic acid belong to groups of their own.

**Charles Darwin** and his son **Francis** studied grass seedlings. They covered the tip of the seedling sheath, the **coleoptile**, and saw that without a tip exposed to light, the seedling does not bend towards the light. They described their experiments in 1880 in the book “The Power of Movement in Plants”. In the 1920s the Dutch botanist **Frits Went** placed cut-off tips on small blocks of agar. The blocks then caused a bend themselves, which proved that a substance travels.

If a seedling is lit from one side only, the auxin moves to the **shaded side**. There the cells stretch more than on the bright side. That is why the shoot bends towards the light. This movement is called **phototropism**. The **PIN proteins** take care of the directed transport: they usually sit on only one side of the cell membrane and channel auxin out in a particular direction.

How does auxin make cells longer? According to the **acid growth theory**, auxin activates proton pumps in the cell membrane. They pump protons into the cell wall, and it becomes acidic. As a result, enzymes such as the **expansins** become active and loosen the wall. The internal pressure of the cell, the **turgor**, can now stretch the cell.

abschnitte.titel: Auxins in the garden and in the field
abschnitte.text: In horticulture, **cuttings** are often dipped in a rooting powder with auxins such as indole-3-butyric acid. This makes new roots form faster at the cut. The synthetic auxin **2,4-D**, on the other hand, works as a weedkiller. It makes broadleaved weeds grow out of control until they die. Cereals, as grasses, are less sensitive and are spared.

gewusst: The name auxin comes from the Greek word for “to grow” or “to increase”.
Even tiny amounts of auxin are enough to bend a seedling.

teile.einleitung: Baker’s yeast makes bread and plaited loaves nicely light. It consists of tiny fungi that you can only see under the microscope. People have been using it for thousands of years.
wichtigste: Baker’s yeast is a single-celled fungus.
Its scientific name is Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
The yeast feeds on sugar and in the process forms the gas carbon dioxide.
The gas bubbles make the dough rise and make the holes in the bread.
Yeast dough rises best in a warm place.
In the hot oven the yeast dies.
Instead of yeast you can also use sourdough.

abschnitte.text: **Baker’s yeast** consists of tiny fungi that are made of only a single cell. A cube of yeast contains billions of these cells. The scientific name is **Saccharomyces cerevisiae**. Saccharomyces means roughly “sugar fungus”, because the yeast processes sugar. The same yeast is also used for brewing beer.

In the dough, the yeast eats **sugar**. Some of this comes from the starch in the flour. In the process it forms the gas **carbon dioxide**. The gas makes many little bubbles, and the dough becomes bigger and lighter. This process is called **fermentation**. When baked, the dough becomes firm, and the bubbles stay as holes in the bread.

Yeast likes to work in a **warm place**. That is why the dough is often left covered in a warm kitchen. In the cold it rises only very slowly, and in the fridge hardly at all. In the **hot oven** the yeast dies. That is why the bread no longer rises after baking.

Fresh yeast is bought as a **cube**, and keeps only a short time in the fridge. **Dried yeast** is dried yeast as a powder in a sachet and keeps much longer. You can also bake bread without bought yeast, for example with **sourdough**. This is an old, fermenting dough. It makes the bread rise and gives it a slightly sour taste.

gewusst: Even in ancient Egypt, bread was baked with fermenting dough.
Yeast cells multiply by little daughter cells growing out of them, which is called budding.

teile.einleitung: Afforestation means planting young trees in a targeted way where a new forest is to grow. In Switzerland it has a long history. After severe floods in the 19th century, people began to put trees back on bare mountain slopes.
wichtigste: Afforestation means planting young trees in a targeted way.
The young trees are called seedlings and are raised in forest nurseries.
After severe floods in the 19th century, Switzerland afforested mountain slopes.
On steep avalanche slopes, defences protect the young trees.
If forest is removed for a building project, replacement afforestation is generally required.
Today a mixture of tree species suited to the site is planted.

abschnitte.text: In **afforestation**, **young trees are planted in a targeted way**. These little trees are called **seedlings**. They are raised in a **forest nursery** until they are strong enough. Then they are put into the ground at intervals of a few metres. Many decades pass before a proper forest grows from them.

In the 19th century, many mountain slopes in Switzerland were **cleared of trees**. The wood was needed for heating, building and industry. Without forest, rainwater ran off quickly, and **severe floods** occurred. After that, Switzerland began to **afforest the slopes on a large scale**. In **1876** the first federal forest law came into force, which protected the forest in the mountains.

Many afforestations in the mountains serve as **protection forest** against avalanches, rockfall and debris flows. On steep **avalanche slopes**, however, the young trees are themselves in danger. Sliding snow can snap them or sweep them away. That is why **defences** of wood or steel are also built, which hold the snow in place. When the trees are big enough, they take over this job themselves.

In the past, afforestation on the **Central Plateau** often used almost only **spruces**. They **grow fast** and supply good **timber**. But such pure spruce forests are vulnerable to storms, drought and bark beetles. Today a **mixture of species suited to the site** is preferred. These are trees that fit the soil and the climate of the place. Often the forest is also left to grow back by itself, which is called **natural regeneration**.

In Switzerland the forest is well protected by law. Anyone who wants to remove forest, for example for a building project, needs a permit for **clearing**. This is only granted in exceptional cases. As a rule, the law then requires **replacement afforestation** in the same area. In this way the total forest area is preserved.

gewusst: The forest area of Switzerland has grown clearly since the 19th century, and today about a third of the country is wooded.
Part of the new forest comes about without any planting at all, because trees grow by themselves on abandoned alpine pastures.

teile.einleitung: When you count animals or plants in an area, at first you quickly find many new species, and later fewer and fewer. A species accumulation curve shows exactly this. With it, researchers estimate whether they have already found almost all the species.
wichtigste: The curve shows the species found in relation to the collecting effort.
If it flattens out clearly, most species have probably been recorded.
If it still rises steeply at the end, many species are still missing.
With rarefaction, species numbers are compared at equal effort.
Singletons are species that were found with only one individual.
You average over many random orders of the samples.

abschnitte.text: A **species accumulation curve** shows how many species you have found in total, depending on the **collecting effort**. The effort can be the number of samples, traps or animals counted. At the beginning the curve rises steeply, because almost every sample brings new species. Later only rare species are added, and the curve becomes flatter. It is also called a **collector’s curve**.

If the **curve flattens out clearly**, most species have probably been recorded. More samples would bring little that is new. If it **still rises steeply at the end**, many species are still missing, and **more samples are needed**. But the shape of the curve depends on the **order of the samples**. That is why you average over **many random orders** and so get a smooth curve.

Two areas can only be compared fairly if the effort was equally large. Anyone who searches twice as long usually finds more species. **Rarefaction** therefore calculates how many species you would expect in both areas at **equal effort**. In this way you compare, for example, 100 animals counted here with 100 animals counted there.

Rare species reveal how much is still missing. **Singletons** are species that were found with **one individual** only, **doubletons** those with two. The estimator **Chao1** calculates: species found plus F1² divided by 2 times F2. Here F1 is the number of singletons and F2 the number of doubletons. An example: 30 species, 8 singletons and 4 doubletons give 30 plus 64 divided by 8, that is **38 species**.

The **species-area relationship** is similar. It describes the fact that more species live in larger areas. The formula is **S = c times A to the power of z**.
