Here S is the number of species, A the area, and c and z are numbers that depend on the region. This relationship applies, for example, to islands of different sizes.

gewusst: With insects in tropical forests, the curve often does not flatten out even after huge effort, because there are so many rare species there.
The estimator Chao1 is named after the statistician Anne Chao.

teile.einleitung: Bio Suisse is the umbrella organisation of Swiss organic farmers. Its sign is the Bud, which you can find on many organic products in the shop. Bio Suisse lays down which rules apply to Bud products.
wichtigste: Bio Suisse is the umbrella organisation of Swiss organic farmers.
Its label is called the Bud.
The association was founded in the 1980s and has its seat in Basel.
The whole farm must be run organically.
Converting to organic takes two years.
The Bud with the Swiss cross means at least 90 percent of the raw materials come from Switzerland.
Bud products from abroad may not be transported by air.

abschnitte.text: Bio Suisse was founded in 1981, at that time under a different name. Several organic organisations joined together to create common rules. Today the association represents organic farms in Switzerland. Its **seat** is in **Basel**. Bio Suisse owns the **Bud** trademark and writes the guidelines for it.

An important rule is: the **whole farm** must be run organically. A farmer may not farm only one field organically and the rest conventionally. A farm that newly switches to organic needs a **conversion period** of two years. Only after that does it get the full Bud. Regular inspections check whether the rules are being followed.

There is the Bud with and without the Swiss cross. If it bears the **Swiss cross**, at least 90 percent of the raw materials come from Switzerland. The Bud without the cross is often found on products from abroad, for example on bananas or coffee. These products too must meet the rules of Bio Suisse.

The rules of the Bud go further than the state organic ordinance in some points. For example, Bud products from abroad may not be transported by **aeroplane**, because that needs a lot of energy. There are also precise regulations for animal husbandry, additives and processing. The animals should, for example, be able to go outdoors regularly.

gewusst: The Bud is one of the best-known labels in Switzerland.
Processors such as bakeries or cheese dairies can also make Bud products if they follow the rules.

teile.einleitung: Birches produce huge amounts of tiny seeds every year. They are so light that the wind can carry them far away. That is why young birches grow in many surprising places.
wichtigste: Birch seeds are tiny and very light.
Each seed has a transparent wing on the left and right.
The seeds ripen in the catkins of the birch and are spread by the wind.
A large birch produces many thousands of seeds in one year.
Young birches need a lot of light to grow.
The lesser redpoll likes to eat birch seeds.

abschnitte.text: A birch seed is only a few **millimetres** in size. In the middle sits the actual little nut, and to its left and right it has two **transparent little wings**. So it looks almost like a tiny insect. With a **hand lens** you can see its shape much better. The seeds form in the long **catkins**, which fall apart in autumn and winter.

Because the seeds weigh almost nothing, even a light breath of wind carries them away. This is called **wind dispersal**. This way birch seeds land in many places, even in **gutters** and **wall cracks**. There young birches sometimes sprout. On the snow in winter you often see many small birch seeds lying.

A birch produces **many thousands of seeds** every year. Only a few of them find a good place. Young birches need **a lot of light**. In the dark forest they have hardly a chance. In clearings, on fallow land or after a forest fire, on the other hand, they grow quickly. That is why the birch is called a **pioneer plant**.

Many birds eat birch seeds. The **lesser redpoll** even carries the birch in its name, as it is called Birkenzeisig in German. It is a small finch with a red cap. Skilfully it picks the seeds out of the catkins. The siskin and tits also like to take birch seeds.

gewusst: Birches were among the first trees to return to Switzerland after the last Ice Age.
Because birch seeds are so light, they can fly several hundred metres.

teile.einleitung: The sycamore maple is a large broadleaved tree that grows in Switzerland high up into the mountains. Well known are its winged fruits, which fly through the air like little propellers. Its pale wood is very valuable.
wichtigste: The leaf of the sycamore maple has five lobes like a hand.
Its winged fruits spin like a propeller as they fall.
Children stick them on their nose as nose pinchers.
On old trees the bark flakes off in scales.
It often grows as a single large tree on alpine pastures.
In autumn the leaves turn yellow.
The back of a violin is often made of maple wood.

abschnitte.text: The leaf of the **sycamore maple** is large and has **five lobes**. It is reminiscent of an open hand. On the flag of **Canada** there is also a maple leaf, but other kinds of maple grow there. In older sycamore maples the **bark** peels off in flat scales. Underneath you can see paler patches.

The fruits of the sycamore maple have a **wing**. Usually two hang together. As they fall they spin like a little **helicopter** and so fly far from the tree. Children like to split the winged fruits open and put them on their nose. That is why children call them **nose pinchers**.

The sycamore maple grows well in **mountain forest** and climbs high in Switzerland. It often stands as a single large tree on **alpine pastures**. There it gives the cattle shade. In autumn its leaves turn **yellow** to golden yellow, and then fall. Some old sycamore maples are several hundred years old.

**Maple wood** is pale, hard and often beautifully patterned. That is why it is popular with joiners and instrument makers. The back of a **violin** is often made of maple. Furniture, chopping boards and wooden spoons are also made from it, because the wood stays clean and smooth.

gewusst: The sycamore maple can grow over 30 metres tall.
Maple syrup does not come from the sycamore maple, but mainly from the sugar maple of North America.

teile.einleitung: Biodiversity means the variety of life on Earth. This includes the variety of species, their genes and their habitats. This variety ensures that nature works and gives us food, clean water and air.
wichtigste: Biodiversity is the variety of species, genes and habitats.
The Convention on Biological Diversity names three levels: genes, species and ecosystems.
This convention was opened for signature in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.
The tropical rainforest is the most species-rich land biome.
An endemic species occurs naturally only in a narrowly limited area.
Biodiversity hotspots are species-rich, highly threatened regions with many endemic species.
In Switzerland about a third of the assessed species are considered threatened.

abschnitte.text: The word **biodiversity** is made up of bios for life and diversitas for variety. It covers three levels: the variety of **genes** within a species, the variety of **species** and the variety of **ecosystems** such as forests, bogs or coral reefs. So far researchers worldwide have described around 2 million species. Probably, however, there are many more that nobody knows.

The most species-rich place on land is the **tropical rainforest**, where hundreds of beetle species can live on a single tree. Coral reefs in the sea are also full of life. The researcher **Norman Myers** coined the term **biodiversity hotspot** for regions that are very species-rich, have many **endemic species** and are highly threatened. Examples are Madagascar, the Andes and the Mediterranean region.

To compare variety, experts first count the species in a place. But it is also important how evenly the animals or plants are spread across the species. The **Shannon index** takes both into account, the number of species and the evenness. A meadow with twenty equally common species of flowers is therefore more diverse than one on which almost only one species grows.

Many species work together: insects pollinate plants, worms and fungi make the soil fertile, forests store water. These services are called **ecosystem services**. A diverse ecosystem withstands droughts, diseases or pests better. Many medicines originally come from plants, fungi or animals.

In 1992 the Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature in **Rio de Janeiro**, and almost all countries in the world have joined it. In 2022 the states agreed in Montreal on new goals, for example to protect around 30 percent of land and sea areas by 2030. Switzerland too has signed the convention. It also has its own Biodiversity Strategy.

In Switzerland around 56,000 species are known, from tiny fungi to the ibex. Thanks to the Alps, the Jura, the Central Plateau and Ticino there are very different habitats. According to the Red Lists of the Federal Office for the Environment, **FOEN**, however, about a third of the assessed species are considered threatened (as of 2023). Bogs, dry meadows and natural river banks have suffered especially.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of living things that can reproduce with each other.
A habitat with all the living things that interact in it.
A species that occurs naturally only in a particular area.
A particularly species-rich and endangered region of the Earth.

gewusst: Almost three quarters of all described animal species are insects.
On a species-rich Swiss flower meadow, over 50 plant species can grow on a few square metres.
Madagascar is so special that most animal and plant species there occur nowhere else.

teile.einleitung: A barometer is a measuring instrument that shows the air pressure. The air above us has weight and constantly presses on everything on the ground. Because air pressure changes with the weather, the barometer helps in forecasting the weather.
wichtigste: A barometer shows the air pressure.
The name comes from Greek, baros means weight.
Evangelista Torricelli built the first mercury barometer in 1643.
Air pressure is nowadays usually measured in hectopascals.
At sea level the average air pressure is 1013.25 hectopascals.
Rising air pressure often points to fine weather, falling pressure to bad weather.
The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure.

abschnitte.text: A **barometer** measures the **air pressure**, that is, how strongly the air presses on a surface. Above every square centimetre of ground there is a column of air that weighs about as much as a kilogram. We do not feel this, because our body presses back from inside. The name comes from the Greek word baros, meaning weight.

In 1643 the Italian **Evangelista Torricelli** filled a glass tube with **mercury** and stood it upside down in a dish. The mercury sank only to a height of about 76 centimetres, because the air pressure held it up. With this he had built the first barometer. In 1648 the Frenchman Blaise Pascal had it measured that the column stands lower on a mountain, because less air presses there.

Today the **aneroid barometer** is mostly used. In it is a flat metal capsule from which almost all the air has been removed. When the air pressure rises, the capsule is squeezed together, and when it falls, it expands again. A pointer passes on this tiny movement to a scale, and many smartphones also have a small pressure sensor built in.

Air pressure is given in **hectopascals**, and at sea level it is on average 1013.25. A **high-pressure area** usually brings calm, sunny weather. A **low-pressure area** often brings clouds, wind and rain. On old barometers there are therefore words such as Fair, Changeable and Rain.

The higher you climb, the less air lies above you, and the air pressure falls. On the Jungfraujoch at around 3,500 metres, it is only about two thirds as high as at the sea. That is why barometers are also used as **altimeters**, for example in aircraft and hiking watches. At great height, water boils below 100 degrees, because the pressure is lower.

The Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, **MeteoSwiss**, measures air pressure at many weather stations across the country. The differences in air pressure between the north and south sides of the Alps show, for example, whether the **foehn** is blowing. In the past, beautiful barometers of wood and brass hung on the wall in many Swiss parlours. Some people still tap the glass lightly today to see where the pointer moves.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the air presses on a surface.
A unit for air pressure, abbreviated hPa.
An area of high air pressure, usually with fine weather.
An area of low air pressure, often with rain and wind.

gewusst: When an aircraft takes off, your ears pop, because the air pressure changes quickly.
With water instead of mercury, a barometer would have to be over 10 metres tall.
Torricelli was a pupil of the famous scientist Galileo Galilei.

teile.einleitung: Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland, BDM for short, observes over many years how the variety of species in Switzerland is changing. For this, experts regularly count plants and animals on fixed plots across the country.
wichtigste: The BDM is run by the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN).
Data have been collected in the field since 2001.
The indicator Z7 uses plots of 1 square kilometre.
On Z7 plots, vascular plants, butterflies and breeding birds are recorded.
The indicator Z9 uses small plots of 10 square metres.
On Z9 plots, vascular plants, mosses and molluscs are examined.
In many habitats the plant communities are becoming more alike.

abschnitte.text: **Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland** is a programme of the Confederation. It is run by the **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)**. Monitoring means observation over a long time. Since **2001** experts have been collecting data in the field for it. This way you can see whether the variety of species is increasing, decreasing or staying the same.

The indicator **Z7** is called “Species diversity in landscapes”. Its sample plots are each **1 square kilometre** in size. On these plots **vascular plants**, **butterflies** and **breeding birds** are recorded. For this the experts walk set routes and note what they find.

The indicator **Z9** is called “Species diversity in habitats”. It works with small plots of **10 square metres**. There **vascular plants**, **mosses** and **molluscs**, for example snails, are examined. These plots lie in meadows, forests, fields and other habitats.

The plots lie on a **regular grid** across the whole of Switzerland. So they are not chosen according to beautiful places. This makes the results **representative** of the whole country. One important result: in many habitats the plant communities are becoming more alike. This is called **homogenisation**. Common species spread, while specialised species become rarer.

gewusst: The same plots are visited again and again, so changes can be compared well.
The BDM shows not only declines, some species such as a few warmth-loving butterflies have increased.

teile.einleitung: The asteroid belt is a huge zone in the solar system in which countless chunks of rock orbit the Sun. It lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. The chunks are leftovers from the time when the planets formed.
wichtigste: The asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Hundreds of thousands of known asteroids orbit the Sun there.
The largest body in the belt is the dwarf planet Ceres.
All the asteroids together have only a small fraction of the mass of our Moon.
The distances between asteroids are usually huge.
Jupiter’s gravity prevented a planet from forming here.
Many meteorites on Earth come from the asteroid belt.

abschnitte.text: The **asteroid belt** is a wide ring around the Sun in which very many **asteroids** orbit. Asteroids are chunks of rock and metal that are much smaller than planets. The belt lies between the orbits of **Mars** and **Jupiter**, about two to three and a half times as far from the Sun as the Earth. An asteroid usually takes three to six years to go once round the Sun.

About 4.6 billion years ago, the planets formed from dust and rock. In the region of today’s belt, the strong **gravity** of giant Jupiter disturbed this growing together. That is why no planet formed here, and many small chunks were left over. Asteroids are therefore like time capsules from the early days of the solar system.

The largest body in the belt is **Ceres**, almost 1,000 kilometres across. Giuseppe Piazzi discovered it on 1 January 1801, and since 2006 it has counted as a **dwarf planet**. The second largest is Vesta, over 500 kilometres across. Ceres alone contains a large part of the mass of the whole belt.

The NASA probe **Dawn** orbited the asteroid Vesta in 2011 and the dwarf planet Ceres from 2015. On Ceres it discovered bright spots of salt, which surprised the experts. Other probes have brought samples of asteroids to Earth. These samples help us to understand what the planets were made from.

In films, spaceships often fly through a dense swarm of rocks. In reality there are usually hundreds of thousands of kilometres between two asteroids. Space probes have therefore been able to cross the belt without any problem. If you stuck all the asteroids together, the ball would be smaller than our Moon.

When asteroids collide, smaller fragments are produced. Some of them end up on a path towards the Earth and fall down as **meteorites**. Most meteorites in museums come from the asteroid belt. Meteorites have also been found in Switzerland, for example in the area around Twannberg in the Bernese Jura.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small body of rock or metal that orbits the Sun.
A round body that is smaller than a planet and has not cleared its orbit.
A piece from space that has landed on Earth.
The path on which one body in space circles another.

gewusst: The dwarf planet Ceres was counted as a planet for almost 50 years.
The total mass of the asteroid belt is only a few per cent of the mass of the Moon.

teile.einleitung: Leaves look very different: round, narrow, lobed or like a little shield. The **leaf shape** is typical for many plants. That is why it helps in identifying trees and flowers.
wichtigste: The leaf shape describes the outline of the leaf blade.
The maple has palmately lobed leaves, as on the flag of Canada.
The pedunculate oak has leaves with rounded lobes and bays.
Willows often have lanceolate leaves, grasses linear ones.
The beech has egg-shaped leaves.
In the nasturtium the stalk attaches in the middle: the leaf is peltate.

abschnitte.text: Every plant species has its typical **leaf shape**. This means the outline of the **leaf blade**, that is, the flat surface of the leaf. Together with the **leaf margin** and the **leaf arrangement**, you can recognise many trees this way. For the different shapes there are fixed technical terms. They often compare the leaf with familiar things.

The leaf of the **beech** is **egg-shaped** to elliptical and about 5 to 10 centimetres long. The **silver birch** has small, triangular to **diamond-shaped** leaves with a doubly serrated margin. **Kidney-shaped** leaves are broader than long and deeply notched at the stalk, as in wild ginger. In **peltate** leaves such as the nasturtium, the stalk sits below the middle of the round blade.

**Lanceolate** leaves are much longer than broad and taper to a point like a lance. They are typical of many **willows**, for example the white willow. **Linear** leaves are narrow, and their margins run almost parallel. This is what the leaves of most **grasses** look like.

Some leaves have deep cuts that form **lobes**. The leaf of the **maple** is **palmately lobed**: several pointed lobes stick out like the fingers of a hand. A maple leaf is the symbol of Canada and can be seen on its flag. The **pedunculate oak** has **sinuately lobed** leaves with rounded lobes and deep bays between them.

gewusst: The leaves of the nasturtium repel water: drops of water roll off like little beads.
On a single tree, sun leaves and shade leaves can differ in size.

teile.einleitung: In every habitat many different living things live together. The whole community of these plants, animals, fungi and tiny organisms is called a **biocoenosis** or living community. Its members depend on each other in many ways.
wichtigste: A biocoenosis is the community of all living things in a particular habitat.
The habitat itself is called the biotope, and together biotope and biocoenosis form an ecosystem.
The term was introduced by the German zoologist Karl Möbius in 1877.
Even tiny bacteria belong to the biocoenosis, but water and stones do not.
The plant part is called the phytocoenosis, the animal part the zoocoenosis.
Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms and close the cycle of matter.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century the zoologist **Karl Möbius** studied oyster beds in the North Sea. In doing so he noticed that the oysters do not live alone. Many other species live together with them and depend on each other. For this community he coined the word **biocoenosis** in 1877. It comes from Greek and means roughly “living together”.

The biocoenosis includes all the **living things** of a biotope: plants, animals, fungi and microorganisms. In a forest soil these are for example trees, mosses, earthworms, beetles, fungi and countless **bacteria**. Non-living things such as water, oxygen, light or minerals do not belong. But they shape the habitat in which the community lives. The plant part is called the **phytocoenosis**, the animal part the **zoocoenosis**.

In a living community there are **producers**, **consumers** and **decomposers**. Plants make food with sunlight. Animals eat plants or other animals. Decomposers such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms break down dead plants and animals. In doing so, minerals are released, which plants take up again. This creates a cycle.

Between the species there are many relationships. Fox and field mouse stand in a **predator-prey relationship**: the fox hunts the mouse. Predators keep the number of their prey animals in check. If all predators disappear, the prey species often multiplies strongly. Then it can, for example, eat too many plants and upset the balance.

Some species are especially important for the whole community. They are called **keystone species**. The **beaver** dams streams with its dams. This creates ponds, wetlands and deadwood, from which amphibians, dragonflies, fish and birds benefit. In Switzerland the beaver has been spreading again since its reintroduction.

gewusst: In the nutrient-poor raised bog, the **sundew** catches small insects with sticky leaf hairs and so gains extra nutrients.
A handful of forest soil contains more living things than there are people on Earth, most of them tiny bacteria.

teile.einleitung: Mountain farmers work meadows and pastures in steep, high-lying areas. Their work is strenuous, because machines often cannot drive on the slope. At the same time they look after the landscape of the Swiss mountains.
wichtigste: The Confederation divides agricultural land into the valley zone, the hill zone and mountain zones I to IV.
Mountain zone IV has the most difficult conditions.
At altitude the growing season of the grass is shorter.
Two-axle mowers with a low centre of gravity tip over less easily on a slope.
In very steep places hay is raked by hand.
Swiss Mountain Aid supports mountain farming families.
Mountain farmers look after the cultural landscape.

abschnitte.text: The **Confederation** divides the agricultural land of Switzerland into zones. There are the valley zone, the hill zone and the **mountain zones I to IV**. The higher the zone, the harder the farming. **Mountain zone IV** covers the highest and steepest locations. Mountain farmers receive payments from the Confederation because their work is particularly demanding.

At altitude it is cooler, and the **snow** stays longer in spring. That is why the time in which grass grows is shorter than in the valley. Mountain farmers can therefore mow less often. In mountain zone IV many jobs are only possible by hand. In summer many mountain farmers take their cattle up to the **alp**.

For steep meadows there are special machines. **Two-axle mowers** and motor mowers are built low and wide and have a low centre of gravity. This way they tip over less easily on a slope. In very steep places, mountain farmers have to rake the **hay together by hand** and sometimes even carry it. Where no road leads, small **goods cableways** bring hay or milk down to the valley.

Mountain farmers do not only produce milk, cheese and meat. By mowing and grazing, they prevent meadows from becoming **overgrown with scrub** and turning into forest. This way species-rich **flower meadows** are preserved. This **cultural landscape** is important for plants, animals and tourism.

**Swiss Mountain Aid** is a foundation that supports mountain farming families with donations. It finances, for example, new stables, paths or water pipes. This way it helps ensure that the mountain regions stay inhabited. Many volunteers also help out on mountain farms in summer.

gewusst: On some very steep mountain meadows the grass is still mown with a scythe today.
Many famous Swiss cheeses such as alpine cheese are made in summer on the alp.

teile.einleitung: A field conservation strip is a strip at the edge of a field that is managed especially gently. There, rare arable wild plants are meant to be able to grow again. The harvest still takes place quite normally.
wichtigste: A field conservation strip lies at the edge of a field.
It promotes above all arable wild plants.
No weedkillers are used.
Without nitrogen fertiliser, the cereal stays sparse.
The cereal is harvested quite normally.
The skylark and many insects benefit from it.

abschnitte.titel: What a field conservation strip is
abschnitte.text: A **field conservation strip** is a strip at the **edge** of a cereal field or other field. It remains part of the field and is grown like the rest. Only the care is **gentler**. In Switzerland, field conservation strips are among the areas with which farmers can promote biodiversity.

In the conservation strip, people do without **herbicides**, that is, weedkillers. Otherwise exactly the wild plants that are meant to be protected would disappear. In addition, no **nitrogen** fertiliser is applied. Without this fertiliser the cereal grows **less densely**. In this way enough light reaches the ground, and the light-loving wild plants can grow. The cereal is then harvested **quite normally** together with the rest of the field.

A field conservation strip is not the same as a **flower fallow**. In the conservation strip a **crop for harvest** still grows, for example wheat. A flower fallow, by contrast, is sown with wild plants and is **not harvested**. It stays for several years. Both measures help nature, but in different ways.

In the conservation strip, **arable wild plants** such as poppy or cornflower bloom again. They supply **nectar** and **pollen** for wild bees, butterflies and other insects. Birds benefit too. The **skylark** nests on the ground in fields. In dense, tall cereal it finds hardly any room, but in sparse stands it does.

gewusst: The song of the skylark can often be heard high in the air while it hovers, fluttering, above the field.
Many arable wild plants like best to germinate in autumn together with the winter cereal.

teile.einleitung: Arable farming means working fields to grow plants such as cereals, potatoes or maize. In Switzerland most arable land lies on the Central Plateau. Healthy soil is the most important asset in this.
wichtigste: Most of Switzerland’s arable land lies on the Central Plateau.
Wheat is the most important bread cereal.
Barley is grown mainly as animal feed.
The plough loosens and turns the soil.
Heavy machines compact wet soil.
Soil erosion washes away unprotected earth.

abschnitte.text: The **Central Plateau** is flat, has fertile soils and a mild climate. That is why most of Switzerland’s fields lie there. In the mountains it is mostly too steep and too cool. There you find mainly meadows and pastures. On the Central Plateau, cereals, maize, potatoes, sugar beet, rapeseed and vegetables, among others, are grown.

**Wheat** is the most important bread cereal. It contains a lot of gluten protein, so the dough rises well. **Barley** is grown mainly as **feed** for pigs, cattle and chickens, and a small part is used for brewing beer. With **silage maize**, the whole plant with its cobs is chopped. Fermented in a **silo**, it serves in winter as energy-rich feed for cows.

The **plough** cuts open the top layer of soil and turns it over. In this way plant remains are worked in and the soil is prepared for sowing. The **seed drill** then places the grains into the soil in even rows, at the right depth and with the right spacing. With **direct drilling**, seed is sown without ploughing. The seed goes straight into the soil with the remains of the previous crop. This protects soil life and saves fuel.

If heavy machines drive over a **wet field**, the soil is **compacted**. Then there are no pores for air and water, and roots and earthworms have a hard time. If a field lies bare without plant cover, heavy rain can wash fertile earth down the slope. This is called **soil erosion**. **Cover crops** and mulch, that is, a layer of plant remains, protect the soil from this.

Farmers do not plant the same thing in the same field every year. They alternate the crops, which is called **crop rotation**. In this way diseases and pests become less frequent, and the soil is not depleted in one direction. Plants such as clover or peas can even fix nitrogen from the air and improve the soil.

gewusst: Arable farming has existed in central Europe since the Neolithic, that is, for several thousand years.
In a handful of healthy field soil live more organisms than there are people on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Albrecht von Haller was a physician, naturalist and poet from Bern in the 18th century. He studied plants and the human body and wrote a famous poem about the Alps. He is regarded as one of the greatest scholars of his time.
wichtigste: Haller was born in **Bern** in 1708 and died there in 1777.
He studied medicine, among other places in Leiden under the famous physician **Herman Boerhaave**.
His poem **“The Alps”** of 1729 made the mountains popular in Europe.
From 1736 he taught anatomy, surgery and botany in **Göttingen**.
In 1768 he published a great flora of Switzerland.
He was pictured on the 500-franc note of the sixth banknote series.

abschnitte.text: After a journey through the Alps, the young Haller wrote the poem **“The Alps”** in 1729. In it he praises the simple life of the mountain dwellers and the beauty of mountain nature. In the past, many people regarded the mountains as wild and threatening. Haller’s poem was read all over Europe and made the Alps a **place of longing**.

Haller studied medicine, among other places in Leiden under **Herman Boerhaave**, the most influential teacher of medicine of his time. In 1736 he was called to the newly founded University of **Göttingen**. There he taught anatomy, surgery and botany and built up a botanical garden. He stayed in Göttingen for 17 years and returned to Bern in 1753.

Haller carried out many experiments to find out how the body works. He distinguished the **irritability** of muscles from the **sensibility** of nerves. Muscle fibres contract when they are stimulated, whereas nerves pass on sensations. Because of such experiments, Haller is regarded as the founder of **experimental physiology**, that is, the study of how the body works.

Haller was also a great expert on plants. In 1768 his work **“Historia stirpium indigenarum Helvetiae”** appeared, a description of the native plants of Switzerland. It was one of the most thorough national floras of its time. From 1758, on behalf of Bern, he ran the **salt works at Roche** in Vaud. During this time he studied the plants of Vaud and Valais.

Haller wrote an incredible amount. For the journal **“Göttingische Gelehrte Anzeigen”** he wrote thousands of book reviews. In this way he followed what researchers all over Europe were finding out. Later the Swiss National Bank honoured him: on the **500-franc note** of the sixth banknote series his picture could be seen.

gewusst: Haller came from a Bernese patrician family, that is, one of the leading families of the city.
Besides his research, Haller also wrote novels about the state and government.
In Bern a statue in front of the university and a street recall him.

teile.einleitung: Biological plant protection means keeping plants healthy with natural means. It uses beneficial organisms, plant preparations and preventive measures. This is just as important in the organic garden as in agriculture.
wichtigste: Biological plant protection fights pests with natural enemies and agents.
Bacillus thuringiensis helps against feeding caterpillars.
Nettle liquid manure and cold-water nettle extract help against aphids.
Horsetail brew is sprayed as a preventive measure against fungal diseases.
Crop protection nets keep out insects such as the cabbage root fly.
Nematodes in the watering water fight the larvae of the black vine weevil.
A healthy soil makes plants more resilient.

abschnitte.text: It is best if plants do not fall ill in the first place. A **healthy, loose soil** provides strong plants that are less susceptible to pests. The right location and enough space between the plants also help. A fine **crop protection net** over the vegetable bed keeps out insects such as the **cabbage root fly**.

In the organic garden, agents are often made yourself. Against **aphids** you use **nettle liquid manure** or a **cold-water nettle extract**. For this, nettles are soaked in water. **Horsetail brew** is sprayed as a preventive measure against **fungal diseases**. It contains a lot of silica, which is meant to strengthen the leaves.

Many living things help against pests. **Nematodes** are tiny worms that are added to the watering water. They fight the larvae of the **black vine weevil** in the soil. In greenhouses, **parasitic wasps** are released against the **whitefly**. The bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis** works against feeding caterpillars.

In the garden you can attract beneficial organisms. Ladybirds, lacewings and earwigs eat aphids. Birds and hedgehogs eat caterpillars and slugs. Hedges, flower meadows, brushwood piles and nest boxes offer them shelter. This creates a balance in which pests multiply less strongly.

gewusst: During its development a ladybird larva eats many aphids.
You can lure earwigs into fruit trees with an upside-down flowerpot filled with wood wool.

teile.einleitung: The alpine aster is a small mountain flower with violet petals and a yellow centre. It shines in high summer among stones and grass. Its name means “star”.
wichtigste: The alpine aster has **violet** petals and a **yellow** centre.
Each stem usually carries only **one** flower head.
It grows about 5 to 20 centimetres tall.
It likes to grow on sunny, stony turf, often on limestone.
It belongs to the **daisy family**.
It mostly blooms in July and August.

abschnitte.text: The word **“aster”** comes from Greek and means **star**. The petals stand all around like the rays of a star. In the alpine aster they are **violet**. In the middle shines a **yellow** disc. The whole flower head is about 3 to 5 centimetres across.

The alpine aster belongs to the **daisy family**, like the ox-eye daisy or the sunflower. What looks like a single flower consists of many small individual flowers. The yellow flowers in the middle are tiny tubes. The violet “petals” on the outside are also individual flowers. Together they attract insects such as bees and butterflies.

The alpine aster likes **sun** and dry, **stony** soil. It often grows on limestone, on mountain turf and on rocky slopes. It is a small plant and usually only grows 5 to 20 centimetres tall. Each stem as a rule carries only one flower head. In this way it is well adapted to the wind and cold in the mountains.

The alpine aster blooms in high summer, mostly in **July and August**. Because it likes stony soil, people like to plant it in a **rock garden**. There it recalls the mountains. In nature you should leave it standing so that everyone can enjoy it.

gewusst: The alpine aster is found not only in the Alps but also in other mountain ranges of Europe and Asia.
In gardens there are varieties of the alpine aster with white or pink flowers.

teile.einleitung: Atropine is a strong plant poison. It occurs in deadly nightshade and in other nightshade plants. But in small, carefully measured amounts it is also an important medicine.
wichtigste: Atropine is named after deadly nightshade, whose scientific name is Atropa belladonna.
It belongs to the tropane alkaloids.
Deadly nightshade belongs to the nightshade family.
Atropine blocks the messenger substance acetylcholine.
A typical sign of poisoning is a dry mouth.
Atropine makes the heart beat faster.
In medicine it is used as an antidote for poisoning with nerve agents.

abschnitte.text: **Deadly nightshade** (Atropa belladonna) also grows in Swiss forests, often in forest clearings. It belongs to the **nightshade family**, like the potato and tomato. Its shiny black berries look harmless, but are **very poisonous**. Even a few berries can be life-threatening for children. The poison **atropine** is named after it.

The genus name **Atropa** comes from **Atropos**, one of the three **goddesses of fate** in Greek mythology. According to the legend, she cut the thread of life of human beings. The second name **belladonna** is Italian and means “beautiful woman”. In the past, women would drip the juice into their eyes to make their pupils large. This was thought beautiful at the time, but it was dangerous.

Atropine belongs to the **tropane alkaloids**. In the nervous system it blocks the messenger substance **acetylcholine**. This messenger substance controls many processes that we do not steer consciously, for example saliva and the heartbeat. When it is blocked, the result is a **dry mouth**, the **pupils become wide**, and the **heart beats faster**. In poisoning, confusion and fever are added, and you need medical help immediately.

In a carefully measured amount, atropine is a **medicine**. Eye doctors use related drugs to widen the pupil for an examination. When the heartbeat is too slow, atropine can make the heart beat faster again. It is especially important as an **antidote for poisoning with nerve agents**, for example with certain plant protection products. There it partly cancels out the dangerous effect of these substances.

Atropine does not occur only in deadly nightshade. **Thorn apple** also contains it, a plant with large white trumpet-shaped flowers and spiny fruits. It is also found in **henbane** and in angel’s trumpet. All these plants are poisonous. You should not touch them, and should wash your hands after contact.

gewusst: The berries of deadly nightshade taste slightly sweet, which makes them especially dangerous for children.
Some animals such as rabbits tolerate deadly nightshade much better than humans.

teile.einleitung: The Asian longhorned beetle is a large black beetle with white spots. It comes from China and Korea and was brought to Europe with packing wood. Its larvae eat their way through the wood of healthy broadleaved trees.
wichtigste: The beetle originally comes from China and Korea.
It was brought to Europe mainly with packing wood such as pallets.
The larvae damage the wood of trunk and branches.
In Europe it attacks maples particularly often.
Adult beetles are shiny black with white spots and very long antennae.
In Switzerland, infested trees are felled and destroyed.

abschnitte.text: The **Asian longhorned beetle** (Anoplophora glabripennis) belongs to the **longhorn beetles**. The adult beetle is **shiny black** with **white spots**. It grows to about 2 to 4 centimetres long. Striking are the **very long antennae**, which are ringed in black and white. They can be longer than the whole body.

The beetle originally lives in **China and Korea**. It came to Europe and North America mainly with **packing wood**, for example with **pallets** and crates. The larvae hid in them. To prevent this, there is the international standard **ISPM 15**. It requires, for example, that packing wood be heated **in its core to at least 56 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes**. Treated wood carries a special mark.

The **larvae** eat their way through the **wood of trunk and branches**. This creates long tunnels, which weaken the tree. Branches can break off, and whole trees can die. Unlike many other beetles, it also attacks **healthy trees**. In Europe it hits **maple** particularly often, but also poplars, willows, birches and other broadleaved trees.

An infestation shows itself in **perfectly round exit holes** about **1 centimetre across**. The finished beetles leave the tree through them. At the foot of the trunk or in forks of branches you often find **boring dust**. You can also see funnel-shaped places in the bark where the female laid her eggs. Anyone who notices something like this should report it to the authorities.

In Switzerland the beetle counts as a **particularly dangerous harmful organism**, and a find must be reported. Since 2011, several infestation sites have been discovered. **Infested trees are felled and destroyed**, usually by chipping and burning. Around the site, the trees are checked for several years, partly with specially trained **sniffer dogs**. In this way some infestation sites have been wiped out again.

gewusst: Sniffer dogs can smell the scent of the larvae and the boring dust in wood.
Development from larva to finished beetle usually takes one to two years.

teile.einleitung: The **leaf stalk** connects the leaf surface with the stem or twig. It carries the leaf, supplies it and turns it towards the light. We even eat some leaf stalks.
wichtigste: The leaf stalk carries the leaf blade and connects it with the shoot.
Through it run the vessels for water and sugar.
A leaf without a stalk is called a sessile leaf.
The angle between leaf stalk and shoot is called the leaf axil, and a bud often sits there.
In rhubarb you eat the thick leaf stalks.
Instead of a stalk, grasses mostly have a leaf sheath.

abschnitte.text: Through the leaf stalk run the **vessels**. They bring water and minerals into the leaf and carry sugar out. Without a stalk the blade would be cut off from supply. The leaf stalk can **bend** and **turn** through growth. This way it brings the blade into a good position towards the **light**. If the stalk is missing, the blade sits directly on the shoot. This is then called a **sessile leaf**.

Between the upper side of the leaf stalk and the shoot lies an angle, the **leaf axil**. There a **side bud** often forms, from which a new shoot can later grow. At the base of the leaf stalk, in some plants small, leaf-like appendages grow, the **stipules**. You find them for example in the rose. In the pea they are especially large and help with photosynthesis.

The leaves of the **trembling aspen** move at the slightest breath of air. The reason is their **flattened-at-the-sides** leaf stalk. It bends easily to the side. This way the leaves flutter and rustle almost constantly. This is where the saying “to tremble like aspen leaves” comes from.

The red or green sticks of **rhubarb** are leaf stalks. You cook compote from them or bake cakes. The large leaf blades are not eaten, because they contain a lot of **oxalic acid**. In celery too you eat the leaf stalks. **Grasses** mostly have no real stalk. Their leaf base forms a **leaf sheath**, which encloses and supports the stem like a tube.

gewusst: In autumn a separating layer forms at the base of the leaf stalk. There the leaf later comes away cleanly.
The saying “to tremble like aspen leaves” comes from the fluttering leaves of the trembling aspen.

teile.einleitung: The leaf is, besides root and shoot, one of the three basic organs of seed plants. Leaves are especially important for the plant because they make food with sunlight. They also regulate the water balance and the gas exchange with the air.
wichtigste: Leaves make sugar from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, which is called photosynthesis.
In the process oxygen is produced, which is released into the air.
A typical foliage leaf consists of leaf base, leaf stalk and leaf blade.
Tiny stomata on the leaf let gases in and water vapour out.
The chlorophyll in the chloroplasts makes the leaves green.
Some leaves are modified, for example into spines, tendrils or needles.
Broadleaved trees shed their leaves in autumn in order not to lose water in winter.

abschnitte.text: A foliage leaf is divided into **leaf base**, **leaf stalk** and **leaf blade**. The blade is the flat, broad surface that catches a lot of light. The leaf veins, also called vascular bundles, carry water and minerals in and sugar out. On top, a layer of wax, the cuticle, protects the leaf from drying out.

In the leaf cells lie small green bodies, the **chloroplasts**. They contain the pigment **chlorophyll**, which captures light energy. With this energy they build glucose from water and carbon dioxide. As a by-product oxygen is produced, on which almost all life on Earth depends.

On the underside of the leaf sit thousands of tiny pores, the **stomata**. They can open and close, a bit like a mouth. Through them carbon dioxide gets into the leaf, and oxygen and water vapour go out. The evaporation pulls water up from the roots like a drinking straw.

Botanists distinguish **simple leaves** as in the beech and **compound leaves** as in the ash or horse chestnut. The leaf margin can be smooth, serrated, toothed or lobed. The arrangement on the stem also differs, for example alternate or opposite. With these features you can identify plants.

In many plants, leaves have taken on new tasks. The spines of a cactus are modified leaves that protect against animals and lose little water. The pea holds on with **leaf tendrils**, and the onion stores nutrients in thick leaves. Carnivorous plants such as the sundew catch insects with sticky leaves.

In winter the ground is often frozen, and the roots can hardly take up water. That is why broadleaved trees such as beech, maple and lime drop their leaves. Beforehand they take nutrients back, and in doing so the chlorophyll is broken down and yellow and red pigments come to the fore. Conifers such as spruce and fir keep their needles, because these are well protected by a thick layer of wax.

begriffe.erklaerung: The flat, broad surface of a leaf.
Tiny green parts in plant cells in which photosynthesis takes place.
Small pores in the leaf through which gases pass in and out.
A protective layer of wax on the leaf surface.
The leaf veins that transport water and nutrients.

gewusst: The spines of cacti are actually modified leaves.
A single leaf can have many thousands of stomata per square centimetre on its underside.
The giant water lily Victoria from the Amazon region has floating leaves up to about three metres across.

teile.einleitung: Ammonification is an important step in the nitrogen cycle. In it, bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and waste and release the nitrogen bound in them as ammonium. This makes the nitrogen available to plants again.
wichtigste: In **ammonification**, nitrogen bound in organic matter is released as **ammonium**.
It is carried out mainly by **bacteria and fungi**.
The nitrogen comes from **proteins**, **nucleic acids** and **urea**.
The enzyme **urease** splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
Ammonification takes place with and without oxygen.
In well-aerated soils it is usually followed by **nitrification**.

abschnitte.text: When plants and animals die, their organic matter is left behind. **Decomposers** such as bacteria and fungi break it down. In doing so they split **proteins** into amino acids and release **ammonium** (NH₄⁺) or **ammonia** (NH₃) from them. This process is called **ammonification**. It is a central part of the **nitrogen cycle**.

In living things, nitrogen is bound mainly in **amino acids** and proteins. **Nucleic acids**, the building blocks of genetic material, also contain nitrogen. Added to this are waste products such as **urea**. Cellulose, starch and fats, on the other hand, contain no nitrogen. In ammonification, only the nitrogen from the nitrogen-containing substances is released.

abschnitte.titel: Urease and the smell of slurry
abschnitte.text: The enzyme **urease** is found in many bacteria. It splits urea very quickly into **ammonia** and carbon dioxide. That is why ammonia quickly forms in stables and **slurry pits**. The gas escapes and causes the sharp smell of stored slurry. Ammonium and ammonia are in **equilibrium**: at a high, alkaline pH there is more volatile ammonia, which can be lost as a gas.

A great many different microorganisms can release ammonium. Ammonification therefore takes place **aerobically** (with oxygen) and **anaerobically** (without oxygen). It even happens in wet, oxygen-poor soils. In well **aerated** soils, the ammonium is then quickly oxidised by **nitrification** to nitrite and nitrate. This completes the path from dead biomass to plant nutrient.

gewusst: Ammonia losses from slurry are an environmental issue in Switzerland, because ammonia can over-fertilise sensitive forests and moors.
Trailing hoses put slurry directly onto the soil, so less ammonia escapes.

teile.einleitung: A biome is a large-scale community of living things with typical climate, plants and animals. The Earth can be divided into such large life zones, for example desert, rainforest or tundra. If you know the biomes, you understand why completely different landscapes grow on each continent.
wichtigste: A biome is a large life zone of the Earth with similar climate, similar plants and animals.
Above all temperature and precipitation decide which biome arises in a place.
Important land biomes are tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, grassland, deciduous forest, coniferous forest and tundra.
There are also biomes in the sea and in waters, for example coral reefs or the deep sea.
The same biomes can lie on different continents, for example deserts in Africa and in Australia.
In the mountains the life zones follow one above another, similar to from the equator to the pole.
The tropical rainforest is the most species-rich land biome on Earth.

abschnitte.text: The word **biome** comes from the Greek word bios for life. It means a very large area in which the climate is similar and therefore similar plants grow. Certain animals then go with the plants. A biome is therefore bigger than a single **ecosystem** such as a pond or a small wood.

Most important are the **temperature** and the amount of rain in a year. Where it is warm and very wet, rainforest grows. Where it is warm but very dry, a desert arises. Where it is cold for a long time, only mosses, lichens and low shrubs grow, which is called **tundra**.

The **tropical rainforest** lies around the equator, for example on the Amazon, in the Congo Basin and in South-East Asia. More than half of all known animal and plant species on land live there. The **savanna** is a grassland with single trees, and in Africa elephants, zebras and lions live there. Deserts such as the Sahara, on the other hand, get hardly any rain.

In central Europe, and so in Switzerland, without humans there would be **mixed deciduous forest** with beeches and oaks almost everywhere. Further north follows the huge coniferous forest, the **taiga**, which stretches through Russia, Scandinavia and Canada. Still further north lies the treeless tundra. Around the poles lie the ice deserts of the Arctic and Antarctic.

Anyone who climbs a mountain in Switzerland travels through several life zones. At the bottom grow deciduous forests, further up spruces, larches and Swiss stone pines. Above the **forest line**, usually at about 1800 to 2200 metres, follow alpine pastures and dwarf shrubs. At the very top there is only rock, snow and glaciers, similar to the Arctic.

Seas, lakes and rivers are also divided into life zones. **Coral reefs** in warm, shallow seas are especially species-rich. The deep sea is dark and cold, yet astonishing animals live there. Fresh water such as Lake Geneva or the Rhine again forms its own habitats.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large life zone of the Earth with typical climate, plants and animals.
A habitat with all the living things that live together in it, for example a pond.
A huge coniferous forest in the far north of Europe, Asia and North America.
A cold, treeless landscape with mosses, lichens and low shrubs.
The height in the mountains above which no more forests grow.

gewusst: The taiga is the largest forest area on Earth and stretches almost once around the North Pole.
Antarctica too counts as a desert, because very little precipitation falls there.
A walk from the valley up to a high Alpine summit leads through similar life zones to a journey from Switzerland to Greenland.

teile.einleitung: With a bug viewer you can look at small animals very closely. It is a transparent cup with a magnifying glass in the lid. It is important that you treat the animals well while doing so.
wichtigste: A bug viewer is a transparent cup with a magnifying glass in the lid.
It is suitable for small animals such as ladybirds, ants or woodlice.
Gently slide animals in with a leaf or a brush.
Never put the bug viewer in the blazing sun.
Watch the animal only for a short time.
Afterwards release it where you found it.

abschnitte.text: A **bug viewer** is a transparent cup. In the lid there is a **magnifying glass** that shows everything bigger. This way you can look at small animals enlarged without touching them. It is suitable for very small animals such as **ladybirds**, ants or woodlice. Many bug viewers have small air holes in the lid.

Small animals are very delicate. So you do not pick them up with your fingers. It is best to slide them **gently** into the cup with a leaf or a brush. You can also put the cup over the animal and carefully slide a leaf underneath. Then you close the lid.

In the bug viewer you can count the legs. A **spider** has eight legs. That is why it is not an insect, because **insects** have six legs. On a **woodlouse** you can clearly see its many little legs, usually fourteen. It has no wings, fur or feathers. Woodlice are, by the way, related to crabs.

In the cup the animal is under **stress**. It can dry out or get too hot. That is why you watch it only for a **short time**. Never put the bug viewer in the **blazing sun**, because it quickly gets very hot in the cup. Afterwards you release the animal exactly where you found it, because that is its habitat.

gewusst: Under the magnifying glass you can see that flies have eyes made of many small single eyes.
Woodlice need moisture, which is why they like to live under stones and leaves.

teile.einleitung: The African baobab, also called the monkey-bread tree, is a giant tree from the savannas of Africa. It has a very thick trunk in which it stores water. Some of these trees are over 1,000 years old.
wichtigste: The baobab grows in Africa south of the Sahara.
It is also called the baobab.
It stores water in its thick trunk.
In the dry season it sheds its leaves.
Baobabs can live to over 1,000 years.
Its flowers are pollinated at night by fruit bats.

abschnitte.text: The **African baobab** grows in the **savannas** of Africa south of the Sahara. Under the name **baobab** it is known in many countries. In the savanna there is a long **dry season** in which hardly any rain falls. The tree is well adapted to it. It is among the longest-lived trees in the world. Some specimens are well **over 1,000 years** old.

The trunk of the baobab is enormously thick. Its wood is soft and, like a sponge, can **store** a great deal of **water**. In this way the tree survives long dry seasons. In the dry season it sheds its **leaves** so that it loses less water. Without leaves, the short, thick branches look like **roots**. That is why people say the tree stands **upside down**.

The fruits of the tree are large and have a hard, velvety shell. They are called **monkey bread**, because **baboons** and other animals like to eat them. People too use the pulp. The large **white flowers** open in the evening. At night **fruit bats** visit them, drink nectar and **pollinate** them as they do so.

In the book **“The Little Prince”** by **Antoine de Saint-Exupéry**, baobabs appear. On his tiny planet the little prince has to pull up the young trees again and again. Otherwise they would grow so big that they would burst the planet.

gewusst: Some hollow baobabs are so large that people can fit inside them.
In several African countries the baobab is regarded as the tree of life, because almost all its parts are used.

teile.einleitung: The climate is getting warmer, and summers are getting drier. Not all trees that grow in Swiss forests today cope with this. Experts are therefore looking for tree species that will also thrive in future.
wichtigste: With climate change, the trees that suit a place are changing.
The beech is likely to struggle in low, dry areas in future.
Oaks are considered especially future-proof on the Central Plateau.
The wild service tree is a rare, warmth-loving native tree.
The Douglas fir from North America is being tested as a possible tree of the future.
Trial plantings in many places show which species cope.
Foreign tree species often offer less habitat for native animals.

abschnitte.text: Trees often live for over a hundred years. A tree planted today must therefore cope with the climate of the future. What matters is a **tree species suited to the site**: it fits the soil, water and climate at the particular place. With **climate change**, however, the species that fit a place are changing. That is why foresters are already thinking today about the forest of tomorrow.

The **beech** is today one of the commonest broadleaved trees in Switzerland. But it needs enough moisture. In the hot, dry summer of **2018** it showed clear damage at low altitudes. Experts expect it to have difficulty in future in the lowest and driest areas. At higher altitudes, however, it is likely to carry on growing well.

**Sessile and pedunculate oaks** cope comparatively well with warmth and drought. That is why they are being encouraged more on the Central Plateau today. The **wild service tree** is also considered a tree of the future. It belongs to the rose family, is rare, likes to grow in warm, dry places and supplies very valuable wood. Other warmth-loving native species are, for example, the Norway maple or the small-leaved lime.

In many places in Switzerland there are **trial plantings** at different altitudes. There, native and foreign tree species are planted and observed for years. Beeches and oaks from **southern Europe** are also tested. These trees of the same species have adapted to heat there. People check whether their offspring also grow well here.

abschnitte.titel: Foreign species with pros and cons
abschnitte.text: The **Douglas fir** comes from North America. It grows fast and tolerates drought better than the spruce. That is why it is being tested as a possible tree for a warmer climate. One disadvantage of foreign species: fewer **native insects** and other animals usually live on them. That is why they are mixed in, if at all, only in small proportions.

gewusst: A mixed forest with many tree species is more resilient than a forest with only one species.
In North America the Douglas fir is among the tallest trees of all.

teile.einleitung: An old-wood island is a small patch of forest where the trees are left to grow old and decay on their own. No timber is cut there. This creates a habitat for many animals, fungi and plants that depend on old and dead wood.
wichtigste: In an **old-wood island** the trees stay standing until they decay naturally.
Individual valuable trees with holes or fungi are called **habitat trees**.
Living things that depend on wood are called **xylobionts**.
Old-wood islands act as **stepping stones** between larger reserves.
The rare **white-backed woodpecker** needs deciduous forests rich in dead wood.
Old-wood islands are usually smaller than natural forest reserves and are often protected only for a set period.

abschnitte.text: In a managed forest, trees are usually felled long before they are old. A lot of habitat is lost this way. In an **old-wood island**, no timber is harvested. The trees are allowed to grow old, die and decay. This produces a lot of **dead wood**. Old-wood islands are complemented by individual **habitat trees**, also called biotope trees. These are trees with woodpecker holes, cracks or fungi, which are left standing because of their value to nature.

Dead wood is anything but dead. Many living things depend on it. They are called **xylobionts**, which means wood dwellers. They include numerous **beetles**, fungi and lichens. They break the wood down or live in holes and crevices. The **tinder fungus**, for example, grows on weakened and dead beech trees and forms large, bracket-shaped fruiting bodies. It breaks the wood down as **white rot**.

A particularly demanding resident is the **white-backed woodpecker**. This rare woodpecker looks for insect larvae mainly in rotting deciduous wood. It only occurs where there is a lot of dead wood. An overview by Müller and Bütler (2010) showed that many demanding dead-wood species need around **20 to 50 cubic metres** of dead wood per hectare, depending on the type of forest.

Many dead-wood species can only spread over short distances. That is why a **network** of protected areas is important. **Natural forest reserves** are large and secured for the long term. **Old-wood islands** are smaller and in Switzerland are often protected for a certain period through contracts. They act as **stepping stones** between the reserves. This allows animals and fungi to move from one area to the next.

gewusst: In the past, people used the tinder fungus to light fires, which is how it got its name.
In a natural forest with no timber harvesting, a tree can live for several hundred years before it decays.

teile.einleitung: Plants in pots need good soil to grow healthily. **Potting soil** holds water, gives the roots support and contains nutrients. In the garden, earthworms and compost help to make the soil fertile.
wichtigste: Good potting soil contains nutrients that feed the plant.
The plant takes up the nutrients with the water through the roots.
Earthworms make garden soil loose and fertile.
Compost is soil made from rotted plant remains.
Good soil is loose, so that air and water reach the roots.

abschnitte.text: Potting soil is a mixture made specially for plants. It is **loose**, so that **air** and **water** reach the roots well. It stores water so that the plant does not dry out quickly. It also contains **nutrients**. The plant takes them up with the water through the **roots**. After some time the nutrients are used up, and then the plant needs fresh soil or fertiliser.

In the garden many small helpers work in the soil. The **earthworm** digs tunnels and eats dead plant remains. Through its tunnels air and water get into the soil. Its droppings are very rich in nutrients. This makes the soil **loose** and **fertile**.

From **kitchen scraps**, leaves and grass cuttings, **compost** forms over time. Small living things such as bacteria, fungi and worms break down the remains. After a few months it has become dark, crumbly and nutrient-rich **compost soil**. Many Swiss municipalities collect green waste and make compost from it.

gewusst: In Switzerland, potting soil is more and more often made without peat, because bogs are destroyed for peat extraction.

teile.einleitung: An identification key helps you find out what a plant is called. You answer simple questions about its features step by step, and so you arrive at its name in the end.
wichtigste: An identification key leads through features to the name of a plant species.
In a dichotomous key you choose between two possibilities at every step.
The “Flora Helvetica” is the well-known identification book for the plants of Switzerland.
With the “Flora Vegetativa” you can identify plants even without flowers.
Important features are leaf arrangement, leaf margin and leaf shape.
If the result does not fit, you go back and check your decisions.
A hand lens helps to see small features such as tiny hairs.

abschnitte.text: An identification key is a series of questions about features. In a **dichotomous key** there are exactly two possibilities at every step, which exclude each other. “Dichotomous” comes from Greek and means “divided in two”. Depending on the answer, you jump to a next step. This way you gradually arrive at the genus or the species.

Many questions concern the leaves. If two leaves sit opposite each other at a node, this is called **opposite**. If there is only one leaf per node, this is called **alternate**. An **entire** leaf has a smooth margin without teeth. A **pinnate** leaf consists of several leaflets to the left and right of a central axis, as in the ash or the rowan.

The **Flora Helvetica** by Lauber, Wagner and Gygax describes the ferns and flowering plants of Switzerland. It contains photos, descriptions and identification keys and is also available as an app. The **Flora Vegetativa** uses features of leaves, stems and growth form. With it you can identify plants even when they are not flowering.

For small features such as hairs or fine teeth on the leaf margin, you take a **hand lens** with you. You look closely at the plant before answering a question. If you end up at a plant that does not fit at all, one answer was usually wrong. Then you go back step by step and check the uncertain decisions. At the end you compare the result with the description or a picture.

gewusst: Some keys lead not only to the species but down to the subspecies.
There are identification keys not only for plants, but also for animals, mushrooms and even rocks.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss pine nut is the seed of the Swiss stone pine, a conifer of the Alps. Unlike many other conifers, the Swiss stone pine does not let the wind spread its seeds. Animals take care of that, above all a bird, the spotted nutcracker.
wichtigste: The Swiss pine nut is the seed of the Swiss stone pine, also called the Arolla pine.
Swiss stone pine seeds have no wing.
A ripe cone does not open by itself, animals break it open.
A Swiss stone pine cone needs about two years to ripen.
Young cones are violet.
A Swiss pine nut is about 1 centimetre in size.

abschnitte.titel: The Swiss stone pine, a tree of the mountains
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss stone pine** (Pinus cembra) is also called the **Arolla pine** or Zirbe. It grows in the Alps up to the **tree line** and withstands great cold. Its needles stand in bundles of five. In Switzerland it is common, for example, in the **Engadine** and in the Valais. Swiss stone pines can live for several hundred years.

**Young cones** are **violet**, and later they turn brown. A cone needs **about two years** to ripen. Inside are the **Swiss pine nuts**, which are about **1 centimetre** in size. The seeds of the Swiss stone pine lack **a wing**, of the kind that the seeds of the spruce, for example, have. That is why the wind cannot carry them far.

A ripe cone **does not open by itself**. **Animals break it open** to get at the nuts. The most important helper is the **spotted nutcracker**, a member of the crow family. In autumn it gathers many nuts and hides them in the ground as a winter store. It finds many of its hiding places again, even under snow. New Swiss stone pines grow from the forgotten nuts.

The **red squirrel** also likes to eat Swiss pine nuts. Mice and other animals take their share as well. The nuts are rich in fat and are therefore valuable winter food. People eat Swiss pine nuts too. In the Grisons they are used, for example, for pastries and sweets.

gewusst: A single spotted nutcracker can hide many thousands of Swiss pine nuts in one autumn.
Swiss stone pine wood has a strong scent and is often used for parlours, furniture and beds.

teile.einleitung: Artemisinin is an active substance from sweet wormwood. It works against malaria, a dangerous disease in warm countries. Its discoverer, Tu Youyou, received the Nobel Prize for it in 2015.
wichtigste: Artemisinin is obtained from sweet wormwood.
It is used mainly against malaria.
Tu Youyou received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2015 for the discovery.
What mattered was an extract made at a low temperature instead of boiling.
An endoperoxide bridge in the molecule is important for its effect.
Artemisinin is given together with a second active substance to prevent resistance.

abschnitte.text: **Sweet wormwood** (Artemisia annua) is a plant from the daisy family. In **traditional Chinese medicine** it has been used against fever for a very long time. The active substance **artemisinin** is obtained from its leaves. Chemically it belongs to the **sesquiterpene lactones**, a group of natural substances.

**Malaria** is caused by tiny single-celled organisms, the **plasmodia**. They are passed on by the bite of certain mosquitoes, the **Anopheles mosquitoes**. The disease causes high fever and can be fatal without treatment. Children in Africa south of the Sahara are especially affected. Against older drugs such as chloroquine, many of the parasites became **resistant** over time, that is, insensitive.

The Chinese researcher **Tu Youyou** searched old writings in the 1960s and 1970s for remedies against malaria. The first extracts from wormwood worked badly. In an old text she found the hint to soak the plant in cold water. She then extracted the active substance **at a low temperature instead of by boiling**, and it worked. In 2015 she received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine** for it.

In the artemisinin molecule there is a special link of two oxygen atoms, the **endoperoxide bridge**. It is crucial for the effect. When the substance comes into contact with iron in the parasite, very reactive particles form, which damage the parasite. Artemisinin works quickly, but stays in the body only for a short time.

Artemisinin or its derivatives are almost always given together with a **second active substance**. This **combination therapy** is meant to **prevent resistance** and kill the remaining parasites. Improved substances were developed from artemisinin, for example **artemether** and **artesunate**. **Artesunate** is injected for **severe malaria**. Combination therapies are now among the most important remedies against malaria.

gewusst: Tu Youyou was the first woman from China to receive a Nobel Prize in a natural science.
The hint about soaking in cold water came from a Chinese book more than 1,600 years old.

teile.einleitung: A **flower meadow** is full of colours in spring and summer. Here ox-eye daisies, bellflowers, clover and many other plants grow. For bees, bumblebees and butterflies it is an important feeding place.
wichtigste: Most meadow flowers bloom in spring and summer.
The ox-eye daisy has white petals and a yellow centre.
After its yellow blossom, the dandelion becomes a seed head.
Bees collect nectar and pollen on the meadow.
Butterflies suck nectar with their long tongue.
The buttercup is poisonous when fresh, and cows leave it standing.

abschnitte.text: The **ox-eye daisy** has white petals and a yellow centre. It looks like a big daisy. The **bellflower** has blue or violet blossoms in the shape of a little bell. The **meadow sage** blooms blue-violet and is related to the sage from the herb garden. **Clover** usually has three leaflets and round flower heads, often red or white.

The **dandelion** blooms bright yellow. After that it forms a white ball of seeds with little parachutes, the **seed head**. The wind carries the seeds away. The **buttercup** also has yellow blossoms, which shine. When fresh it is **poisonous**. That is why cows leave it on the pasture. In hay, dried, it is harmless.

**Bees** fly from blossom to blossom and collect **nectar** and **pollen**. Honeybees make honey from the nectar. **Butterflies** suck the sweet nectar out of the blossoms with their long **tongue**. In doing so the insects carry pollen on and pollinate the plants. The more different flowers a meadow has, the more insect species find food there.

A colourful meadow does not arise by itself. It is **mown** once or twice a year, otherwise bushes and trees grow over time. Too much fertiliser lets mainly grasses grow, and the flowers disappear. In Switzerland many species-rich meadows have been lost. Farmers therefore receive payments if they manage meadows gently.

gewusst: A clover leaf with four leaflets is rare and is regarded as a lucky charm.
On a species-rich mountain meadow in Switzerland, over 50 different plant species can grow.

teile.einleitung: **Blue Carbon**, in German “blauer Kohlenstoff”, is carbon that plants on coasts and in the sea store. Mangroves, seagrass meadows and salt marshes lock up especially much of it in the soil. Protecting them is therefore also considered a contribution to climate protection.
wichtigste: Blue Carbon is carbon that is stored in coastal and marine ecosystems.
The focus is on mangroves, seagrass meadows and salt marshes.
The carbon is stored mainly in the sediments on the bottom.
Oxygen-poor, wet sediments slow down decomposition, so the carbon stays stored for a long time.
A UN report made the term internationally known in 2009.
When mangroves are cleared, stored carbon is released.

abschnitte.text: In photosynthesis, plants take up **carbon dioxide** (CO2) from the air or the water. They build the carbon into their leaves, stems and roots. When this carbon is stored in coastal and marine ecosystems, it is called **Blue Carbon**. The term became known through a report by **UNEP**, **FAO** and **UNESCO** from **2009**. It stressed the role of oceans and coasts as **carbon sinks**.

Research looks mainly at three coastal ecosystems: **mangroves**, **seagrass meadows** and **salt marshes**. Per area they store especially much carbon in the soil. Coral reefs do not count, because their lime formation tends to release CO2. Mangroves are forests in tropical tidal zones. Many have breathing roots sticking up vertically out of the mud, the **pneumatophores**. They supply the roots in the oxygen-poor mud with air.

Most of the carbon is not in the plants themselves, but in the **sediments**. These soils are constantly saturated with water and therefore **low in oxygen**. Without oxygen, decomposers work only very slowly. Dead plant material therefore accumulates over **centuries to millennia**. This creates very large, lasting stores.

**Seagrasses** are not algae, but **flowering plants**. They have roots and leaves and form flowers and seeds under water. Their ancestors were land plants that returned to the sea. In the Mediterranean grows **Neptune grass** (Posidonia oceanica), which occurs only there. It forms thick mats of roots and rhizomes that can grow over millennia.

Many of these habitats are threatened. In **South-East Asia** and **Latin America**, large areas of mangrove were cleared for **shrimp farming ponds**. In doing so, not only is habitat for fish, crabs and birds lost. The carbon stored in the soil is also released again. That is why many countries try to protect and restore coastal ecosystems.

gewusst: Mangroves also protect coasts from storm surges, because their dense roots slow the waves.
Neptune grass meadows are among the oldest known living things on Earth: some stands are probably many thousands of years old.

teile.einleitung: In organic farming, work is done as far as possible in harmony with nature. Organic farmers do without chemical-synthetic fertilisers and pesticides. In Switzerland organic farming has a long tradition.
wichtigste: In organic farming no genetically modified plants may be grown.
Organic farmers fertilise mainly with dung and compost.
Weeds are mostly controlled mechanically with a hoe or a harrow.
Hans and Maria Müller founded organic-biological farming in Switzerland.
The research institute FiBL has its seat in Frick AG.
Graubünden has the highest share of organic farms.
Biodynamic farming goes back to Rudolf Steiner.

abschnitte.text: In **organic farming** the soil is meant to stay fertile and nature to be burdened as little as possible. Organic farmers fertilise mainly with **dung** and **compost**. They do without chemical-synthetic fertilisers and sprays. **Genetically modified plants** are forbidden. An important principle is crop rotation: on a field, different plants take turns.

Organic farmers control weeds mostly **mechanically**. They use a hoe or a **harrow**, a device with many fine tines. Against pests they use beneficial insects and preventive measures. This takes more work, and the yield is often smaller. That is why **organic products** in the shop are often more expensive.

The couple **Hans and Maria Müller** are regarded as the founders of organic-biological farming in Switzerland. They developed their ideas from the 1940s. In **Frick AG** stands the Research Institute of Organic Agriculture, the **FiBL**. It researches how organic farming can succeed even better. The canton of **Graubünden** has the highest share of organic farms, mainly thanks to many mountain farms.

A special form is **biodynamic farming**. It goes back to **Rudolf Steiner**, who gave lectures on it in 1924. Biodynamic farms use special preparations made from herbs, dung and minerals. They see the farm as a whole made of soil, plants and animals. Their label is called Demeter.

gewusst: The FiBL is one of the largest research institutes for organic farming in the world.
In organic farming the animals are supposed to get plenty of outdoor access and feed from their own farm.

teile.einleitung: Species diversity means how many different kinds of animals, plants, fungi and tiny living things there are. It is an important part of biodiversity. Some habitats are especially rich in species, and much has not even been discovered yet.
wichtigste: Around 2 million species have been scientifically described worldwide.
Insects make up most of the known animal species.
The tropical rainforest is regarded as the habitat richest in species on land.
Coral reefs are called the “rainforest of the seas”.
From the poles to the equator, species diversity increases.
In Switzerland, dry meadows are among the habitats richest in species.
Invasive species can push out native species.

abschnitte.text: **Biodiversity** includes three levels: the diversity of **habitats**, the diversity of **species** and the **genetic diversity** within a species. **Species diversity** counts how many different species there are. Around **2 million species** have been scientifically described worldwide. But experts suspect that there are many more that nobody knows. Every year thousands of new species are discovered.
