**Insects** make up most of the known animal species. Of the **beetles** alone, several hundred thousand species are known. Add to that butterflies, flies, ants, bees and many more. Mammals, by comparison, are a small group with a few thousand species. Many insects are tiny and live hidden, so many are still unknown.

abschnitte.titel: Where there are especially many species
abschnitte.text: From the **poles towards the equator, species diversity increases**. On land, the **tropical rainforest** is the habitat richest in species. On a single tree there, hundreds of insect species can live. In the sea, **coral reefs** are especially rich in life. That is why they are often called the **“rainforest of the seas”**.

Thanks to mountains, valleys, lakes and rivers, Switzerland too has many habitats. **Dry meadows** and **dry pastures** are especially rich in species. Many flowers grow on them, and many butterflies, grasshoppers and wild bees live there. Such meadows are low in nutrients and are fertilised very little. Many of them have disappeared because the land was fertilised, built on or no longer mown.

Some species are brought by humans into new areas. If they spread strongly and **push out native species**, they are called **invasive species**. An example in Switzerland is the **Canadian goldenrod** from North America. It blooms **golden yellow** and often grows on **railway embankments**, at the edges of paths and on waste ground. Where it forms dense stands, other plants have hardly any room left.

gewusst: Many experts estimate that there are several million still unknown species on Earth.
A single gram of soil can contain millions of bacteria from thousands of species.

teile.einleitung: The brown trout is a typical fish of Swiss streams. It needs cool, clear water rich in oxygen. Because rivers are getting warmer, it has a hard time in many places today.
wichtigste: The brown trout lives in cool, oxygen-rich streams and the upper reaches of rivers.
Typical are black and red spots, the red ones often with a pale ring.
It belongs to the salmon family and has a small adipose fin.
It spawns from about October to January in pits in the gravel.
It eats insects, insect larvae and freshwater shrimps.
The lake trout belongs to the same species, but lives in the lake.
Proliferative kidney disease hits it hard in warm water.

abschnitte.text: The **brown trout** belongs to the **salmon family**, like the salmon and the grayling. Typical of this family is the small **adipose fin** on the back between the dorsal fin and the tail. The brown trout has black and red spots, the red ones often with a pale ring. Its colouring can vary greatly depending on the water. Some fish are very dark, others pale and silvery.

The brown trout needs **cool**, clear and **oxygen-rich** water. That is why it lives mainly in streams and in the upper reaches of rivers, even high in the mountains. It likes to hide under roots, stones or overhanging banks. From there it lies in wait for prey carried along by the current. It defends its territory against other trout.

The brown trout is a **predator**. It eats mainly insect larvae that live in the stream, and insects that fall onto the water surface. **Freshwater shrimps** are also on its menu. Large trout also eat small fish. Because it snaps insects from the surface, it is often fished for with artificial flies.

Brown trout **spawn** from about October to January, that is, in late autumn and winter. The female beats a pit into the **gravel bed** with her tail. There she lays the eggs, which are washed by fresh water. In the cold water the eggs develop slowly over the winter. If the gravel is clogged with mud, the eggs get too little oxygen.

The **lake trout** belongs to the same species as the brown trout. It grows into a large fish in the lake and climbs up the inflowing streams to spawn. The **rainbow trout**, on the other hand, comes from North America and was introduced in Switzerland. A great danger is **proliferative kidney disease** (PKD). It is caused by a parasite and is often fatal at water temperatures above about 15 degrees.

gewusst: Brown trout and lake trout look very different, but are the same species.
The rainbow trout has a pink shimmering stripe on its side.

teile.einleitung: Omnivores eat both plants and animals. Because they do not depend on a single food, they do well in many habitats. Humans too are omnivores.
wichtigste: The technical term for omnivores is **omnivores**.
Omnivores eat plant and animal food.
Wild boar, brown bear, red fox, badger and carrion crow are omnivores.
Humans have the typical **teeth** of an omnivore.
Omnivores find a substitute more easily when a food is missing.

abschnitte.text: The Latin word “omnis” means “all”. That is why omnivores are also called **omnivores**. They eat plants such as fruit, seeds and roots, but also animals such as insects, worms or carrion. Besides them there are **herbivores** and **carnivores**. Omnivores stand, so to speak, in between.

The **wild boar** eats acorns, roots, mushrooms, worms, insects and also carrion. The **red fox** hunts mainly mice, but in late summer it also eats many berries and windfall fruit. The **badger** eats fruit, roots, insects and mice, but its most important food is often **earthworms**. The **brown bear** usually eats more plants than meat: berries, grasses and roots, plus insects and carrion.

Omnivores also live in Swiss cities. The **carrion crow** eats seeds, fruit, worms, insects, waste and carrion. That is why it almost always finds something in the city. Other birds are choosier: the common swift catches only insects in the air. Foxes too live in many cities today and sometimes search through rubbish bags.

From its **teeth** you can tell what an animal eats. Humans have **incisors** for biting off, **canines** for holding and **molars** for grinding. This mixture suits mixed food. Omnivores have a great advantage: when one food is missing, they find a substitute more easily. They are less dependent on a single source of food.

gewusst: A badger can eat a great many earthworms on a damp night.
Carrion crows are very clever and sometimes drop nuts on the road so that they break open.

teile.einleitung: An anthill is the home of an entire ant colony. The large mounds in the forest are built by red wood ants from needles, twigs and soil. In Switzerland these ants are protected.
wichtigste: The large mounds in the forest are built by **red wood ants**.
The **queen** lays the eggs, and the workers look after the brood.
Wood ants have been **protected** in Switzerland since 1966.
To defend themselves they spray **formic acid**.
They collect sweet **honeydew** from aphids.
A large colony can have many hundreds of thousands of ants.

abschnitte.text: **Red wood ants** build mounds that can grow to more than a metre high. To do this they gather needles, small twigs and pieces of plants. The nest also reaches deep into the ground. They prefer to build in **sunny spots**, such as at the edges of forests or in clearings. The ants need warmth for their brood.

Very many ants live together in an anthill, in a large colony **many hundreds of thousands**. The **queen** lays the eggs from which the colony grows. With wood ants there are often several queens in one nest. The many **workers** look after the brood, build the mound and fetch food. They all work together like one big team.

If an anthill is disturbed, the ants spray **formic acid**. It stings and drives enemies away. Ants also have a special friendship with **aphids**. The aphids give off a sugary juice, the **honeydew**. The ants drink it and in return protect the aphids from enemies.

Wood ants are very useful to the forest. One colony catches a great many **insects**, including pests that weaken trees. That is why they are called the **health police of the forest**. In Switzerland, red wood ants have been **protected since 1966**. Their nests must not be damaged. If you see an anthill, it is best to look at it from a little distance and leave it untouched.

gewusst: Ants find their way using scent trails that they leave on the ground.
An anthill works like a heater: in spring it is often much warmer inside than outside.

teile.einleitung: On a farm, food is produced and animals are kept. Farmers look after fields, meadows and the soil. In Switzerland there are many family farms.
wichtigste: A person who runs a farm and has trained for it is called a farmer.
The apprenticeship lasts three years in Switzerland.
Hay and straw are stored in the barn.
Manure is a natural fertiliser and is stored on the manure heap.
With crop rotation the soil stays healthy.
In the farm shop you can buy products directly from the farm.
On 1 August many farms invite people to a Buurezmorge, a farmers’ breakfast.

abschnitte.text: Someone who runs a farm and has trained for it is a **farmer**. The apprenticeship lasts three years in Switzerland. There is a lot to do on a farm: feeding animals, milking, tending fields and looking after machines. Often the whole family helps. Many farms have cows, while others grow mainly cereals, vegetables or fruit.

The animals live in the **stable**. In the **barn**, hay, straw and equipment are stored, and they stay dry there. The manure from the stable is collected in a heap, the **manure heap**. Many farms also have a small **farm shop**. There they sell eggs, potatoes, milk or cheese directly from the farm.

A **field** is land that is ploughed and sown, for example with cereals or beet. On the **pasture**, on the other hand, grass grows, which the animals eat. Against birds that eat the seeds, some farmers put up a **scarecrow**. It looks like a person and is meant to scare the birds away.

A farmer does not plant the same thing on the same field every year. He alternates, for example wheat, then maize, then beet. This is called **crop rotation**. In this way the soil stays healthy and pests spread less. As natural fertiliser the farmer spreads **manure** on the fields. This is a mixture of dung and straw that gives nutrients back to the soil.

On the **national holiday**, many Swiss farms invite people to a big breakfast. It is called a **Buurezmorge** or 1 August brunch. There you eat plaited bread, cheese, butter and jam from the farm. This way people from the town also get to know life on a farm.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are farms from the Central Plateau up to high in the mountains.
A cow eats a great deal of grass or hay every day, often more than 50 kilograms of fresh grass.

teile.einleitung: When we think of a leaf, we usually mean the flat green surface. It is called the **leaf blade**. Here the plant captures sunlight and makes its food.
wichtigste: The leaf blade is the flat, mostly green main part of a foliage leaf.
A typical foliage leaf consists of leaf base, leaf stalk and leaf blade.
The flat, broad shape catches a lot of light for photosynthesis.
The outer end of the blade is called the leaf tip.
If the blade is not divided, it is called a simple leaf.
Shade leaves are usually larger and thinner than sun leaves.

abschnitte.titel: The structure of a foliage leaf
abschnitte.text: A typical foliage leaf has three main parts. With the **leaf base** it attaches to the shoot. The **leaf stalk** carries the **leaf blade**, the actual leaf surface. At the outer end of the blade lies the **leaf tip**. Through the blade run the leaf veins, which supply and support it.

The blade is mostly **thin**, **flat** and **broad**. This way it can take up as much **sunlight** as possible. The plant needs this light for **photosynthesis**, in which sugar is made from water and carbon dioxide. Leaves in the shade are often larger and thinner than leaves in the sun. This way they make good use of the little light with little material.

If the blade forms a continuous surface as in the **beech**, it is called a **simple leaf**. If it is divided into separate leaflets, it is called a **compound leaf**. An example is the horse chestnut with its leaflets arranged like fingers.

Many plants in the rainforest have a long, drawn-out **drip tip**. Rainwater runs off quickly over it. This way the leaf does not stay wet for long, and algae and fungi grow less well on it. The **giant water lily** (Victoria) from the Amazon region has round floating leaves over 2 metres across with an upturned rim.

gewusst: The leaves of the giant water lily are among the largest undivided leaves in the world and have spiny ribs on the underside.
The giant water lily is named after the British Queen Victoria.

teile.einleitung: Plants can influence one another with chemical substances. This phenomenon is called allelopathy. Some plants give off substances that inhibit the germination and growth of their neighbours.
wichtigste: In **allelopathy**, plants influence other plants through substances they release.
The term was coined in 1937 by the Austrian botanist **Hans Molisch**.
The walnut tree produces the inhibitor **juglone**.
The invasive **tree of heaven** releases ailanthone and is spreading in Ticino.
The **novel weapons hypothesis** explains why some introduced plants are so successful.
In agriculture, cover crops and mulch help against weeds.

abschnitte.text: Plants release various substances into their surroundings through their **roots**, leaves or falling foliage. Some of these inhibit or promote the germination and growth of other plants. This effect is called **allelopathy**. The term was coined in 1937 by **Hans Molisch** in a book about the influence of one plant on another. The word is put together from Greek “allelon” (of one another) and “pathos” (suffering).

A well-known example is the **walnut tree**. In its leaves, roots and fruit husks, precursors of the substance **juglone** are formed. Juglone inhibits the germination and growth of many plants. That is why often only a few other plants grow under walnut trees. Gardeners therefore prefer not to plant delicate vegetables directly beneath them.

Some introduced plants spread especially strongly. The **novel weapons hypothesis** of Callaway and Ridenour explains it this way: their defensive substances work strongly in the new area because the native species have never had to deal with them. The **tree of heaven**, which comes from China, produces **ailanthone** and is spreading strongly above all on the southern side of the Alps, for example in Ticino. **Garlic mustard**, introduced in North America, uses root secretions to inhibit the **mycorrhizal fungi** on which native trees depend.

Allelopathy can also be used deliberately. Certain **cover crops** such as rye release inhibiting substances as they break down. If their remains lie on the field as **mulch**, fewer weeds germinate. **Sorghum** gives off from its root hairs the substance **sorgoleone**, which inhibits the photosynthesis of neighbouring weeds. In this way less weedkiller is needed.

gewusst: Allelopathic substances can not only inhibit but sometimes also promote the growth of other plants.
Sorgoleone is an oily substance that sits as small droplets on the root hairs of sorghum.

teile.einleitung: The **copper beech** is a special form of the European beech with dark red leaves. Because of its colour it was often planted in parks and castle gardens. Some old copper beeches are real celebrities.
wichtigste: The copper beech is a form of the European beech with red leaves.
A red pigment covers the green chlorophyll.
In spring, when it comes into leaf, the leaves shine most strongly.
From its seeds grow many green young trees.
Copper beeches can become over 200 years old.
The municipality of Buch am Irchel in the canton of Zurich has a copper beech in its coat of arms.

abschnitte.text: The leaves of the copper beech also contain green **chlorophyll**. But a **red pigment** in the outer layer covers it. The leaves shine most strongly in **spring**, when they come into leaf. In the course of summer they become **darker** and often a little greenish. Despite the red colour, the copper beech can carry out photosynthesis quite normally.

The fruits of the copper beech are **beechnuts**. These are small, **three-edged** nuts. Usually two of them sit in a spiny husk. The red leaf colour is not passed on to all offspring. From the seeds, **red and green** young trees therefore grow. Gardeners therefore often propagate especially beautiful copper beeches by **grafting**.

Because of its beautiful red leaves, the copper beech was gladly planted in **parks** and **castle gardens**. Old specimens often stand by castles and villas. There are also bred forms with hanging branches like a weeping willow. They are called **weeping copper beeches**. Beeches live to about **200 to 300 years**. Many copper beeches in parks were planted over 100 years ago.

abschnitte.titel: The copper beech of Buch am Irchel
abschnitte.text: In the municipality of **Buch am Irchel** in the **canton of Zurich** stands a copper beech that has been known since **1680**. It is among the oldest known copper beeches. The municipality has even put it in its **coat of arms**. Copper beeches like this arose through a natural change in the genes of an ordinary European beech.

gewusst: Many copper beeches in Europe are said to descend from a few old trees that were already known centuries ago.
The name European beech (in German Rotbuche, red beech) does not come from the leaves, but from the slightly reddish wood.

teile.einleitung: Bracken is one of the largest ferns in our woods. It often forms dense stands in clearings and at woodland edges. The whole plant is poisonous, including to grazing animals.
wichtigste: Bracken usually grows half a metre to two metres tall.
It often grows in large stands in woodland clearings.
Underground it spreads with long rhizomes.
The whole plant is poisonous.
It is dangerous for cows and horses.
In autumn its fronds turn brown.

abschnitte.text: **Bracken** usually grows **0.5 to 2 metres** tall. If it can lean on bushes, it grows even taller. The leaves of ferns are called **fronds**. They are divided several times into leaflets and look like small trees. Like all ferns, bracken does not produce flowers but reproduces by means of tiny **spores**. It is one of the most widespread plants in the world and grows in Europe, Asia and Africa.

Bracken needs some light. That is why you find it mainly in **woodland clearings**, at **woodland edges** and on unused pastures. There it often forms large, **dense stands**. Other plants have hardly any room beneath it, because the fern takes their light. In **autumn** the fronds turn **brown** and die back. In spring it sprouts anew.

Underground, bracken has long, branching **rhizomes**. With them it spreads far. In Finland, some were even found that were **60 metres** long. From one spot usually only **one frond** grows. Because the rhizome is so long, many fronds still stand side by side. That is why it is very hard to get rid of bracken again.

Bracken contains poisonous substances in **all parts**. If **cows** or **horses** eat a lot of it, they become ill. The poison even remains in **dried** fern, for example when it gets into hay. People too should not eat bracken, although young shoots are eaten in some countries.

gewusst: If you cut the stalk of bracken through at a slant, you can see in the cross-section a pattern that recalls an eagle. That is where the German name Adlerfarn, “eagle fern”, comes from.
Ferns existed long before the dinosaurs.

teile.einleitung: ATP synthase is a tiny protein motor in the membranes of cells. It makes ATP, the most important energy carrier of all living things. It is driven by a flow of protons.
wichtigste: ATP synthase forms ATP with the help of a proton gradient.
Peter Mitchell explained this with the chemiosmotic theory and received the Nobel Prize in 1978.
In chloroplasts, the protons flow from the thylakoid lumen into the stroma.
One part of the enzyme turns like a rotor.
The formation of ATP using light energy is called photophosphorylation.
Uncouplers stop the formation of ATP.

abschnitte.text: **ATP** stands for adenosine triphosphate. It is the energy currency of the cell: almost all processes that need energy use ATP. **ATP synthase** puts ATP together from ADP and phosphate. It sits in the membranes of the **mitochondria** and of the **chloroplasts** of plants. In chloroplasts its formation with the help of light is called **photophosphorylation**, in mitochondria **oxidative phosphorylation**.

In chloroplasts, ATP synthase consists of two main parts. **CF0** is embedded in the membrane and lets the protons through. **CF1** projects into the stroma and forms the ATP there. The C stands for chloroplast. The flow of protons sets a ring in the membrane and the **gamma subunit** attached to it turning. This **rotor** changes the shape of the centres in the head part, where ATP is made.

abschnitte.titel: Protons like water at a dam
abschnitte.text: In photosynthesis, the electron transport chain pumps protons into the inner space of the thylakoids, the **thylakoid lumen**. There their concentration is high. Following the gradient, the protons flow back through ATP synthase into the **stroma**. This is like water flowing through a turbine. Substances that make the membrane permeable to protons are called **uncouplers**. Then electron transport carries on, but ATP synthase no longer gets any drive.

**Peter Mitchell** was the first to explain that a **proton gradient** across a membrane drives the formation of ATP. For this **chemiosmotic theory** he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in **1978**. **André Jagendorf** confirmed it in 1966: in the dark he moved chloroplasts from an acidic to a basic solution, and they made ATP without light. **Paul Boyer** and **John Walker** worked out exactly how the enzyme works. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in **1997**.

gewusst: ATP synthase is one of the smallest rotary motors known in nature.
Every day a person builds up and breaks down about as much ATP as they weigh themselves.

teile.einleitung: Tree ferns are ferns that form a trunk and can grow as tall as trees. They grow mainly in damp, mild regions of the tropics and subtropics. Their relatives existed already in the time of the dinosaurs.
wichtigste: Tree ferns grow mainly in tropical and subtropical mountain forests.
The largest grow up to about 20 metres tall.
Their trunk is an upright rootstock without real wood.
The trunk forms no annual rings.
The fronds grow as a tuft at the top of the trunk.
The silver fern is a national symbol of New Zealand.
Trade in many tree ferns is regulated by the Washington Convention on endangered species.

abschnitte.text: **Tree ferns** are the largest living ferns today. The largest reach heights of around **20 metres**. They love damp, mild regions, especially tropical **mountain and cloud forests**. They are also common in New Zealand and Australia. Like all ferns, they form no flowers, but reproduce with tiny **spores**.

The trunk of a tree fern is not real wood. It is an upright-growing **rootstock**. Towards the bottom it becomes ever thicker through a dense mantle of many roots. Ferns have no growth layer that forms new wood every year. That is why there are no **annual rings** in the trunk of a tree fern.

Tree ferns usually have no branches. All the leaves, which in ferns are called **fronds**, grow together from the **top of the trunk**. There they form a tuft, similar to a palm. New fronds are at first rolled up and unfurl slowly. The fronds can grow several metres long.

The **silver fern** has fronds with a silvery-white underside. It is a well-known **national symbol of New Zealand** and can be seen on shirts, coins and coats of arms. **Dicksonia antarctica** comes from south-east Australia and Tasmania. It grows slowly and is gladly kept as a potted plant in central Europe, including Switzerland.

Many tree ferns were dug up for the garden trade. Their trunks were also used as a **growing medium** for orchids. As a result some species became rare. That is why trade in many tree ferns is restricted by the **Washington Convention on endangered species**. This agreement regulates the worldwide trade in endangered animals and plants.

gewusst: Relatives of today’s tree ferns grew already many millions of years ago.
The New Zealand national rugby team plays with the silver fern on its shirt.

teile.einleitung: Wild garlic is a wild plant that grows in damp woods in spring and smells strongly of garlic. Many people gather its leaves for pesto or soup. You have to be very careful, though, because there are poisonous look-alikes.
wichtigste: Wild garlic smells strongly of garlic.
You eat mainly the leaves, best in spring before flowering.
Pesto is often made from wild garlic.
It can be confused with the poisonous lily of the valley and autumn crocus.
To check, rub a leaf and smell it.
Wild garlic flowers white and is related to chives.

abschnitte.text: **Wild garlic** grows in damp **broadleaved woods** and floodplain forests, often in large stands. It is also widespread in Switzerland. It belongs to the genus **Allium**, like onion, garlic and **chives**, to which it is most closely related. From a small bulb in the ground grow broad, light green leaves. In April and May **white, star-shaped flowers** appear in an umbel.

Wild garlic smells and tastes **of garlic**, but a little milder. You eat mainly the **leaves**. It is best to harvest them **in spring before flowering**, when they are tender. **Wild garlic pesto** is very popular. You can also put the leaves in soup, butter, bread or quark. Because heat weakens the flavour, they are usually added only at the end.

Wild garlic can be confused with poisonous plants. The **lily of the valley** has similar leaves and grows in similar places. The young **autumn crocus** also looks similar. Both plants are very poisonous. To check, **rub a leaf** and smell it: only wild garlic smells of garlic. Because the smell stays on your fingers, take a fresh leaf for every test or wash your hands.

The German name, Bärlauch, comes from the **bear**. An old story says that bears eat wild garlic after hibernation to get their strength back. Whether this is true is not certain. In some areas the plant is also called **wild garlic** in German. Its scientific name is Allium ursinum, which also means bear’s leek.

gewusst: In places with a lot of wild garlic, the whole forest smells of garlic in spring.
After flowering, the leaves of wild garlic disappear completely in early summer, and only the bulb in the ground survives.

teile.einleitung: Agroecology means applying the rules of nature to farming. Instead of relying only on fertiliser and sprays, it makes use of diversity, natural cycles and beneficial insects. Agroecology is at once a science, a practice and a social movement.
wichtigste: Agroecology applies ecological principles to farming.
Mixed cropping makes better use of light, water and nutrients.
Legumes fix nitrogen from the air with nodule bacteria.
Standard-tree orchards are a Swiss example of agroforestry.
Ladybirds eat aphids and are important beneficial insects.
The FiBL in Frick AG is a leading institute for organic farming.

abschnitte.text: **Agroecology** relies on **diversity**, natural cycles and the knowledge of local farming families. One example is **mixed cropping**: several crops grow at the same time on the same area. They make better use of **light**, water and nutrients and can confuse pests. The risk is also spread. Such a system is regarded as **resilient**: it can cushion disturbances such as **droughts** or pest attacks and recover.

Plants need **nitrogen** to grow. **Legumes** such as clover, peas or beans live together with **nodule bacteria** on their roots. These bacteria, the rhizobia, make nitrogen from the air available to plants. That is why legumes are deliberately built into the **crop rotation**. They fertilise the soil in a natural way.

In **agroforestry**, trees are combined with crops or livestock. A traditional example in Switzerland is the **standard-tree orchard**. Large fruit trees stand on meadows that are mown or grazed. Such orchards offer habitat to many birds and insects.

Instead of using poison, you can let animals help. **Ladybirds** and especially their **larvae** eat large quantities of **aphids**. Such **beneficial insects** are an important part of agroecological systems. In East Africa the **push-pull method** was developed. The plant **Desmodium** in the maize field drives pests away with its scent (push). Grasses such as **Napier grass** at the field edge attract them (pull). The method manages without insecticides.

In **Frick** in the canton of Aargau, the **Research Institute of Organic Agriculture**, **FiBL** for short, has its headquarters. It was founded in **1973** and is among the leading institutes for organic farming worldwide. Today it has sites in several countries.

gewusst: A single ladybird larva can eat hundreds of aphids during its development.
Standard fruit trees can live for many decades and shape the landscape in many places in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The pineapple is a sweet, juicy fruit from warm countries. It originally comes from South America. With its scaly skin and its green crown of leaves, it looks very special.
wichtigste: The pineapple comes from **South America**.
It is a **multiple fruit** made of many berries grown together.
It takes **more than a year** before a plant bears a fruit.
A new plant can grow from the **crown of leaves**.
Fresh pineapple contains **bromelain**, which breaks down protein.
In German it is called **“Ananas”**, in English **“pineapple”**.

abschnitte.text: The pineapple comes from **South America**. The people there had been growing it for a long time. **Christopher Columbus** got to know it on his travels and brought news of it to Europe. Later it was planted in many warm countries. In the 20th century, **Hawaii** was famous for its huge pineapple fields. Today most pineapple is grown in other countries.

A pineapple is not really a single fruit. It is a **multiple fruit**. Many small flowers produce berries that **grow together** into one large fruit. The scales on the skin show where the individual flowers sat. Each plant usually produces only one large fruit at a time, and it takes **more than a year** for it to ripen.

Fresh pineapple sometimes tingles on the tongue. This is because of a substance called **bromelain**. It breaks down **protein** and can therefore irritate the tongue. In tinned pineapple, the substance is usually inactive because of the heating. That is why it does not tingle.

You can do an experiment with the **crown of leaves** of a pineapple. You twist it off and let it dry out a little. Then you put it in soil. The crown can grow **roots**, and a new pineapple plant grows. But it needs plenty of warmth, light and patience before it bears a fruit.

gewusst: The German word “Ananas” and the English word “pineapple” both describe the same fruit. “Pineapple” originally meant pine cone, because the fruit reminded people of one.
The pineapple belongs to the bromeliad family. Many of its relatives grow on trees in the rainforest.

teile.einleitung: Biodiversity promotion areas are areas on farms that serve mainly nature. There plants and animals find habitat. In Switzerland they are part of the rules that farmers must meet to receive direct payments.
wichtigste: For direct payments a farm needs proof of ecological performance.
Most farms must have at least 7 percent of their farmland as biodiversity promotion area.
Extensively used meadows may not be fertilised.
In the valley area they may be mown from 15 June at the earliest.
High-stem field fruit trees also count.
Quality level II requires especially many indicator plants.
In the past these areas were called ecological compensation areas.

abschnitte.text: Swiss farmers receive **direct payments** from the Confederation. For this they must provide **proof of ecological performance**. Part of this is that most farms must declare at least **7 percent** of their agricultural land as biodiversity promotion area. In the past these areas were called **ecological compensation areas**.

Often these are **extensively used meadows**. Extensive means that they are used little. They may not be fertilised. In the valley area they may be mown from **15 June** at the earliest. This way many flowers can bloom and form seeds, and insects find food.

Biodiversity promotion areas include not only meadows. **High-stem field fruit trees**, hedges and field copses also count. On arable land there is the **flower fallow**: there native wild herbs are sown that flower for several years. Such areas offer shelter to birds, insects and small mammals.

There are different levels. For **quality level II** an area must show especially many **indicator plants**, that is, plants that point to valuable habitats. For this there are higher payments. In **networking projects** areas are laid out so that they link habitats. This way animals can move from one place to another.

gewusst: High-stem fruit trees shape the landscape in many parts of Switzerland.
On a species-rich meadow many different plant species can grow.

teile.einleitung: Stoneworts are green algae that grow on the bed of clear lakes and ponds. With their whorled side branches they look like little candelabras. They are regarded as a sign of clean water.
wichtigste: Stoneworts owe their German name, “Armleuchteralgen”, which means candelabra algae, to their whorled side branches.
Important genera are Chara and Nitella.
The shoot is divided into nodes and long internodes.
They are anchored in the bed with thread-like rhizoids.
Many Chara species deposit lime and feel rough.
If they return to a lake, the water quality has improved.

abschnitte.text: Stoneworts are **green algae**. On their shoot the side branches stand in **whorls**, that is, in a circle at the same height. This is reminiscent of a **candelabra** with many arms. Well-known genera are **Chara** and **Nitella**. Stoneworts are close relatives of land plants and often grow up to half a metre long or longer.

The shoot is divided into **nodes** and long sections in between, the **internodes**. The side branches grow at the nodes. The algae have no roots. They are anchored in the bed with thread-like **rhizoids**. Many species of the genus **Chara** deposit **lime** on their surface. That is why they feel **rough and brittle**.

The internodes often consist of a single, very long cell that can reach several centimetres. In these **giant cells** you can see well under the microscope how the inside of the cell moves. This movement is called **cytoplasmic streaming**. Researchers also study **electrical signals** that travel through the cell in stoneworts. In this way the algae help us to understand processes in plant cells in general.

Most stoneworts need **clear, nutrient-poor water**. If a lake is over-fertilised, the water becomes cloudy with algal blooms, and the stoneworts disappear. If they return later, this shows an **improvement in water quality**. Dense stands are very useful for a lake: they **bind nutrients**, **stabilise the sediment** and **keep the water clear**. They also give fish and small animals shelter and food.

gewusst: In some lakes, stoneworts form real underwater meadows on the bottom.
The lime that stoneworts deposit can build up on the lake bed over a long time and contribute to so-called lake marl.

teile.einleitung: Bananas are among the most popular fruits in the world. The banana plant looks like a tree, but is a giant herbaceous plant. The bananas in Swiss shops often come from South America.
wichtigste: The banana plant is a herbaceous plant, not a tree.
Its false trunk consists of tightly rolled leaves.
Bananas grow upwards towards the light and so become curved.
Bananas are harvested green and ripen afterwards.
Ecuador exports the most bananas.
Eating bananas no longer have hard seeds.
Plantains are eaten boiled or fried.

abschnitte.text: The **banana plant** can grow several metres tall and looks like a tree. But it has no woody trunk. Its **false trunk** consists of tightly rolled leaves. That is why it counts as a **herbaceous perennial**. Each false trunk bears fruit only once. Then it dies, and new shoots grow from the ground.

Bananas grow in large bunches on a fruit stalk. Young bananas first hang downwards. Then they grow upwards towards the **light**. This gives them their typical curved shape. A bunch can become very heavy and carry many dozens of bananas.

Bananas are harvested **green** and unripe. This way they survive the long journey on the ship. In ripening rooms in Europe they then turn yellow and sweet. Ecuador in South America is the largest **exporter** of bananas. Many bananas in Swiss shops come from South America or Central America.

Wild bananas have many hard **seeds**. In the cultivated eating bananas, only tiny dark dots can still be seen. That is why they are propagated through shoots from the ground. Besides the sweet bananas there are **plantains**. They are starchy and hardly edible raw. In many tropical countries they are a staple food.

gewusst: Botanically speaking, the banana is a berry.
The banana plant is one of the largest herbs in the world, because it forms no wood.

teile.einleitung: Many T-shirts, socks and jeans are made of cotton. The soft fibres grow on a plant in warm countries. Before it becomes a piece of clothing, many steps are needed.
wichtigste: From cotton, fabrics are made for T-shirts, socks and bed linen.
The white fibres sit in burst-open capsules on the seeds.
Cotton needs a lot of warmth, sun and water.
India and China are among the biggest producers.
The fibres are spun into yarn.
Most jeans are made of denim, a cotton fabric.

abschnitte.text: **Cotton** is a plant that grows as a shrub. After flowering it forms **capsules**. When they are ripe, they burst open. Then white, soft **fibres** swell out. These fibres sit on the seeds of the plant and look like little balls of cotton wool.

Cotton needs a lot of **warmth** and sun. That is why it is grown in warm countries. **India** and **China** are among the countries that grow the most cotton. In Switzerland no cotton grows in fields. Growing it needs a great deal of **water**, and the fields often have to be irrigated.

After the harvest, the fibres are separated from the seeds and cleaned. Then they are **spun** into a thread, the **yarn**. From the yarn, fabrics are woven or knitted. In the past there were also many spinning and weaving mills in eastern Switzerland that processed cotton.

From cotton, many clothes are made, for example **T-shirts**, socks and bed linen. Cotton is soft, pleasant on the skin and absorbs moisture well. Most **jeans** are sewn from **denim**. This is a strong cotton fabric, usually dyed blue.

gewusst: For a single cotton T-shirt, growing the plant often needs several thousand litres of water.
There is organic cotton, which is grown without chemical sprays.

teile.einleitung: Lycophytes are a very old group of vascular plants. Today they are mostly small, but about 300 million years ago their tree-high relatives formed whole forests, from which coal was formed.
wichtigste: The class is called Lycopodiopsida in science.
Typical are microphylls, small leaves with only one leaf vein.
Lycophytes are the sister group of all other living vascular plants.
The scale tree (Lepidodendron) shaped the coal forests of the Carboniferous.
The group includes clubmoss, spikemoss (Selaginella) and quillwort (Isoetes).
The name Lycopodium literally means wolf’s foot.

abschnitte.titel: A plant class of its own
abschnitte.text: The lycophytes form the class **Lycopodiopsida**. They have conducting tissue for water and nutrients and therefore belong to the **vascular plants**. Typical are their small leaves, the **microphylls**. Each of these little leaves has only a **single leaf vein**. In the family tree, the lycophytes are the **sister group of all other vascular plants**: so they split off from the ferns and seed plants very early.

In the geological period called the **Carboniferous**, about 300 million years ago, huge lycophytes grew. The best known is the **scale tree** (Lepidodendron). It grew many metres tall, and its bark showed a pattern like scales. Together with seal trees and horsetails it formed swampy forests. From the dead plants, **coal** formed over time.

Today three groups mainly live. The **clubmosses** in the narrower sense, such as the stag’s-horn clubmoss, creep over the ground. The **spikemoss** (Selaginella) forms two kinds of spores: small **microspores** and large **megaspores**. The **quillwort** (Isoetes) grows in lakes and swamps and looks like a tuft of rushes. Quillworts also occur in Swiss mountain lakes.

From a spore a small **prothallus** grows first, also called a **gametophyte**. In the stag’s-horn clubmoss it lives **underground** and has no chlorophyll. It is fed by **fungi** with which it lives closely together. Many years can pass before a new plant grows from it. That is why clubmosses spread only very slowly.

gewusst: The genus name Lycopodium comes from Greek and means wolf’s foot, probably because of the furry shoot tips.
Petrified pieces of bark of the scale tree are often found in coal mines.

teile.einleitung: A biotope is the habitat of a community of plants and animals. It can be a pond, a bog, a hedge or a piece of forest. Together with the living things, the biotope forms an ecosystem.
wichtigste: A biotope is the habitat of a living community.
The word is made up of “bios” for life and “topos” for place.
A pond is an example of a biotope.
A floodplain is the habitat along a river that is regularly flooded.
Stepping-stone biotopes link larger habitats.
Raised bogs are among the biotopes of national importance.
Deadwood is a habitat for beetles, fungi and woodpeckers.

abschnitte.text: The word **biotope** comes from Greek: “bios” means life, “topos” means **place**. A biotope is therefore the habitat of a **living community**. The living community itself is called a **biocoenosis**. The biotope includes the non-living conditions, for example in a pond the **water temperature**, the light and the soil. Biotope and living community together form an **ecosystem**.

A **pond** is a typical biotope. Further examples are bogs, hedges, dry meadows or **floodplains**. A floodplain is the habitat along a river that is regularly flooded. In a pond for amphibians you do not put fish, because **fish eat spawn and tadpoles**. This way frogs, toads and newts can develop well.

Many habitats are cut up by roads, settlements and fields. A **stepping-stone biotope** is a small habitat that links larger habitats. Animals can move from one stepping stone to the next, like over stones in a stream. These can be a garden pond, a hedge or a flower meadow.

The Confederation keeps inventories of **biotopes of national importance**. These include **raised bogs**, fens, floodplains, amphibian spawning sites and dry meadows and dry pastures. These areas are specially protected. In the forest too, valuable habitats arise: **deadwood** is deliberately left lying. It is a habitat for beetles, fungi and woodpeckers.

gewusst: Raised bogs grow extremely slowly, often only about one millimetre a year.
Even a small garden pond can attract dragonflies and newts.

teile.einleitung: The Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, or APG for short, is an international team of researchers. It arranges all flowering plants in a shared system based on comparisons of DNA. This system has greatly changed the study of plants.
wichtigste: APG stands for **Angiosperm Phylogeny Group**.
The first version of the system appeared in **1998**.
The version **APG IV** appeared in **2016** and recognises 64 orders and 416 families.
The system is based on **comparisons of DNA sequences**.
It only accepts **monophyletic groups**.
**Amborella trichopoda** is regarded as the sister group of all other flowering plants.

abschnitte.text: In the past, plants were arranged mainly by their **shape**, for example by flowers and leaves. But plants that look similar are not always closely related. The **APG** therefore arranges the families according to **molecular analyses of relationships**, that is, by comparing DNA sequences. The first version, **APG I**, appeared in **1998**. It was followed by APG II (2003), APG III (2009) and **APG IV (2016)**. It was the first widely supported system based on DNA.

The APG system only accepts **monophyletic** groups. Such a group includes one ancestor and **all** of its descendants. That is why old groups were dropped, for example the **dicotyledons** in the old sense. The version APG IV appeared in the Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society. It recognises **64 orders** and **416 families**.

abschnitte.titel: The root of the family tree
abschnitte.text: Right at the base of the flowering plants stands **Amborella trichopoda**, a shrub from **New Caledonia**. It is the only species in its order. Its line split off first from all other flowering plants. After that, the **Nymphaeales**, which include the water lilies, and the **Austrobaileyales** branch off. Together with the Amborellales they form the so-called **“ANA grade”**.

Many well-known plants belong to two large groups: the **rosids** and the **asterids**. The **pea** belongs to the Fabales, an order of the rosids. The **sunflower** belongs to the Asterales, the **potato** to the Solanales. Both orders count as asterids. Tomato, lavender and coffee are also asterids.

gewusst: Water lilies belong to the oldest lines of flowering plants.
Many identification guides and botanical gardens have rearranged their order according to the APG system.

teile.einleitung: Bioindicators are living things from which you can read the state of the environment. Their occurrence or condition reveals whether air, water or soil are clean or polluted. Especially well known are lichens as indicators of air quality.
wichtigste: Bioindicators show environmental conditions through their occurrence or condition.
Many lichens react sensitively to sulphur dioxide.
Lichens take up water and substances over their whole surface.
Fruticose lichens are especially sensitive.
The yellow wall lichen spreads when there is a lot of nitrogen in the air.
In lichen mapping, lichens on tree bark are recorded.
The saprobic system rates water quality using organisms.

abschnitte.text: A **bioindicator** is a living thing whose occurrence or condition shows environmental conditions. Some species need clean air or clean water. If they are missing, that is a warning sign. Other species like certain substances and spread when a lot of them is present. Bioindicators show the effect of pollution over a longer time.

**Lichens** are a partnership of fungus and alga. They have no roots and take up water and substances over their whole surface. That is why they react sensitively to pollutants in the air, especially to **sulphur dioxide**. **Fruticose lichens** are considered especially sensitive. In the past there were areas in towns with almost no lichens. They were called **lichen deserts**.

In **lichen mapping** you record which lichens grow on tree bark. From this you can draw conclusions about the air quality. The **yellow wall lichen** indicates a lot of nitrogen in the air, for example from agriculture and traffic. In many Swiss towns more lichens grow again today than 50 years ago. The reason: the exhaust gases from heating systems and factories have become cleaner.

In waters too there are bioindicators. The **saprobic system** rates water quality using organisms that tolerate different amounts of organic pollution. Some insect larvae live only in clean, oxygen-rich water. Other animals cope even with polluted water. Depending on which animals you find, you can judge the water quality.

gewusst: On land, the stinging nettle indicates nitrogen-rich soils.
Lichens grow very slowly, some only a few millimetres a year.

teile.einleitung: A brushwood pile looks unremarkable, but it is a valuable habitat. Between the piled-up branches, many animals find shelter, food and a place to spend the winter. That is why nature conservationists encourage brushwood piles in gardens, at the edges of forests and in farming.
wichtigste: A brushwood pile consists of piled-up branches and twigs.
Hedgehogs like to hibernate in brushwood piles.
You should not simply set fire to a brushwood pile, because animals may be sleeping in it.
The wren likes to build its nest in dense brushwood.
The slow worm likes to hide under brushwood piles.
Fungi and insects break down the wood over the years.

abschnitte.titel: More than a pile of wood
abschnitte.text: A **brushwood pile** consists of **piled-up branches and twigs**, of the kind that arise when hedges and trees are cut. Between the branches many **hollow spaces** form. There it is sheltered, a little warmer in winter and shady in summer. A good pile is one that is big enough and may stay for a long time. At the bottom you can lay thicker branches, and at the top finer twigs.

The **hedgehog** likes to use brushwood piles as a refuge and **hibernates** in them. The **slow worm**, a legless lizard, likes to hide under the branches. Lizards, toads, mice and many beetles also find shelter here. The **wren** is a small brown bird with a **cocked tail**. It likes to build its nest in **dense brushwood**.

In time the wood becomes rotten. **Fungi and insects** break it down over the years. This produces valuable soil. Many beetle larvae and wild bees live in dead wood. To keep the habitat going, new branches are laid on top again and again.

In farming, brushwood piles are made specially for **weasels**, for example for the stoat. Weasels hunt mice and need safe hiding places along hedges and field edges. Often the brushwood pile is combined with a **nesting chamber made of wood**. It is a **protected place for the young**. Several such piles in a row help the weasels to move safely through the landscape.

abschnitte.titel: Do not simply set it alight
abschnitte.text: Sometimes brushwood piles are burnt, for example for a fire on 1 August. This is dangerous for animals, because **hedgehogs and other animals can sleep in them**. It is better to pile up the wood for a fire only shortly beforehand. An old brushwood pile should be moved over before it is lit. A related idea is the **Benjes hedge**: it is made of **loosely piled branches**, in which shrubs sprout in time.

gewusst: The Benjes hedge is named after the German landscape gardener Hermann Benjes.
Birds carry seeds into a Benjes hedge, and new shrubs grow from these seeds in time.

teile.einleitung: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is a bacterium that lives in the soil. It can build its own genes into plant cells and so trigger growths. Because it does this naturally, it is called a “natural genetic engineer”.
wichtigste: Agrobacterium tumefaciens builds its own genes into plants.
For this it uses the Ti plasmid.
A section called T-DNA is transferred.
The vir genes control the transfer.
Infected cells form opines, which serve the bacterium as food.
In 1983, one of the first genetic modifications succeeded with tobacco.

abschnitte.text: **Agrobacterium tumefaciens** lives in the soil. It enters a plant through **wounds** at the root collar or on the trunk. Wounded tissue gives off substances such as **acetosyringone**. These attract the bacterium. At the infected spot a growth later develops, called a **crown gall**. In nature the bacterium infects mainly **dicotyledonous plants** such as fruit trees, grapevines or roses.

Besides their main genetic material, bacteria often have small rings of DNA, the **plasmids**. Agrobacterium has the **Ti plasmid**. Ti stands for “tumour-inducing”. On this plasmid lies a section, the **T-DNA** (transfer DNA). It is built into the genetic material of the plant cell. The **vir genes**, also called virulence genes, control this process. They are switched on by the substances from wounded tissue. Their proteins cut the T-DNA out and smuggle it into the plant cell.

abschnitte.titel: A food source of its own
abschnitte.text: The transferred genes make the plant cells grow strongly. In addition, the cells make **opines**. These are substances that almost only Agrobacterium can use. In this way the bacterium creates its own **food source**, which the plant produces for it.

Researchers use exactly this mechanism. They remove the genes that trigger growths from the T-DNA and insert **desired genes**. The bacterium then builds these into the plant. In **1983**, one of the first genetic modifications of a plant succeeded this way with **tobacco**. Tobacco is easy to keep in the laboratory and can be grown into whole plants from single cells. With cereals such as maize or rice, the method succeeded only later with improved techniques. There the **gene gun** was often used for a long time.

gewusst: The word tumefaciens comes from Latin and means roughly “producing swelling”.
Long before humans invented genetic engineering, this bacterium was already transferring genes between different living things.

teile.einleitung: We speak of a biological invasion when a non-native species gets a foothold in a new area and spreads strongly. Often humans brought the species deliberately or by accident. Invasive species can seriously endanger native plants and animals.
wichtigste: A biological invasion occurs when a non-native species establishes itself and spreads strongly.
Charles Elton founded invasion biology in 1958.
The cane toad was introduced to Australia in 1935 and itself became a plague.
The Nile perch in Lake Victoria led to the extinction of many cichlid species.
Introduced crayfish transmit crayfish plague to the noble crayfish.
Often a species spreads only after a long lag phase.
According to IPBES, invasive species were involved in around 60 percent of documented extinctions.

abschnitte.text: The British ecologist **Charles Elton** published the book “The Ecology of Invasions by Animals and Plants” in 1958. With it he founded **invasion biology**. Not every introduced species becomes a problem. Many disappear again or stay rare. Often there is also a long **lag phase**: for decades the species hardly spreads, then suddenly very strongly.

In 1859 the settler **Thomas Austin** released wild rabbits in Australia. They multiplied rapidly and ate large stretches of land bare. In 1935 the **cane toad** was introduced to fight beetles in sugar cane. It is poisonous and spread over large parts of the country. Many native animals that eat it die from it.

In **Lake Victoria** in Africa the **Nile perch** was introduced. As a result many endemic cichlid species died out that existed only there. On the Pacific island of **Guam** the introduced **brown tree snake** wiped out most native forest birds. Islands are especially vulnerable, because their animals often know no enemies.

In Switzerland too there are invasive species. North American crayfish such as the **signal crayfish** transmit **crayfish plague**. They themselves are mostly resistant, but the native **noble crayfish** dies of it. The world biodiversity council **IPBES** concluded in 2023 that invasive species were involved in around 60 percent of documented extinctions.

gewusst: The brown tree snake probably came to Guam with ships or aircraft.
Trade and travel have greatly speeded up the spread of species.

teile.einleitung: A **flowerpot** is the home of a houseplant or balcony plant. It looks simple, but is cleverly built. With the right pot and a little care, the plant stays healthy.
wichtigste: The hole in the bottom of the pot lets excess water drain away.
The saucer catches the draining water.
Classic red-brown flowerpots are made of fired clay.
Gravel or pot shards at the bottom help the water drain well.
If a plant gets too big, you repot it into a bigger pot.

abschnitte.text: Almost every flowerpot has a **hole** at the bottom. Through this hole **excess water can drain away**. This way the roots do not stand in the wet all the time. This is important, because roots also need **air**. If they stand in water for a long time, they can rot. At the very bottom people often put a layer of **gravel** or **pot shards**, so that the water drains well.

Under the pot you put a **saucer**. It catches the water that runs out at the bottom. This way the **windowsill** and the floor stay dry. If water stays in the saucer for a long time after watering, you should empty it. Otherwise the roots are standing in water again after all.

The well-known **red-brown** flowerpots are made of **fired clay**. Clay lets some air and moisture through, so the soil in it dries faster. Pots made of **plastic** are lighter and hold the water longer. There are also pots made of ceramic, wood or metal.

Plants grow, and at some point the pot becomes too small. Then the roots often already grow out of the hole. Now you put the plant into a **bigger pot** with **fresh soil**. This is called **repotting**. The best time for it is usually spring, when the plants begin to grow vigorously.

gewusst: Clay pots have been made for thousands of years, and the ancient Egyptians also grew plants in vessels of clay.
A clay pot that has soaked up water becomes noticeably heavier than a dry one.

teile.einleitung: We call plants with beautiful, often coloured blossoms flowers, such as rose, tulip or edelweiss. They grow on meadows, in forests, in the mountains and in our gardens. Flowers delight people, and at the same time they are important food for bees and other insects.
wichtigste: A flower needs water, light and soil with nutrients, or it wilts.
The snowdrop often peeks out of the snow already in late winter.
The rose often has sharp thorns on its stem.
The edelweiss is a white, felty mountain flower and very well known in Switzerland.
Tulips grow again every spring from a bulb.
With colours and scent, flowers attract insects that pollinate them.
Many wild flowers in Switzerland are rare and protected.

abschnitte.text: In everyday speech, a flower is a plant with a striking **blossom**. A flower usually has roots, a stem, leaves and one or more blossoms. The blossom is the part from which seeds later arise. Experts therefore often speak of flowering plants.

Flowers need water, sunlight, air and soil with nutrients. A pot flower that is not watered lets its leaves hang and **wilts**. Too much water also harms, because the roots can then rot. Cut flowers in a vase last longer if you change the water regularly and cut the stems at an angle.

The **snowdrop** often flowers as early as February, sometimes in the middle of the snow. After it come crocuses, daffodils and tulips. Tulips and daffodils grow from a **bulb**, in which the plant stores nutrients over winter. In summer ox-eye daisies, poppies and sunflowers bloom, in autumn asters and autumn crocuses.

The **rose** is regarded as the queen of flowers and has sharp thorns on its stem. There are thousands of kinds of rose in many colours. The tulip originally comes from Central Asia and became so popular in the Netherlands in the 17th century that single bulbs were more expensive than a house. Today the Netherlands is the most important country for the flower trade.

The **edelweiss** is white, feels like felt and grows on limestone rocks in the Alps. The fine felt protects the plant from cold, wind and strong sun. Gentian, alpenrose and black vanilla orchid are also well-known mountain flowers. Many of them are protected, so you should leave them in nature and only photograph them.

With bright colours, scent and sweet **nectar**, flowers attract bees, bumblebees and butterflies. The insects carry pollen from flower to flower and so ensure pollination. A colourful flower meadow is therefore a valuable habitat. Anyone who sows native wild flowers in the garden or on the balcony helps the insects.

begriffe.erklaerung: The coloured part of the flower from which seeds and fruits later arise.
An underground store from which tulips grow anew every year.
When a flower becomes limp and dry because it has too little water.
Sweet juice in the blossom that bees and butterflies drink.

gewusst: In the 17th century in the Netherlands, single tulip bulbs were as expensive as a house.
With its white felt the edelweiss is well protected against cold and strong mountain sun.
The sunflower turns its young buds with the sun during the day.

teile.einleitung: A floodplain forest grows along rivers and is flooded regularly. Such forests are wild, damp and full of life. In Switzerland they have become rare and are now protected.
wichtigste: A floodplain forest is flooded regularly by a river.
In the softwood floodplain close to the water, willows and poplars grow.
Typical of the hardwood floodplain are ash, oak and elm.
Around 90 per cent of Swiss floodplains have disappeared over time.
Today floodplains cover only about 0.5 per cent of the country’s area.
Since 1992 there has been a federal inventory of floodplains of national importance.

abschnitte.text: A **floodplain forest** grows near a river and is **flooded regularly**. The trees then stand in water for a time. The soil is often damp and rich in nutrients, which the flood brings with it. Only trees that can withstand flooding can grow here. Climbers such as **traveller’s joy** and **hop** climb up the trunks.

Close to the water lies the **softwood floodplain**. Here mainly **willows** and **poplars** grow. They are flooded often and for long periods. Further from the river and a little higher lies the **hardwood floodplain**. It is **flooded less often**. Typical tree species there are **ash**, **oak** and **elm**.

Floodplains count as especially **species-rich habitats**. The reason: **floods create new habitats again and again**. Besides the forest there are gravel banks, pools, oxbow lakes and swamps. In them live amphibians, dragonflies, fish, birds and many rare plants. Dead wood also stays where it falls and provides food for beetles and fungi.

Floodplain forests are also useful to people. They **take up water** and **slow down floods**. The water spreads over the area and flows on more slowly. The soil also filters the water and tops up the **groundwater**. Many municipalities get their drinking water from such areas.

In the past there were large floodplains along almost all Swiss rivers. Through straightening, dams, power stations and new building land, **around 90 per cent** of them have disappeared. Today floodplains cover only **about 0.5 per cent of the country’s area**. Since **1992** there has been a **federal inventory of floodplains of national importance**, which protects the most valuable areas. In addition, rivers are being restored in many places so that floodplain forests can form again.

gewusst: Although floodplains cover only a tiny part of Switzerland, a large part of all native species occur there.
The seeds of willows and poplars fly away on white hairs and like to sprout on fresh gravel.

teile.einleitung: Because of climate change, the habitats of many species are shifting. Some species cannot follow fast enough. In assisted migration, humans bring them in a targeted way to areas that will suit them in future. The idea is controversial.
wichtigste: Assisted migration is the targeted relocation of species to areas that will suit them climatically in future.
The term means a migration that is helped along.
The species is brought to places where it did not occur before.
A frequently mentioned risk: the species could become invasive in the new area.
In forestry, seed from warmer origins of the same species is used.
A well-known example is the conifer Torreya taxifolia from Florida.

abschnitte.text: **Assisted migration** means a **migration that is helped along**. It refers to the **targeted relocation** of species to areas that will **suit them climatically in future**. This is a particular issue for species with a **low ability to spread**. They cannot shift their range fast enough when the climate changes. These include many plants and small animals that only cover short distances.

In a classic **reintroduction**, a species is brought back to where it lived before. An example is the ibex in the Swiss Alps. In assisted migration, by contrast, a species is **brought to places where it did not occur before**. This is a bigger intervention in nature. That is why it is much discussed among experts.

**Torreya taxifolia** is a seriously threatened conifer from Florida. In its small natural area, many trees are dying. A **citizens’ group** therefore began planting trees **far to the north** of its previous range. Supporters see in this a chance to save the species. Critics complain that this happened without thorough scientific examination.

abschnitte.titel: In the forest of the future
abschnitte.text: In forestry there is a more cautious form, **assisted population migration**. In it, **seed from warmer origins of the same species** is used, but within its range. An example would be beeches from a drier, warmer region that are planted further north. In Switzerland, too, researchers are testing in trial plantings which tree species and origins cope with a warmer climate.

A frequently mentioned risk is that the relocated species becomes **invasive** in the new area and pushes out native species. Diseases and pests could also be brought along. Many experts therefore demand clear conditions. The species should be **seriously threatened without help**, and the **risk in the target area** should be thoroughly **examined** beforehand. Others think it is more important to link habitats so that species can migrate by themselves.

gewusst: The citizens’ group that is bringing Torreya taxifolia northwards calls itself the “Torreya Guardians”.
Even today, tree species that cope better with heat and drought than the previous ones are sometimes planted in forests.

teile.einleitung: Albedo is the reflectivity of a surface for sunlight. It states how much light a surface throws back and how much it absorbs. That is why fresh snow is so dazzlingly bright and black asphalt is so hot in summer.
wichtigste: Albedo means the reflectivity of a surface for sunlight.
The word comes from the Latin albus, which means white.
Light surfaces have a high albedo, dark ones a low one.
Fresh snow throws back the greater part of the sunlight.
The open sea absorbs almost all the light and warms up as a result.
The Earth as a whole throws back about 30 per cent of the sunlight.
Albedo plays an important role for the climate.

abschnitte.text: The **albedo** measures what share of the sunlight a surface throws back. It is given as a number between 0 and 1 or in per cent. An albedo of 0 means that all the light is absorbed, at 1 everything is reflected. The name comes from the Latin word **albus** for white.

**Fresh snow** has a very high albedo and throws back about 80 to 90 per cent of the light. Forests and fields are usually only at 10 to 25 per cent. The open sea is particularly dark and often throws back less than 10 per cent. What is not thrown back is **absorbed** and turned into heat.

In summer a black T-shirt in the sun becomes much hotter than a white one. That is why people in hot countries often wear light clothing and paint houses white. On ski slopes you need sunglasses because the snow dazzles so strongly. Light roofs in cities can also help to reduce heat in summer.

Altogether the Earth throws back about 30 per cent of the sunlight into space, mainly through clouds, ice and snow. When ice melts, dark ground or dark sea comes to light. These surfaces take up more heat, so that even more ice melts. This self-reinforcing cycle is called the **ice-albedo feedback**.

When snow on glaciers melts away early in the year, the grey ice underneath is exposed. This ice has a lower albedo and therefore melts faster. On the **Rhone Glacier**, parts are therefore covered in summer with white **fleece blankets**. The blankets throw back the sunlight and slow the melting at that spot.

Planets and moons also have an albedo, which astronomers measure. The **Moon** looks bright at night but has an albedo of only about 0.12, and its rock is actually dark grey. Venus, with its dense white clouds, is among the brightest planets. From the albedo, researchers can infer what the surface of a celestial body is made of.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how strongly a surface throws back light.
The taking up of light, which turns into heat in the process.
A process that reinforces or weakens itself.
The throwing back of light at a surface.

gewusst: The Moon is about as dark as worn asphalt and still shines brightly in the night sky.
Saharan dust on Swiss glaciers makes the snow darker and makes it melt faster.

teile.einleitung: Albert Frey-Wyssling was a Swiss botanist and professor at ETH Zurich. He investigated how plant cells are built on the very smallest scale, far finer than can be seen with an ordinary microscope.
wichtigste: Frey-Wyssling was professor of plant physiology at **ETH Zurich**.
From 1957 to 1961 he was **rector** of ETH Zurich.
He investigated the fine structure of cells below the limit of the light microscope.
He studied above all the cell wall made of **cellulose microfibrils**.
He made early use of polarization microscopy and later of the electron microscope.
In his youth he did research in Sumatra on **rubber**.

abschnitte.text: After his studies, Frey-Wyssling worked for some years at an experimental station for **rubber** in Medan on the island of Sumatra. Rubber is the raw material for gum and comes from the milky sap of certain trees. In 1932 he returned to ETH Zurich. There he then taught and did research for decades.

A light microscope can no longer show very small things clearly. Frey-Wyssling wanted to know how the cell is built **below this limit**. For this he used **polarization microscopy**: ordered molecules change polarized light in a typical way. From this he concluded how the molecules are aligned. Later, as one of the first botanists, he used the **electron microscope**, which works with beams of electrons instead of light and shows much finer structures.

He studied the wall of plant cells especially thoroughly. It consists of long cellulose molecules that join together into fine threads, the **microfibrils**. These lie embedded in a ground mass. How the threads are aligned determines the **strength** of the cell wall. With this work Frey-Wyssling became a pioneer of ultrastructure research and of cell biology.

gewusst: Besides his research, as rector from 1957 to 1961, Frey-Wyssling led the whole of ETH Zurich.
Cellulose from plants is also found in paper and cotton.

teile.einleitung: Alpine farming means that animals are kept on high mountain pastures in summer. There the milk is often made into cheese straight away. In Switzerland, alpine farming has a tradition going back centuries, with many customs.
wichtigste: On the alp the animals eat mountain grass and **alpine herbs**.
Cheese is made in the **dairy hut**, where the alp staff often live too.
The milk is heated in a large **copper cauldron**.
Many alps belong to **alp cooperatives**, corporations or municipalities.
In the past, **alp pigs** were fed with the whey.
Customs include the **alp blessing** and the **Chästeilet** in the Justistal.

abschnitte.text: In summer, farmers take their animals up to the alp. There they graze on the natural **mountain meadows**, which are rich in herbs and flowers. This time is called **summering**. Meanwhile the grass in the valley can be mown and stored as hay for the winter. Many alps do not belong to a single farmer, but to **alp cooperatives**, corporations or municipalities. The members may summer their animals there and share the work.

abschnitte.titel: Making cheese in the dairy hut
abschnitte.text: The most important building on the alp is the **dairy hut**. In it stand the **cheese cauldron** and the cheese press. The cauldron is a large kettle, often made of **copper**, which hangs over the fire. The milk is warmed in it and curdled with **rennet**. A lot of **whey** is left over when cheese is made. In the past, **pigs** were fattened with it on many alps, so nothing was wasted.

Bells help the herdsman to find the animals on the wide pasture. One special bell is the **treichel**. It is forged from sheet metal and has a deep sound. Treichel bells are hung on cows or carried in parades. When the animals go up to the alp and come down again, you can hear their sound from far away.

On some alps the herdsman speaks or sings the **alp blessing** in the evening, also called the **Betruf**. He calls it out across the alp through a wooden milk funnel. The blessing is meant to protect animals and people during the night. It is found mainly in Catholic alpine regions. In the **Justistal** in the canton of Bern, the **Chästeilet** takes place in autumn: the summer’s cheese is shared out fairly among the farmers, according to how much milk their cows gave.

gewusst: The Chästeilet in the Justistal attracts many spectators every year.
Alpine cheese tastes a little different from alp to alp, because the cows eat different herbs everywhere.

teile.einleitung: Arnica is a bright yellow mountain flower from the daisy family. It grows on poor meadows and is known as a medicinal plant. But you must not eat it, because it is poisonous.
wichtigste: Arnica has yellow to orange flowers.
It belongs to the daisy family.
Another name is Bergwohlverleih.
The leaves on the stem grow in opposite pairs.
It flowers in summer.
Arnica ointments are used externally for bruises.
Arnica cannot stand a lot of fertiliser on the meadow.

abschnitte.text: **Arnica** (Arnica montana) has large, **yellow to orange** flower heads. As in all **members of the daisy family**, a flower head is made up of many small individual flowers. At ground level it forms a rosette of leaves. On the stem the leaves stand **in opposite pairs**. This is how you can tell it apart from similar yellow flowers.

Arnica grows on **poor meadows and pastures**, especially in the mountains. In Switzerland it is found mainly in the Jura and the Alps. It prefers rather acidic, nutrient-poor soils. It cannot stand **a lot of fertiliser** at all, because then other plants get stronger and push it out. Because such meadows have become rarer, arnica too has become rarer in many places.

Arnica **flowers in summer**, usually from June to August. Then its flowers shine far across the mountain meadows. Many insects such as bees and butterflies visit it. Later small fruits with a crown of hairs form, which the wind carries away.

abschnitte.titel: A medicinal plant for the skin
abschnitte.text: Arnica is an old **medicinal plant**. Its old name **Bergwohlverleih** shows how much good people expected of it. Ointments, gels and tinctures with arnica are used **externally**, for example for **bruises**, contusions and sprains. You should not put it on open wounds. Some people react sensitively to it on the skin.

Arnica is **poisonous** if you eat it or drink it as tea. It can cause stomach pain and heart problems. So the rule is: use it only externally, and only ready-made products from a pharmacy or chemist. In many areas wild arnica is also **protected** and must not be picked.

gewusst: For medicines, arnica is nowadays often grown in fields, so that the wild populations are spared.
The name Arnica montana means that the plant grows in the mountains: montana means “in the mountains”.

teile.einleitung: Bees are busy insects that carry pollen from flower to flower. The best known is the honeybee, which lives in large colonies and makes honey. Without bees there would be much less fruit, vegetables and flowers.
wichtigste: Bees are insects with six legs and four wings.
They collect nectar and pollen in the flowers.
In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower and pollinate the plants.
The honeybee lives in a colony with a queen, many workers and drones.
Honeybees make honey from nectar.
With a dance, bees show each other where there is food.
In Switzerland there are around 600 species of wild bee.

abschnitte.text: Bees are **insects**: they have six legs, four transparent wings and a body made of head, thorax and abdomen. Their body is covered with fine hairs on which pollen sticks. Honeybees collect the pollen in small baskets on their hind legs. Female bees have a **sting** with which they defend themselves.

A **honeybee** lives in a colony that in summer can number several tens of thousands of animals. There is only one **queen**, who lays all the eggs, in summer up to 2000 a day. The **workers** clean, feed, build combs, guard the hive and collect food. The male bees are called **drones**, they do not sting and are there only for mating with a young queen.

Bees suck sweet **nectar** from the flowers with their tongue. In the hive they pass it on to other bees, who remove water from it and add substances from their body. Then they store it in six-sided cells of wax, the **combs**. For a single jar of honey, bees have to visit millions of flowers.

When a bee has found good food, it performs a **waggle dance** in the hive. The direction and duration of the dance tell the other bees in which direction and how far away the flowers are. This bee language was decoded by the Austrian researcher **Karl von Frisch**. For this he received the Nobel Prize in 1973.

While collecting, bees carry **pollen** from flower to flower and so pollinate them. Many fruit trees such as apple, cherry and pear need this help to bear fruit. Rapeseed, strawberries and many wild flowers also benefit. Besides the honeybee, bumblebees and wild bees are just as important here.

In Switzerland many beekeepers keep honeybees, often as a hobby. Besides the honeybee, around 600 species of **wild bee** live here, which mostly live alone and make no honey. Bees are threatened by a lack of flower meadows, pesticides and the **varroa mite**, a parasite from Asia. Flowering gardens, meadows and balconies help them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who keeps honeybees and harvests honey.
A structure of many six-sided wax cells in the beehive.
A male honeybee.
A small parasite that weakens honeybees.
Sweet juice in flowers.

gewusst: A honeybee beats its wings about 200 times per second, which is where the buzzing comes from.
A worker lives in summer for only about five to six weeks.
Bees can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to us.

teile.einleitung: Biomass is the mass of all living things in an area. The term is used in ecology, but also in energy supply. There it means wood, plants and organic waste from which energy is obtained.
wichtigste: In ecology, biomass is the mass of living things in an area.
Plants make up the largest part of the Earth’s biomass.
Among animals, arthropods have the largest biomass.
Biomass is often measured as dry mass.
On land, plant biomass is especially large in the tropical rainforest.
From one trophic level to the next, biomass usually decreases.
Wood chips and biogas are energy from biomass.

abschnitte.text: In ecology, **biomass** is the mass of all living things in an area. Because the **water content** of living things can vary greatly, it is often measured as **dry mass**. For this a sample is dried until no water is left in it. This way different areas can be compared well.
