The largest part of the Earth’s biomass is made up of **plants**, above all the trees with their wood. In second place come the bacteria. Animals make up only a small part. Among them, **arthropods** have the largest biomass. They include insects, spiders and crustaceans.

In an ecosystem there are different **trophic levels**, that is, steps of the food chain. At the bottom are the plants, above them the plant eaters, then the meat eaters. From step to step **biomass usually decreases**. One reason is that at every step a lot of energy is used for movement and warmth. That is why there are far fewer foxes than mice.

Biomass can also supply energy. **Wood chips** are burned in heating systems. In **biogas plants**, **biogas** is produced from liquid manure and green waste. The energy originally comes from the sun, which plants store through photosynthesis. On land, plant biomass per area is especially large in the **tropical rainforest**.

gewusst: The biomass of all humans is much smaller than that of plants.
The biomass of livestock today is greater than that of all wild mammals together.

teile.einleitung: Abiotic factors are the non-living conditions in a habitat. They include light, temperature, water, wind and the properties of the soil. They help to decide which plants and animals can live somewhere.
wichtigste: “Abiotic” means “non-living”.
Examples are light, temperature, water and the pH value of the soil.
In a lake, light decreases sharply with depth.
South-facing slopes in the Alps are sunnier and warmer than north-facing ones.
Temperature determines the position of the tree line.
Warm water contains less oxygen.

abschnitte.text: The prefix “a” means “not”, and the Greek word “bios” means “life”. **Abiotic factors** are therefore **non-living environmental factors**. They include **light**, **temperature**, **water**, wind and the properties of the soil. One example is the **pH value**, which shows how acidic or alkaline the soil is. The opposite are **biotic factors**, that is, influences from other living things such as predators or competitors.

Plants need light for **photosynthesis**. In a lake, the water absorbs sunlight. That is why light decreases sharply with **depth**, and algae and water plants grow only in the upper layers. In a **beech wood**, the **wood anemone** blooms already in early spring. Then the beeches have no leaves yet, and a lot of light reaches the ground. Later it becomes dark on the forest floor.

In the Northern Hemisphere the sun stands in the south at midday. The **south-facing slopes** of an Alpine valley therefore receive more sunshine. They are warmer and drier than **north-facing slopes**, and different plants grow there. The higher you climb, the cooler it becomes. Above a certain height the growing season is too short and too cold for trees. This is how the **tree line** arises.

Less **oxygen** can dissolve in **warm water** than in cold. For fish such as the **grayling**, which love cool water, this becomes dangerous. In the hot summer of **2018**, many grayling therefore died in the Rhine near **Schaffhausen**. A lack of water is also an abiotic factor. **Cacti** have adapted to it: they store water in their thick stems, and their leaves have turned into spines.

gewusst: Just a few metres below the surface of a lake it can be much darker and cooler than at the top.
Animals too depend on abiotic factors: many insects only become active when it is warm enough.

teile.einleitung: Every animal and plant species lives in a particular area, its range. When the climate warms, these areas shift: towards the poles and upwards in height. This range shift can also be observed in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: The range is the area where a species is found.
With warming, many ranges shift towards the poles and to greater heights.
In the mountains it gets about 0.65 °C cooler for every 100 metres of height.
On many European mountain summits, more plant species grow today than before.
The alpine tree line is slowly rising in many places.
Fragmented habitats make it harder for species to follow their climate.

abschnitte.text: The **range** is the area where a species occurs naturally. Its limits often depend on the climate, for example on how cold the winters or how dry the summers are. When it gets warmer, the suitable zone shifts. Many species then move **towards the poles**, in Europe that means north, or **to greater heights**. At the warm edge of their range, on the other hand, they can disappear.

In the mountains the temperature falls by about **0.65 °C per 100 metres of height**. If it gets 1.3 °C warmer, a certain temperature zone therefore lies about **200 metres** higher than before. Long-term observations on European **mountain summits** show that the **number of plant species is increasing** there, because species move up from below. The **tree line** is also slowly rising in many places.

For species that already live right at the top, things get tight. They are pushed higher and higher until **no habitat is left** above them. Experts therefore speak of an **“escalator to extinction”**. Affected are, for example, specialised alpine plants and animals that need cold. The smaller a mountain, the sooner the summit is reached.

How fast climate zones move across the landscape is described by **climate velocity**, for example in kilometres per year. Birds and many insects can fly and follow the climate quite quickly. **Plants** are slower: they spread only by **seeds**, from generation to generation. In addition, the **fragmentation** of habitats hinders many species. Roads, settlements and intensively farmed fields separate the areas from each other.

The forests of Switzerland are changing too. The **Norway spruce** is an important tree species, but it was often planted at low altitudes in the Central Plateau as well. There it suffers more and more from **drought** and **bark beetles**. At low altitudes it is therefore considered particularly at risk. Foresters are increasingly relying on tree species that cope better with warmth and dryness.

gewusst: One degree of warming corresponds to roughly 150 metres of height in the mountains.
On some Alpine summits the number of plant species has risen clearly in recent decades.

teile.einleitung: Ragweed is a plant from North America that has spread in Europe. Its pollen causes severe allergies in many people. That is why it is actively controlled in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Ragweed pollen is one of the **strongest allergy triggers**.
The plant comes from **North America**.
It was often brought in with contaminated **bird seed**.
In Switzerland it must be **reported and controlled by law**.
It flowers in **late summer and autumn**, roughly from August to October.
Its pollen is spread by the **wind**.

abschnitte.text: The most common species is called **common ragweed** in English. Its finely divided leaves are reminiscent of mugwort, and its small flower heads grow in spikes. The plant comes from **North America**. In Europe it spread mainly in the 20th century. Plants that spread strongly in a new area and cause problems are called **invasive**.

abschnitte.titel: Into the garden with bird seed
abschnitte.text: Ragweed seeds were often found in bird seed mixtures in the past. Under the **bird feeders** they fell to the ground and sprouted. This is how ragweed reached many gardens. Today people make sure that bird seed is free of ragweed seeds. It can also be spread through soil and construction machinery.

Ragweed is a **wind-pollinated plant** and produces huge amounts of light pollen grains. These can be carried a long way through the air. Even **very few** pollen grains per cubic metre of air can cause symptoms in sensitive people. The pollen can cause **hay fever** and **asthma**. Because ragweed flowers from August to October, it extends the pollen season into autumn for allergy sufferers.

In Switzerland, ragweed must be **reported and controlled by law**. Anyone who finds it must remove it and report the find to the authorities. This is meant to stop it from spreading. When pulling it out, you wear **gloves**, because the plant sap can irritate the skin. If the plant is already flowering, a **dust mask** protects against the pollen. It is best to pull the plants out with their roots before they flower.

gewusst: A single large ragweed plant can produce thousands of seeds, which stay able to sprout in the soil for many years.
In Greek legend, “ambrosia” was the food of the gods. The plant shares only the name with it.

teile.einleitung: A species is extinct when not a single living thing of that species is left. Many animals have disappeared in recent centuries, often because of hunting or because people introduced foreign animals. An extinct species never comes back.
wichtigste: A species counts as extinct when, after a thorough search, no individual is found any more.
The moas of New Zealand were wiped out after the arrival of the Maori.
The last passenger pigeon, Martha, died in Cincinnati Zoo in 1914.
The thylacine has counted as extinct since 1936.
The aurochs, the ancestor of our domestic cattle, died out in Poland in 1627.
Island species are especially at risk from introduced enemies such as rats and cats.
In Switzerland the last native bear was shot in 1904 in the Lower Engadine.

abschnitte.text: A species is **extinct** when not a single animal or plant of that species is left alive. Because you can never search the whole world, experts only declare a species extinct after a long and thorough search. Extinction has always happened, for example with the dinosaurs. Today, however, many species are disappearing because of humans. An extinct species is lost for ever.

The **moas** of New Zealand were flightless running birds, some over three metres tall. After settlement by the Maori, they were wiped out within a few centuries. The **passenger pigeon** was once the commonest bird in North America, but hunting was so heavy that the last pigeon, named Martha, died in a zoo in 1914. The **great auk** looked like a penguin and lived in the North Atlantic. The last known birds were killed off Iceland in 1844.

The **aurochs** was a large wild bovine and is the ancestor of our domestic cattle. The last animal, a female, died in Poland in 1627. The **thylacine**, also called the Tasmanian tiger, had stripes on its rump and in the end lived only on Tasmania. The last known animal died in Hobart Zoo in 1936. **Steller’s sea cow** in the Bering Sea was discovered in 1741 and was wiped out after only about 27 years, because sailors hunted it for its meat.

Animals on islands die out especially easily. Many of them know no enemies such as **rats**, cats or pigs. Some island birds have even lost the ability to fly. When people bring such animals to an island, the native species have hardly any protection. That is why especially many species have disappeared on islands such as New Zealand or Mauritius.

An animal can also disappear in just one country, while it lives on elsewhere. It is then said to be **locally extinct** there. In Switzerland the last native **brown bear** was shot in 1904 in the Lower Engadine. Since 2005, individual bears have been migrating in again from Italy. The wolf and the lynx also had long disappeared from Switzerland and are back today.

gewusst: Steller’s sea cow could grow to about eight metres long.
The passenger pigeon was so common that its flocks could darken the sky for hours.

teile.einleitung: Biotic factors are all influences that come from living things. They include predators, competitors, parasites or pollinators. Together with abiotic factors such as light and temperature, they determine where and how a living thing can live.
wichtigste: A biotic factor is an influence that comes from living things.
For a roe deer, the lynx is a biotic factor.
Relationships within the same species are called intraspecific.
For the cherry harvest, pollination by insects is important.
Camouflage colours protect prey animals from predators.
Ash dieback is caused by a fungus.
In the 1990s wolves migrated back into Switzerland from Italy.

abschnitte.text: Many influences act on every living thing. **Abiotic factors** come from non-living nature, for example light, water, temperature or soil. **Biotic factors** come from living things. For a **roe deer**, the **lynx** is a biotic factor, because it hunts roe deer. The food the roe deer eats also belongs here.

Relationships between living things of the same species are called **intraspecific**. An example is the competition of roe deer for food or territories. Relationships between different species are called **interspecific**. These include predator and prey, competition, **parasitism** and **symbiosis**, that is, living together for mutual benefit.

Some biotic factors are useful. For a good **cherry harvest**, **pollination** by insects such as bees is very important. Others are dangerous. Prey animals protect themselves from predators with **camouflage colours**. In Switzerland the **wolf** returned: in the 1990s wolves migrated in again from Italy.

Disease-causing organisms are also biotic factors. **Ash dieback** is caused by a **fungus**. It has also occurred in Switzerland since about 2008 and is killing many ash trees. Non-native species that spread strongly and displace native ones are called **invasive neobiota**. They too change the living communities.

gewusst: The fungus that causes ash dieback originally comes from East Asia.
Many plants depend on very particular pollinators.

teile.einleitung: Essential oils are strongly scented substances that plants make in their leaves, flowers, peels or bark. They give peppermint, lavender or lemon their typical smell. Unlike fatty oils, they evaporate easily.
wichtigste: Most essential oils are obtained by steam distillation.
Oils from citrus peel are usually cold pressed.
Essential oils evaporate and leave no lasting grease spot.
Distillation also produces scented water, the hydrolate.
Members of the mint family store their oil in glandular hairs on the leaves.
Well-known ingredients are eugenol, thymol, chamazulene and 1,8-cineole.

abschnitte.text: **Essential oils** are mixtures of many different scented substances. Plants make them, among other reasons, to deter animals that would eat them or to attract insects. In **members of the mint family** such as peppermint and sage, they sit in tiny **glandular hairs** on the leaf surface. If you rub a leaf, these burst open and the scent is released.

Although they are called oils, essential oils are not fats. They are **volatile**, which means they evaporate easily. You can test this simply: a drop of essential oil on paper **evaporates** and leaves **no lasting grease spot**. A drop of cooking oil, that is a **fatty oil**, on the other hand makes a lasting, translucent spot. Essential oils hardly dissolve in water, but dissolve well in alcohol and fat.

Most essential oils are obtained by **steam distillation**. Hot steam flows through the plant parts and takes the scented substances with it. Then the steam is cooled. The oil then floats on the water and can be separated. The scented water that is left behind is called **hydrolate**, an example is rose water. Oils from **citrus peel** are usually obtained by **cold pressing**.

Every oil has typical main components. In the oil of the **clove** it is **eugenol**, which is also used in dentistry. **Thymol** gives thyme oil its strongly **antiseptic**, that is germ-killing, effect. The oil of true chamomile is deep blue, because of the substance **chamazulene**. In eucalyptus oil, **1,8-cineole** is the main component by quantity.

Essential oils are used for perfumes, soaps, foods and in herbal medicine. But they are **very concentrated**. Undiluted, they can irritate the skin, and even small amounts can do harm if swallowed. Some oils such as peppermint or eucalyptus oil are dangerous for **small children**. They should therefore be used only diluted and according to instructions, and kept tightly closed.

gewusst: For one kilogram of rose oil, several tonnes of rose petals are needed.
The blue chamazulene is not yet present in the chamomile flowers themselves, it only forms during distillation.

teile.einleitung: Some plants produce seeds without fertilisation taking place. This phenomenon is called apomixis. The offspring are then usually exact copies, that is clones, of the mother plant.
wichtigste: **Apomixis** means seed formation without fertilisation.
Another technical term for it is **agamospermy**.
The **common dandelion** usually forms its seeds apomictically.
In **brambles** and **lady’s mantle**, many microspecies arose this way.
In **citrus fruits**, several seedlings often grow from one seed.
Many apomictic plants are **polyploid**.

abschnitte.text: Normally a seed forms when two reproductive cells fuse. In **apomixis** it is different: the embryo in the seed forms **without fertilisation**. That is why the offspring are usually **clones** of the mother plant. People also speak of **agamospermy**, which means seed formation without the fusion of reproductive cells. This must not be confused with **autogamy**, self-fertilisation.

A well-known example is the **common dandelion**. It usually forms its seeds without fertilisation. The plants in a meadow are therefore often clones. The **true brambles** (Rubus) also often form their seeds apomictically. This is why hundreds of **microspecies**, hard to tell apart, have been described in Europe. In the Alps, **lady’s mantle** (Alchemilla) is a classic example: most of its species reproduce in this way.

In many **citrus species**, extra seedlings grow from the tissue of the ovule. This is called **nucellar embryony**. Several little plants can thus sprout from a single seed. These are clones of the mother plant. Gardeners can use this to raise plants that are exactly like the mother.

Many apomicts are **polyploid**. This means they have more than two sets of chromosomes, for example triploid dandelions. In them the normal cell division for reproductive cells is often disturbed. Apomixis gets around this problem. For **plant breeding**, apomixis is very interesting: hybrid seed splits up again in the next generation. With apomixis, **hybrid varieties** could reproduce themselves true to type, and their good qualities would be kept.

gewusst: The term apomixis comes from Greek and means roughly “without mixing”.
Some grasses, for example some meadow-grasses, also form their seeds apomictically.

teile.einleitung: The **monkshood** is a beautiful mountain flower with dark blue blossoms. But it is regarded as the most poisonous plant in Europe. That is why it is best admired only with the eyes.
wichtigste: The monkshood flowers dark blue to violet.
Its flower is reminiscent of a helmet, in German once called an iron hat.
It is regarded as the most poisonous plant in Europe, and all parts are poisonous.
The poison can act even through the skin.
In Switzerland it often grows in the mountains on damp meadows and near alpine huts.
Bumblebees fetch nectar from its helmet flowers.

abschnitte.text: The monkshood flowers **dark blue** to violet. The upper petal arches like a **helmet** over the flower. In the past such a helmet was called an **iron hat**, hence the German name Eisenhut. The flowers sit in a long cluster on an upright stem. The plant usually grows **50 to 150 centimetres** tall, rarely up to 2 metres. For a child it often reaches up to the hip or higher.

The monkshood is regarded as the **most poisonous plant in Europe**. **All parts** are poisonous, and the most poison is in the **root tuber**. Even small amounts can be life-threatening. The poison can even act **through the skin** and cause burning and tingling there. That is why you should not touch or pick it with bare hands.

In Switzerland the monkshood is often found **in the mountains**. It likes **damp**, nutrient-rich soils, for example by streams, in tall-herb communities and near **alpine huts**, where cows have fertilised the soil. Because it is so pretty, it is also planted in **gardens**. Cows do not eat it on the pasture.

The helmet flower is not easy for all insects to reach. **Bumblebees** are strong enough to crawl in. With their long tongue they fetch the **nectar**, which is hidden at the top of the helmet. In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower and so **pollinate** the plant.

If a friend wants to pick monkshood flowers, you should **warn** them and fetch an **adult**. If someone has touched the plant, you wash your hands thoroughly. In case of poisoning in Switzerland, **Tox Info Suisse** helps on the emergency number **145**. In case of severe signs you call the emergency number 144.

gewusst: The monkshood belongs to the buttercup family, like the buttercup.
Its scientific name is Aconitum napellus.

teile.einleitung: Species extinction means that animal and plant species disappear from the Earth for ever. Extinction has always happened in the history of the Earth, sometimes even in huge waves. Today, however, species are disappearing much faster than naturally, and humans are the main reason.
wichtigste: A species is extinct when not a single living thing of that species is left.
The background extinction rate is the natural rate of extinction without mass extinctions.
In the history of the Earth there have been five big mass extinctions.
The biggest was the Permian-Triassic event about 252 million years ago.
66 million years ago the dinosaurs disappeared, linked to the impact at Chicxulub.
According to the IPBES, the intergovernmental biodiversity panel, around 1 million species are threatened with extinction.
The main driver on land is the change in land use.

abschnitte.text: A species is **extinct** when its last living member has died, and it never comes back. Even without disasters, individual species die out again and again, and this is the **background extinction rate**. When very many species disappear in a short time, people speak of a **mass extinction**. Many researchers think that we are right now at the start of a sixth mass extinction.

In the last 500 million years there have been five big mass extinctions. The worst was the **Permian-Triassic event** about 252 million years ago, when most of all marine species died out, probably because of gigantic volcanic eruptions. 66 million years ago an asteroid struck at **Chicxulub** in Mexico. After that the dinosaurs died out, except for the ancestors of birds.

The flightless **dodo** lived on the island of Mauritius and was wiped out in the 17th century by sailors and introduced animals. The passenger pigeon was once the commonest bird in North America, with billions of birds. It disappeared through hunting, and the last passenger pigeon, called Martha, died in 1914 in a zoo. The mammoth also disappeared, probably partly because of human hunting.

In 2019 the **IPBES** examined the most important reasons. On land, the change in **land use** comes first, that is, the clearing of forests, the draining of moors and the building of roads and settlements. Other reasons are overfishing and hunting, climate change, pollution and **invasive species**. According to the report, around 1 million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature, the **IUCN**, keeps the **Red List** of threatened species. It sorts species into categories, from not threatened to extinct. The category EW means extinct in the wild, and the species then lives only in zoos or gardens. Switzerland also has its own Red Lists for its animals and plants.

In Switzerland the bear, wolf, lynx, ibex and bearded vulture were wiped out in the past. Through protection and reintroduction, some have returned: the **ibex** was released again from 1911, and the bearded vulture has flown in the National Park again since 1991. The wolf came back by itself from Italy. Such successes show that protection measures can work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A time when very many species die out in a short time.
A list of threatened animal and plant species.
An introduced species that harms native species.
The intergovernmental biodiversity panel, which examines the state of nature.

gewusst: More than 99 per cent of all species that ever lived on Earth are extinct today.
Birds are the last living descendants of the dinosaurs.
The dodo was only described in more detail by Europeans around 1600, and had already disappeared about 100 years later.

teile.einleitung: Alkaloids are natural substances found mainly in plants. They contain nitrogen and mostly taste bitter. Many act strongly on the body: as stimulants, as medicines or as poisons.
wichtigste: All alkaloids contain the element **nitrogen**.
The name comes from “alkali”, because they react **basically**.
Most alkaloids taste **bitter**.
Well-known alkaloids are **caffeine**, **nicotine**, **morphine** and **quinine**.
Plants probably protect themselves with alkaloids from animals that would eat them.
Theobromine from chocolate is poisonous to dogs.

abschnitte.text: Alkaloids are a large group of natural substances. What they have in common is that they contain **nitrogen**. In water they behave like alkalis, that is, **basically**. That is why they were called “alkali-like”, and from this came the name alkaloid. Today thousands of different alkaloids are known.

Plants cannot run away when an animal wants to eat them. Many therefore protect themselves with substances that taste bitter or are poisonous. Alkaloids probably belong to these **defensive substances**. The bitter taste often warns animals and people of something poisonous. The nicotine of the tobacco plant, for example, is a strong poison for insects.

The best-known alkaloid is probably **caffeine**. It is found in coffee beans and tea leaves and makes you wake up. In the cocoa bean there is **theobromine**. Humans break it down quickly, but dogs only very slowly, which is why chocolate is dangerous for dogs. **Nicotine** comes from the leaves of the tobacco plant and is addictive.

Many alkaloids are used as **medicines**. **Morphine** comes from the milky sap of the opium poppy and is a strong painkiller that only doctors may prescribe. **Quinine** from the bark of the cinchona tree was long the most important remedy against malaria. Other alkaloids are very poisonous, for example in deadly nightshade or in the autumn crocus, which also grows in Swiss meadows.

gewusst: Quinine gives tonic water its bitter taste.
In the early 19th century, morphine was one of the first alkaloids that could be obtained pure from a plant.

teile.einleitung: If you run your finger along the edge of a leaf, you feel differences. Some edges are smooth, others have pointed or round teeth. The **leaf margin** is an important feature for identifying plants.
wichtigste: A smooth leaf margin without teeth is called entire.
Serrated margins have pointed teeth directed forwards.
Crenate margins have rounded teeth.
The hornbeam has doubly serrated leaves.
The holly has spiny-toothed leaves.
The beech has a smooth, slightly wavy margin.

abschnitte.text: An **entire** leaf has a smooth margin without teeth or cuts. Examples are the **lilac** and ivy on flowering shoots. The **beech** also has a smooth margin that is slightly **wavy**. Young beech leaves also bear fine hairs on the margin.

In a **serrated** margin, pointed teeth point towards the tip of the leaf like those of a saw. An example is the wild cherry. The **stinging nettle** has a **coarsely serrated** margin with large, pointed teeth. In a **crenate** margin, by contrast, the teeth are round, and the cuts between them are pointed. In the **hornbeam** the large teeth bear small teeth again. This margin is called **doubly serrated**.

The **holly** has hard, prickly teeth on the leaf margin. Especially young plants and low-hanging twigs are spiny. This way the leaves are protected from animals that want to eat them. Higher up on the shrub the leaves are often smoother.

The **sweet chestnut** has long, narrow leaves that can grow over 20 centimetres long. Its margin is coarsely serrated, and every tooth ends in a fine point. On the **south side of the Alps**, especially in **Ticino**, it forms large chestnut woods. Its fruits are the marroni.

gewusst: Researchers have observed that trees in cool regions have toothed leaf margins more often than trees in the warm tropics.
The stinging hairs of the nettle break off at a touch like tiny glass tubes.

teile.einleitung: Abscisic acid is a plant hormone. Plants produce it above all when they are under stress, for example in drought. It helps them to save water and keeps seeds dormant.
wichtigste: Abscisic acid is a plant hormone, often called the “stress hormone”.
In drought it closes the stomata of the leaves.
It keeps seeds dormant.
It is formed from carotenoids.
Chemically it is a sesquiterpene with 15 carbon atoms.
Its level rises sharply in drought, cold or salt.

abschnitte.text: The substance was studied in the **1960s**, when researchers were investigating the shedding of **cotton fruits**. The Latin word abscidere means “to cut off”. That is why it was called **abscisic acid**, abbreviated ABA. Today we know that it plays only a minor role in the shedding of plant parts. Its most important task is a different one: protection against a lack of water.

Leaves have tiny openings, the **stomata**. Water evaporates through them. In drought the level of abscisic acid in the leaf rises, and the stomata **close**. In doing so the hormone opens ion channels in the **guard cells**. Potassium and chloride ions stream out, and water follows. The internal pressure, the **turgor**, falls, and the pore closes. In this way the plant loses less water through **transpiration**.

Often the **roots** are the first to notice that the soil is drying out. They then produce more abscisic acid. With the flow of water, the hormone travels through the conducting channels, the **xylem**, into the leaves. There it triggers protective reactions even before the plant wilts. In **cold** or with a lot of **salt** in the soil, too, the level rises sharply. The hormone then switches on protective genes. That is why it is called a **stress hormone**.

Abscisic acid also ensures that **seeds** do not germinate too early. It keeps them **dormant**. In **maize** plants that cannot produce abscisic acid, the kernels germinate while still on the cob. This phenomenon is called **vivipary**.

Abscisic acid has **15 carbon atoms**. This makes it one of the **sesquiterpenes**, which are built from three isoprene units. The plant makes it from **carotenoids**, that is, from yellow and orange pigments. These are split in the plastids, and an intermediate product is **xanthoxin**.

gewusst: Abscisic acid is not found only in plants but is also produced by some fungi.
The stomata of a leaf can close within minutes when abscisic acid acts.

teile.einleitung: Biodiversity hotspots are areas of the Earth with especially many species that exist only there. At the same time these areas are highly threatened. That is why they are considered especially important for nature conservation.
wichtigste: The concept was coined by the biologist Norman Myers in 1988.
A hotspot has at least 1500 endemic species of vascular plants.
It has lost at least 70 percent of its original vegetation.
Since 2016 Conservation International has distinguished 36 hotspots.
The intact vegetation of the hotspots covers only about 2.5 percent of the land area.
The Mediterranean region is a hotspot in Europe.
The Tropical Andes are considered the most species-rich hotspot.

abschnitte.text: The British environmental researcher **Norman Myers** presented the idea in 1988. He wanted to show where nature conservation can achieve the most. Because money for nature conservation is scarce, it should be used where the most species are saved per area. Later the organisation **Conservation International** took over the concept and developed it further.

An area counts as a hotspot if it meets two conditions. First, it must have at least 1500 **endemic** species of vascular plants. Endemic means that these species occur only there. Second, it must have lost at least 70 percent of its original vegetation. A hotspot is therefore rich in species and at the same time highly threatened.

Since 2016 Conservation International has distinguished **36 hotspots**. Their still intact vegetation covers only about **2.5 percent** of the land area of the Earth. Nevertheless a large share of all plant and vertebrate species lives there. Most hotspots lie in the tropics.

The **Tropical Andes** in South America are considered the most species-rich hotspot in the world. **Madagascar**, together with neighbouring islands, forms its own hotspot and is famous for its lemurs. In Europe the **Mediterranean region** is one, with many plant species that exist only there.

gewusst: In the wild, lemurs occur only on Madagascar.
Hotspots were chosen on the basis of plants, because plants are the foundation for many other living things.

teile.einleitung: Bioplastics are plastics that are made from renewable raw materials or can be broken down biologically. Both do not always apply at the same time. That is why it is worth looking closely.
wichtigste: Bio-based plastics are not automatically biodegradable.
Bio-PE from sugar cane is chemically the same as conventional polyethylene.
PLA usually breaks down well only in industrial composting plants.
PHA are formed by bacteria as storage substances.
The standard EN 13432 regulates industrially compostable packaging.
PLA bottles contaminate the PET collection.
Celluloid was an early plastic made from cellulose.

abschnitte.text: The term bioplastic has two meanings. **Bio-based** means that the plastic comes from plants such as maize or sugar cane. **Biodegradable** means that microorganisms can break it down. Bio-based plastics are not automatically degradable. **Bio-PE** from sugar cane, for example, is chemically the same as normal polyethylene and does not break down.

**PLA** is made from lactic acid, which is obtained from plant starch. **PHA**, the polyhydroxyalkanoates, are formed by bacteria as storage substances in their cells. **Thermoplastic starch** consists of starch processed with plasticisers such as **glycerine**. As early as the 19th century there was a plastic made from cellulose, **celluloid**.

PLA usually breaks down well only in **industrial composting plants** at high temperatures. In the garden or in nature it takes a very long time. The European standard **EN 13432** lays down when a package counts as industrially compostable. Some Swiss municipalities nevertheless do not allow compostable bags in green waste. They can hardly be told apart from normal plastic bags.

Bottles made of PLA look similar to PET bottles. If they get into the **PET collection**, they contaminate the recycled material. That is why they do not belong there. Experts stress: what matters is not only what a plastic is made of, but also how it is disposed of or reused.

gewusst: Celluloid used to be used for film strips and table tennis balls.
Some bacteria store PHA in their cells, similar to how we store fat.

teile.einleitung: The beaver is the largest rodent in Europe and a real master builder. It dams streams with dams and so changes whole landscapes. In Switzerland it once disappeared, but today it lives again on many waters.
wichtigste: The beaver builds dams to hold back the water.
Its tail, the paddle, is broad and flat.
It eats bark, twigs and water plants.
Its gnawing teeth are orange.
The entrance to the beaver lodge lies under water.
About 200 years ago the beaver was extinct in Switzerland.
In 2022 around 4900 beavers lived in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The beaver is well adapted to life in the water. Its dense fur keeps it warm and dry. Between the toes of its hind feet it has webbing. Its tail is called the **paddle**, and it is broad, flat and covered with scales. The paddle serves as a rudder when swimming and stores fat. When in danger the beaver slaps the water loudly with it.

The gnawing teeth of the beaver are **orange**, because their enamel contains iron. They keep growing throughout its life. The beaver is a pure plant eater. In summer it eats herbs and water plants, in winter mainly **bark** and twigs. For this it fells trees on the bank, often willows and poplars.

With branches, mud and stones the beaver builds a **dam**. This way it holds back the water so that the entrance to its den always lies under water. The **beaver lodge** is a heap of branches and earth with a dry living chamber inside. Because the entrance is under water, enemies can hardly get in. The beaver also often digs burrows into steep banks.

The beaver was hunted heavily for its fur, its meat and a scent substance. About 200 years ago it was **extinct** in Switzerland. From 1956 beavers were released again. Since then it has spread strongly, and in 2022 around 4900 animals were counted. Today it is protected. Sometimes there are conflicts when it floods fields or fells fruit trees.

gewusst: The beaver is active mainly at night and at dusk, which is why you rarely see it.
Beaver ponds create habitat for dragonflies, amphibians and fish.

teile.einleitung: The alpenrose is a low shrub that in early summer colours whole mountain slopes pink to red. Despite its name, it is not a true rose but a rhododendron. All its parts are poisonous.
wichtigste: The alpenrose is not a rose but a **rhododendron**.
It belongs to the **heather family**.
It blooms **pink to red**, mostly in June and July.
It is **evergreen**: its leaves stay green in winter.
All parts of the alpenrose are **poisonous**.
In Switzerland the rusty-leaved and the hairy alpenrose grow.

abschnitte.text: The alpenrose has only the name from the rose. In reality it belongs to the **rhododendrons** and thus to the **heather family**. It grows as a low **shrub**, mostly 50 to 100 centimetres tall. In early summer it bears bright pink to red flowers. Then it colours whole slopes red.

In the **rusty-leaved alpenrose**, the underside of the leaves is covered with many small, **rust-brown** scales. That is where it gets its name. It grows on acidic soil. The **hairy alpenrose** has fine hairs like **eyelashes** on the leaf margin. It likes to grow on limestone soil. Where both occur together, there are also hybrid forms.

The alpenrose is **evergreen**. Its leathery leaves stay on the shrub even in winter. In doing so it needs a protective **blanket of snow**. Under the snow it is protected from hard frost and cold wind. That is why it often grows in places where a lot of snow lies in winter.

All parts of the alpenrose are **poisonous**. You must not eat either leaves or flowers. The alpenrose mostly blooms in **June and July**. The higher it grows, the later in the year it blooms. You can see especially beautiful stands at the tree line and above.

gewusst: In Austria and Bavaria the alpenrose is also called “Almrausch”.
Honey from alpenrose flowers is also produced in the Alps and is regarded as a speciality.

teile.einleitung: Woodlice are small grey animals that you find under stones and flowerpots. Although they live on land, they are not insects but crustaceans. In the garden they are useful helpers, because they eat dead plant material.
wichtigste: Woodlice belong to the crustaceans.
An adult woodlouse has 14 legs.
You often find them under damp stones.
They eat mainly rotting plant material.
The pill woodlouse rolls itself into a ball when in danger.
A hard shell protects their body.

abschnitte.text: Woodlice belong to the **crustaceans**, so they are related to crabs and prawns. Most woodlouse species live in the sea, but some also live on land. An adult woodlouse has **14 legs**, which is seven pairs of legs. This sets it clearly apart from insects, which have six legs. Its body is flat and divided into many segments.

Land woodlice need **moisture**, or they dry out. That is why you find them **under damp stones**, under leaves, wood and flowerpots. During the day they hide, and at night they become active. The common woodlouse is called **Kellerassel** in German, which means cellar woodlouse, because you often find it **in damp cellars**. Common woodlice are mostly **grey**.

Woodlice eat mainly **rotting plant material** such as wilted leaves and rotten wood. In doing so they break up the material. Fungi and bacteria can then break it down further more easily. This produces fertile **humus**. In the compost heap, woodlice are therefore welcome helpers.

The woodlouse’s body is protected by a **hard shell**. Because it does not grow with the animal, the woodlouse has to **moult** as it grows. It sheds first the rear half and later the front half. The **pill woodlouse** has a special trick. When it feels threatened, it **rolls itself up into a ball**, so that only the shell can be seen.

gewusst: The females carry their eggs and the newly hatched young for a time in a brood pouch on the underside of the body.
Land woodlice breathe with modified gills and therefore need damp air.

teile.einleitung: With an identification guide you find out what a plant, an animal or a fungus is called. It shows pictures and describes important features. This way you become a nature researcher.
wichtigste: An identification guide helps you find out the name of plants or animals.
It contains pictures and features such as colour, size or voice.
Flowers are often arranged by colour so that you find them more quickly.
You compare the living thing with the pictures in the book.
In Switzerland, collected mushrooms are taken to the mushroom inspection.
For outdoors, a small, light book is handy.
Apps also help with identifying, but you should check the result.

abschnitte.titel: What is an identification guide for?
abschnitte.text: An **identification guide** helps you find out the name of a plant, an animal or a fungus. In it you find **pictures** and **features**. A bird book shows, for example, the colour, size and voice of the birds. For outdoors, small and light books are handy. They are also called **field guides**, and they fit well in a rucksack.

First you look at the animal or the plant **closely**. How big is it, what colour is it, how many legs or petals does it have? Then you look in the book for the picture that fits best and **compare** the features. In some books flowers are arranged by **colour**. You see the colour of the flower straight away, so you find the flower faster.

There are also **mushroom books** with many pictures. But many mushrooms are poisonous and look very similar to edible ones. That is why you should collect mushrooms for eating only with an expert. In Switzerland, collected mushrooms are taken to the **mushroom inspection** before eating. There trained mushroom inspectors check every mushroom.

Today there are also **apps** on the phone that recognise a plant or a bird in a photo. This is handy and quick. But the apps also make mistakes. So you should **check** the result with a book. You learn the most when you look closely yourself.

gewusst: Some identification guides work like a guessing game with questions: you always choose between two possibilities.
There are bird apps that can even recognise birds by their song.

teile.einleitung: Antarctica is the very cold continent at the South Pole. It is almost completely covered by a thick shell of ice and is nearly one and a half times as big as Europe. No people live here permanently, but penguins, seals and researchers from all over the world do.
wichtigste: Antarctica is the continent around the South Pole.
The Antarctic often means the whole region together with the surrounding sea.
Around 98 per cent of the area is covered by ice.
Most of the Earth’s fresh water is found here.
In 1983, minus 89.2 degrees was measured at Vostok station.
The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 protects the continent for peace and research.
Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole, in 1911.

abschnitte.text: At about 14 million square kilometres, **Antarctica** is the fifth-largest continent. Almost its whole area lies under an **ice sheet** that is on average around 2 kilometres thick. In some places the ice is over 4 kilometres thick. This ice holds about 70 per cent of the Earth’s fresh water.

Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent. At the Russian station **Vostok**, minus 89.2 degrees Celsius was measured in 1983. Because it hardly ever snows, Antarctica counts as the largest desert on Earth. In winter it is dark for months, and in summer the sun shines day and night.

On the coasts live **emperor penguins**, the largest penguins in the world, and Adélie penguins. Seals such as the leopard seal and the Weddell seal hunt in the icy sea. Whales come in summer to eat **krill**, tiny crustaceans that exist there in huge numbers. On the land itself only mosses, lichens and two species of flowering plants grow.

abschnitte.titel: The race to the South Pole
abschnitte.text: For a long time Antarctica was a blank spot on the map. The Norwegian **Roald Amundsen** reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911 as the first person ever. The Briton Robert Falcon Scott arrived a good month later and died with his companions on the way back. Their stories are among the best-known adventures in the history of exploration.

In the **Antarctic Treaty** of 1959, states agreed that Antarctica may only be used peacefully. The military and mining are forbidden, and research is at the centre. Around 70 research stations study climate, ice and animals there, and in summer several thousand people live on the continent. In old ice cores, researchers, including some from Switzerland, read what the climate was like hundreds of thousands of years ago.

The highest mountain in Antarctica is **Mount Vinson**, at almost 4,900 metres. Under the ice are hidden whole mountain ranges and over 400 lakes of liquid water. The largest of them is Lake Vostok, which lies under almost 4 kilometres of ice. If all the ice were to melt, sea level would rise by about 58 metres.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge mass of ice that covers a whole land.
Small crustaceans, the main food of many whales and penguins.
An agreement that protects Antarctica for peace and research.
A long cylinder of ice from the depths that contains old air and traces of the climate.

gewusst: Antarctica has no time zone of its own, each research station chooses its own time.
Although Antarctica is full of ice, less precipitation falls in its interior than in the Sahara.
In the icy winter, male emperor penguins incubate the egg on their feet for around two months.

teile.einleitung: The Biodiversity Initiative was a federal popular initiative for the protection of nature. In September 2024 the Swiss people voted on it. It was clearly rejected.
wichtigste: The official title was “For the future of our nature and landscape”.
It was backed among others by Pro Natura, BirdLife Switzerland and the Swiss Heritage Society.
It wanted to anchor more areas and resources for biodiversity in the constitution.
To be accepted it needed a majority of the people and of the cantons.
It was rejected with around 63 percent No.
Basel-Stadt was among the few cantons that said Yes.

abschnitte.text: With a **popular initiative**, citizens can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. For this 100,000 signatures are needed. Then the people vote. An initiative is accepted only with the **popular majority** and the **cantonal majority**. That means: the majority of those voting and the majority of the cantons must agree.

The initiative was officially called “For the future of our nature and landscape”. It wanted the Confederation and the cantons to protect **biodiversity** better. For this, more areas and more money were to be made available for nature. Beautiful landscapes and townscapes were also to be better protected. The backers included **Pro Natura**, **BirdLife Switzerland** and the **Swiss Heritage Society**.

Supporters said that the variety of species in Switzerland is declining and that more protection is needed. Opponents thought there were already enough rules. They warned that the initiative would restrict **agriculture** and the expansion of **renewable energies**. The Federal Council and Parliament recommended rejection. Parliament did without a counter-proposal.

The vote took place on 22 September 2024. The initiative was rejected with around **63 percent No**. Only a few cantons agreed, including **Basel-Stadt**. In many rural cantons the rejection was especially large.

gewusst: In Switzerland citizens can vote directly on changes to the constitution.
Besides the people, a popular initiative also needs the agreement of the majority of the cantons.

teile.einleitung: Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle was a famous botanist from Geneva. He lived from 1778 to 1841 and coined the term taxonomy. With his great work he wanted to describe all known seed plants.
wichtigste: Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle was born in Geneva in 1778.
In 1813 he coined the technical term taxonomy.
His work the “Prodromus” was meant to describe all known seed plants.
With Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck he published the third edition of the “Flore française”.
Before returning to Geneva in 1816, he taught in Montpellier.
The Botanical Garden of Geneva goes back to him.

abschnitte.text: **Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle** was born **in Geneva in 1778**. He became interested in plants early on. He studied in Geneva and then went to **Paris**, where he worked with important naturalists. Later he became a professor at the University of **Montpellier** in southern France. In **1816** he returned to Geneva, where he lived until his death in 1841.

De Candolle wanted to arrange plants according to their natural relationships. In a book of **1813** he coined the technical term **taxonomy**. It describes the science of classifying and naming living things. Together with the French naturalist **Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck** he published the third edition of the **“Flore française”**. This work describes the plants of France.

His greatest project was the **“Prodromus systematis naturalis regni vegetabilis”**. The aim was to **describe all known seed plants**. De Candolle did not manage this alone. After his death his son **Alphonse de Candolle** and many other botanists carried the work on. In the end it comprised 17 volumes.

After returning to Geneva, de Candolle founded a **botanical garden**. From it developed today’s **Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques de la Ville de Genève**. There, plants are still researched today and millions of dried plants are kept. In Geneva, several places recall the famous botanist.

De Candolle kept **mimosas** in **constant light**. Their leaves still opened and closed in a rhythm of about a day. This showed that plants follow an **inner rhythm**. He also described how plants are in **competition for space**. **Charles Darwin** later took up this idea. His son **Alphonse** put forward rules for **botanical names** in **1867**, a basis of today’s naming rules.

gewusst: In scientific plant names, the abbreviation “DC.” stands for Augustin-Pyramus de Candolle as the first describer.
Three generations of the de Candolle family were important botanists: Augustin-Pyramus, his son Alphonse and his grandson Casimir.

teile.einleitung: Clubmosses are ancient plants that creep over the forest floor like little green tendrils. They form no flowers, but reproduce with tiny spores. A well-known representative is the stag’s-horn clubmoss.
wichtigste: The stag’s-horn clubmoss creeps along the ground.
Its shoot can grow several metres long.
The little leaves are small and needle-like.
The spores form in club-shaped spikes.
Clubmosses stay green in winter too.
Their relatives were as big as trees many millions of years ago.

abschnitte.text: The **stag’s-horn clubmoss** does not grow upwards, but **creeps along the ground**. Its shoot can grow **several metres** long and keeps forming small roots. From the main shoot, short side shoots grow upwards. The little leaves are **small and needle-like** and sit close against the stem. This makes the plant look a bit like a green, fluffy rope.

Clubmosses have no flowers and no seeds. They reproduce with **spores**, tiny grains that can only be seen individually with a microscope. In the stag’s-horn clubmoss, the spores form in **club-shaped spikes** on upright stalks. That is where its name comes from. When a spike is ripe, a fine yellow powder trickles out, which the wind spreads.

abschnitte.titel: Powder for a flash of fire
abschnitte.text: The spores of the clubmoss contain a lot of oil and are very fine. If you blow them into a flame, they burn in a flash with a bright jet of flame. **Fire-eaters** use this for their shows. In the past the powder was also used for flash lighting in the theatre. It is also called **witches’ flour**. But you should only play with fire under the supervision of experts.

Clubmosses are among the oldest land plants on Earth. Many millions of years ago there were relatives that grew **as big as trees**. Part of today’s **coal** formed from their forests. Today’s clubmosses, by contrast, are small. Here they grow **in woods and on heaths**, also in Switzerland. They stay **green in winter** and grow very slowly.

gewusst: Clubmoss spores are so water-repellent that a powdered finger can stay dry in water.
Because clubmosses grow so slowly, they are protected in many areas and must not be collected.

teile.einleitung: The apricot is an orange, velvety stone fruit. In Switzerland it grows mainly in the Valais, where it is harvested in summer. In Austria it is called Marille.
wichtigste: The apricot is a stone fruit and belongs to the rose family.
Ripe apricots are orange and have velvety soft skin.
In Austria the apricot is called Marille.
Most Swiss apricots grow in the canton of Valais.
In the Valais the harvest is mainly in July and August.
The bitter kernels inside the stone can be poisonous and should not be eaten.

abschnitte.text: The apricot grows on a small tree from the **rose family**. Its fruit is roundish, orange and has **velvety soft skin**. Inside is a hard **stone**, which is why it counts as a **stone fruit**, like the cherry, plum and peach. The **peach** looks similar to it, but is usually bigger. The flesh is sweet and slightly sour.

The apricot originally comes from Asia and reached Europe along long trade routes. Its scientific name is **Prunus armeniaca**, because people used to believe it came from Armenia. In the German-speaking world it has different names. In Austria and parts of southern Germany people say **Marille**. In Switzerland and Germany the name Aprikose is usual.

The canton of **Valais** is the most important growing area in Switzerland. In the Rhône valley it is sunny, dry and warm in summer, which the trees like. The harvest takes place mainly in **July and August**. A well-known traditional Valais variety is called **Luizet**. One problem is spring: apricot trees **blossom very early**, and a cold night can freeze the blossoms. Farmers then sometimes protect them from the frost with water or fire.

Apricots are eaten fresh, dried or as **jam**. Well known are apricot tart and Marillenknödel (apricot dumplings). In the famous Viennese **Sachertorte** there is a layer of **apricot jam** under the chocolate icing. Dried apricots are a popular store, because they keep for a long time. A spirit is also made from Valais apricots, Abricotine.

In the hard stone lies a kernel like an almond. In many apricots it tastes **bitter**. Bitter kernels contain a substance from which poisonous **prussic acid** can form in the body. That is why you should **not eat** the bitter kernels. The flesh itself, on the other hand, is healthy and contains many vitamins.

gewusst: A single frosty morning in spring can destroy a large part of the Valais apricot harvest.
Apricots and peaches belong to the same plant genus as cherries and plums, the genus Prunus.

teile.einleitung: Assimilation is a term from biology. It describes the building up of the body’s own substances from substances that a living thing has taken in. The best-known example is the photosynthesis of plants.
wichtigste: Assimilation is the building up of the body’s own substances from substances taken in.
Autotrophic living things build up organic substances from inorganic substances.
Heterotrophic living things such as humans have to take in organic substances with their food.
Photosynthesis is also called carbon assimilation.
The opposite term is dissimilation, the breaking down of substances to gain energy.
Legumes use nodule bacteria to take nitrogen from the air.

abschnitte.titel: Building up instead of breaking down
abschnitte.text: The word **assimilation** comes from Latin and means roughly “making alike”. A living thing takes in substances and makes **its own body substances** from them. So it makes the foreign substances like itself. For this it needs **energy**. The opposite term is **dissimilation**: in it, a living thing breaks down its own body substances to gain energy, for example in **cellular respiration**.

Living things that build up their organic substances themselves from **inorganic substances** such as water and carbon dioxide are called **autotrophic**. These include green plants and some bacteria. Living things such as humans and animals are **heterotrophic**. They have to take in organic substances with their **food**. From the food they then build up their own proteins, fats and other substances.

In **photosynthesis**, plants use the energy of **light**. From **carbon dioxide** and **water** they build up **glucose**, and **oxygen** is produced. Because the plant builds carbon into its substances in the process, photosynthesis is also called **carbon assimilation**. From the sugar, starch, cellulose and many other substances are later formed.

For **proteins**, plants need **nitrogen**. Most take it up through the roots as **nitrogen-containing mineral salts**, for example nitrate. This is called **nitrogen assimilation**. **Legumes** such as **clover**, peas and beans have a special feature. In nodules on their roots live **nodule bacteria**, which fix nitrogen from the air and make it available to the plant.

Some bacteria build up organic substances without using light. They gain the energy from **chemical reactions**, for example from sulphur or iron compounds. This process is called **chemosynthesis**. Such bacteria live, for example, at hot springs in the deep sea. There they form the food basis for whole communities of living things.

gewusst: Farmers often sow clover to improve the soil, because thanks to its nodule bacteria it brings nitrogen into the soil.
Almost all the oxygen in the air comes from the photosynthesis of plants, algae and bacteria.

teile.einleitung: The Bern Convention is an international agreement for the protection of Europe’s wild animals and plants. It was signed in Bern in 1979. Today it is also well known because of the discussion about protecting the wolf.
wichtigste: The Bern Convention was signed in Bern on 19 September 1979 and entered into force in 1982.
It protects wild plants and animals and their habitats.
The appendices list protected species and banned means of capture.
States can enter reservations for certain species.
The network of protected areas is called the Emerald Network.
In 2018 Switzerland unsuccessfully proposed lowering the protection of the wolf.
In December 2024 the wolf was downgraded from “strictly protected” to “protected”.

abschnitte.text: The full name is the **Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats**. It was signed in Bern on **19 September 1979** and entered into force in 1982. The Bern Convention is a **treaty under international law**. States join it through ratification and undertake to implement its requirements in their own law.

The convention wants to protect not only individual species but also their **natural habitats**. Particular account is taken of endangered and **migratory species**, for example migratory birds. The contracting states report areas that are especially valuable for these species. Together they form the **Emerald Network**. In the EU, the Natura 2000 network takes on this task.

The Bern Convention has several **appendices** with lists. Appendix I names strictly protected plants, Appendix II **strictly protected animals**, Appendix III **protected animals**. Appendix IV lists means of capture and killing that are banned. On signing or ratification, states can enter **reservations** for certain species. For these species the duties of protection then do not apply or apply only in a limited way.

The **wolf** was long in Appendix II and was therefore strictly protected. In 2018 **Switzerland** proposed downgrading it to protected status. The proposal found no majority at the time. In December 2024 the **Standing Committee** adopted a similar proposal from the EU. The wolf was moved to Appendix III, and the change came into force in March 2025. Supporters see this as an easing for regulation, while nature conservation organisations criticised the decision.

gewusst: The convention is named after the Swiss federal city, because it was signed there.
Some states outside Europe, for example in North Africa, have also joined the Bern Convention.

teile.einleitung: Many plants grow upwards mainly at their tip. The terminal bud holds back the side buds further down. This phenomenon is called apical dominance, meaning the dominance of the tip.
wichtigste: In **apical dominance**, the terminal bud holds back the sprouting of the side buds.
If you cut off the tip, the side buds sprout.
The plant hormone **auxin** is an important signal from the tip.
Since 2008 we have known that **strigolactones** also hold back branching.
In spruces this produces the slim **cone shape**.
When pathogens disturb apical dominance, **witches’ brooms** form.

abschnitte.text: On a shoot there is a **terminal bud** at the tip and many **side buds** beneath it. The tip suppresses the growth of the side buds. As a result the plant grows mainly in **height**. A hobby gardener can easily see this: if you pinch off the shoot tips of **basil**, the inhibition disappears. The side buds sprout, and the plant becomes bushier.

The tip sends out an inhibiting signal that flows from top to bottom. In the 1930s, **Thimann and Skoog** showed that if you cut off the tip and put the hormone **auxin** on the cut surface, the side buds stay inhibited. This proved that auxin is the signal of apical dominance. In 2008, research groups showed that **strigolactones** also hold back the sprouting of side buds. These substances were previously known as a germination signal for parasitic plants.

In **spruces**, the dominance of the main shoot is strongly marked. The leading shoot grows more strongly every year than the side branches, and the upper branches stay shorter. This produces the typical slim **cone shape**. In most broadleaved trees, the buds near the shoot tip sprout most strongly. This is called **acrotony**. In **basitonic** shrubs, on the other hand, the buds at the base sprout most vigorously.

Sometimes you can see dense, broom-like bunches of shoots on trees. These **witches’ brooms** form when fungi, bacteria or phytoplasmas change the hormone balance, often through extra **cytokinin**. Then many side buds sprout at the same time. The **potato tuber** also shows apical dominance. It is a thickened shoot, and its **crown end** corresponds to the tip. The eyes there sprout first and hold back the others.

gewusst: Gardeners use apical dominance on purpose: by cutting the tip they make hedges denser.
The word “apical” comes from the Latin “apex”, which means tip.

teile.einleitung: Bioenergy is energy from biomass, that is, from wood, plants or organic waste. From it you can obtain heat, electricity and fuels. In Switzerland wood is the most important energy source from biomass.
wichtigste: The energy in biomass originally comes from the sun, through photosynthesis.
In Switzerland wood is the most important biomass energy source.
Many district heating plants burn wood chips.
Bioethanol is made by alcoholic fermentation with yeasts.
Biodiesel is made by transesterification of vegetable oil with methanol.
The debate “tank or plate” concerns space on the field.
Small wood-burning stoves give off a lot of fine dust.

abschnitte.text: Plants use sunlight for **photosynthesis**. In doing so they build sugar and other substances from carbon dioxide and water. Energy is stored in these substances. When biomass is burned or converted, this energy is released again. Bioenergy counts as **renewable**, because plants grow back.

In Switzerland **wood** is the most important energy source from biomass. Many municipalities run **district heating plants** that burn **wood chips**. The heat reaches houses and schools through pipes. Firewood must be well **dried**. Otherwise evaporating the water takes a lot of energy, and more smoke is produced.

**Bioethanol** is made when yeasts ferment sugar or starch. This is called **alcoholic fermentation**. Raw materials are for example sugar cane or maize. From wood it is harder, because the wood component **lignin** is difficult to break down. **Biodiesel** is made from vegetable oil such as rapeseed oil. The oil reacts with methanol, which is called **transesterification**.

Bioenergy can replace fossil fuels such as oil. But it also has disadvantages. The debate **“tank or plate”** is about energy crops competing with food for farmland. Small wood-burning stoves give off a lot of **fine dust**, which burdens the airways. Modern plants with filters are much cleaner.

gewusst: Liquid manure and green waste can also be turned into energy in biogas plants.
About a third of the area of Switzerland is forest.

teile.einleitung: The apple is one of the most popular fruits in Switzerland. There are many varieties with red, yellow or green skin. You eat it fresh, cook it into apple purée or press it into cider.
wichtigste: Apples can be **red, yellow or green**.
Because of its many apple trees, Thurgau is jokingly called **“Mostindien”** (cider India).
A cut apple turns brown when **air** reaches the flesh.
**Lemon juice** slows the browning.
An apple **floats** in water because it contains a lot of air.
**Bees** pollinate apple blossoms.

abschnitte.text: There are very many **apple varieties**. Their skin can be red, yellow, green or a mixture. Some taste sweet, others sour. Many apple trees grow in Switzerland, especially in the canton of **Thurgau**. Because so much cider is made there, it is jokingly called **“Mostindien”**. **Apple purée** is made from cooked and mashed apples.

In spring the apple trees bloom white and pink. **Bees** fly from flower to flower and carry the pollen along. Only in this way can many apples grow. In summer the small fruits get bigger and bigger. In autumn most apples are ripe and are harvested.

If you cut open an apple, the flesh turns **brown** after a while. This happens because substances in the flesh react with the **oxygen in the air**. If you drip **lemon juice** on it, the slices stay pale for longer. If you put an apple in a bucket of water, it **floats**. There is a lot of air between its cells, so it is lighter than water.

Sometimes an apple is **“wormy”**. The “worm” in it is really the **caterpillar** of a small moth. It eats its way through the flesh. An apple also plays a part in a famous Swiss legend: **William Tell** had to shoot an apple off the head of his son Walter with a crossbow. He hit it.

gewusst: The ancestors of our apples come from Central Asia, from the area of what is now Kazakhstan.
The moth whose caterpillar lives in the apple is called the codling moth.

teile.einleitung: In an algal bloom, tiny algae in the water multiply so strongly that a lake or even the sea changes colour. It has nothing to do with flowers. Some algal blooms are harmless, others produce dangerous poisons.
wichtigste: An algal bloom is a **mass multiplication** of algae.
Many nutrients such as **phosphate**, warmth and sun encourage it.
**Cyanobacteria**, formerly called “blue-green algae”, can produce poisons.
Dogs should not drink from the lake during an algal bloom.
The **Burgundy blood alga** can turn lakes red.
The amount of **chlorophyll** in the water shows how many algae there are.

abschnitte.text: Algae grow especially fast when the water contains many **nutrients**, above all phosphate. These can come from fertiliser on fields or from wastewater. If warmth and a lot of sun are added, the algae multiply explosively. That is why algal blooms mostly occur in **summer**. When the algae die, a lot of oxygen is used up in the breakdown, which can harm fish.

The organisms formerly called “blue-green algae” are actually **cyanobacteria**. They carry out photosynthesis like plants. Many have small gas bubbles and rise to the surface. There they form green or blue-green, slimy **mats** and streaks. Some species produce **poisons** that are dangerous to people and animals.

For **dogs**, algal poisons are especially dangerous. They drink lake water and afterwards lick their fur. In this way they take in a lot of poison, which can even end fatally. People too should not bathe when algal mats are visible. In Switzerland, cantons and municipalities often warn with notices on the shore.

abschnitte.titel: Red lakes and the red tide
abschnitte.text: The **Burgundy blood alga** can turn lakes red. Its name recalls the **Battle of Murten** of 1476. According to the legend, the blood of the defeated Burgundians turned Lake Murten red; in fact the colour came from this alga. In the sea there is the **red tide**: certain marine algae colour the water red or brown, and their poisons can contaminate fish and shellfish.

All algae contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**. Experts measure how much of it is in the water. The more chlorophyll, the more algae. In Switzerland many lakes used to be heavily over-fertilised. Since sewage treatment plants were built and phosphates in detergents were banned, the water of many lakes has become clearer again.

gewusst: The Burgundy blood alga is actually a cyanobacterium and not a true alga.
Some algal blooms in the sea are so large that they can be seen from space in satellite images.

teile.einleitung: A biogeochemical cycle describes the path of a chemical element through living things, air, water and rock. Important cycles are those of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur. They link living and non-living nature.
wichtigste: A biogeochemical cycle shows the path of an element through living things, air, water and rock.
For nitrogen the largest reservoir is in the atmosphere.
Silicate weathering removes CO₂ from the air over millions of years.
The biological pump carries carbon into the deep sea.
The residence time is the average time an atom stays in a reservoir.
Vladimir Vernadsky is regarded as the founder of biogeochemistry.
Since 1958 the CO₂ concentration has been measured on Mauna Loa in Hawaii.

abschnitte.text: On Earth no atom is lost. Elements move back and forth between **reservoirs** such as air, sea, soil, rock and living things. The **residence time** is the average time an atom stays in a reservoir. It can last days, but also millions of years. The Russian researcher **Vladimir Vernadsky** is regarded as the founder of biogeochemistry.

Plants take in **carbon dioxide** from the air, and living things give it off again when breathing. In the sea, carbon sinks into the depths with dead plankton. This is called the **biological pump**. Over millions of years the **silicate weathering** of rock removes CO₂ from the air and so regulates the climate. Since 1958 the CO₂ concentration has been measured on **Mauna Loa** in Hawaii. From this comes the well-known **Keeling curve**, which shows a rise.

For **nitrogen** the largest reservoir is in the atmosphere. The air consists of about 78 percent nitrogen. Most living things, however, cannot use this nitrogen from the air directly. Certain bacteria convert it into compounds that plants can take up. Later, other bacteria release the nitrogen back into the air.

Sulphur too is in a cycle. Marine algae give off **dimethyl sulphide**, which can contribute to cloud formation. Humans have greatly changed the sulphur cycle. By burning coal and oil containing sulphur, **acid rain** arose in the 1980s. It damaged forests and lakes. With filters and low-sulphur fuels the problem was greatly reduced.

gewusst: The Keeling curve shows an up and down every year, because plants take up more CO₂ in summer.
Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus has no large reservoir in the air, and its cycle runs mainly through rock, soil and water.

teile.einleitung: In biological pest control, natural enemies are used against pests. These can be insects, mites, bacteria, viruses or tiny worms. This way fewer chemical agents are needed.
wichtigste: In Switzerland Trichogramma wasps are used against the European corn borer.
Bacillus thuringiensis forms a protein that kills caterpillars specifically.
The predatory mite Phytoseiulus persimilis helps against spider mites.
Against the codling moth a granulovirus is used.
Insect-pathogenic nematodes fight the larvae of the black vine weevil.
The cactus moth helped against prickly pears in Australia.
The cane toad was introduced in 1935 and itself became a plague.

abschnitte.text: Every pest has enemies in nature. They are called **beneficial organisms** or natural enemies. In **biological pest control** they are deliberately encouraged or released. We speak of **classical** biological control when an introduced pest is fought. Then a natural enemy from its area of origin is settled.

Tiny **parasitic wasps** of the genus **Trichogramma** lay their eggs in the eggs of the **European corn borer**, a maize pest. In Switzerland they are used on a large scale. In greenhouses the predatory mite **Phytoseiulus persimilis** helps against the two-spotted spider mite. In Australia the **cactus moth** was used successfully against introduced prickly pears.

The bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis** forms a protein that kills caterpillars specifically. It is used as a biological insecticide. In fruit growing a **granulovirus** is used against the caterpillars of the **codling moth**. Against the larvae of the **black vine weevil** living in the soil, **insect-pathogenic nematodes** help. These are tiny threadworms that attack insect larvae.

Biological control must be tested carefully. A well-known example of a failure is the **cane toad**. It was released in Australia in 1935 against beetles in sugar cane. It hardly ate the beetles, but it spread strongly and itself became a plague. Today, before a release, people examine closely whether the beneficial organism attacks only the pest.

gewusst: Trichogramma wasps are so small that you can hardly see them with the naked eye.
Ladybirds and their larvae eat many aphids.

teile.einleitung: In a biogas plant, a combustible gas is produced from liquid manure, dung and green waste. Tiny living things break the material down without oxygen. The biogas supplies electricity and heat or is upgraded to biomethane.
wichtigste: Raw biogas consists of around 50 to 75 percent methane.
In the digester, microorganisms break down the substrate without oxygen.
A stirrer mixes the substrate.
The digester is heated so that the microorganisms work well.
Before the engine the gas is desulphurised.
For biomethane, mainly the carbon dioxide is removed.
Gas that cannot be used is burned in an emergency flare.

abschnitte.text: The heart is the **digester**, a large, tight container. Into it goes the **substrate**, for example liquid manure, dung or food leftovers. Without oxygen, **microorganisms** break down the material and form gas. The digester is usually **heated**, because the microorganisms work best at a constant, warm temperature. A **stirrer** mixes the substrate and prevents floating layers.

abschnitte.titel: How long does the substrate stay?
abschnitte.text: How long the material stays in the digester is called the **retention time**. You work it out by dividing the volume by the daily amount. If a digester holds 2000 cubic metres and receives 50 cubic metres daily, the substrate stays in it for **40 days** on average. Liquid manure is often fermented together with other materials. On its own it yields relatively little gas, because the animals have already extracted a lot of energy from it.

**Raw biogas** consists of around 50 to 75 percent **methane**, and the rest is mainly carbon dioxide. In addition there are small amounts of **hydrogen sulphide**. This is corrosive, so it attacks metal. That is why the gas is **desulphurised** before use in the engine. If the gas cannot be used, for example in an engine failure, it is burned in an **emergency flare**. This way no methane gets into the air.

Often the biogas drives an engine that produces **electricity** and **heat**. You can also upgrade the gas to **biomethane**. For this, mainly the carbon dioxide is removed. Biomethane can be fed into the natural gas network or used as a fuel. The residue from the digester, the **digestate**, is used as fertiliser on the fields.

gewusst: In landfills too a gas containing methane forms, called landfill gas.
Methane is a strong greenhouse gas, so it is good if it is used instead of released.

teile.einleitung: Every species of plant and animal has a scientific name that is the same all over the world. This name consists of two parts. This system is called binomial nomenclature.
wichtigste: A species name consists of two parts: genus and species epithet.
The genus is written with a capital letter, the species epithet in lower case.
In printed texts the name is written in italics.
Bellis perennis is the daisy, Pinus cembra the Swiss stone pine.
Urtica dioica is the stinging nettle, Picea abies the Norway spruce.
“sp.” means a species of a genus that has not been identified more precisely.
In zoology genus and species epithet may be the same, in botany they may not.

abschnitte.text: The system goes back to the Swedish naturalist **Carl Linnaeus**. He introduced the two-part names for plants and animals in the 18th century. Before that, species often had long descriptive names. The short names made of Latin or Latin-shaped words made communication much easier. Researchers all over the world therefore know exactly which species is meant.

The first part is the **genus**, for example “Bellis”. It is written with a capital letter. The second part is the **species epithet**, for example “perennis”, and it is written in lower case. Together they make the species name. In books and magazines it is printed in **italics**. Bellis perennis is the daisy.

The **Swiss stone pine** is called Pinus cembra, so it belongs to the genus of pines. The **Norway spruce** is called Picea abies. The **stinging nettle** is called Urtica dioica. If you know only the genus, you write “sp.”, for example “Carex sp.” for a sedge that has not been identified more precisely.

Plants and animals have their own rules. In zoology, genus and species epithet may be the same. The red fox, for example, is called **Vulpes vulpes**. Such names are called **tautonyms**. In botany they are forbidden.

gewusst: Humans also have a scientific name: Homo sapiens.
