The badger is called Meles meles, which is also a tautonym.

teile.einleitung: Angiosperms are the flowering plants. They are the most species-rich group of plants in the world. Their name comes from the fact that their ovules are enclosed in an ovary.
wichtigste: Around 300,000 species of angiosperms are known.
Their ovules lie protected in the ovary.
The fruit develops from the ovary.
They are reliably documented as fossils since the Early Cretaceous, around 130 million years ago.
Darwin called their sudden appearance an “abominable mystery”.
Most have vessels, which conduct water quickly.
The magnoliids include magnolia, laurel, pepper and avocado.

abschnitte.text: The **angiosperms** are the plants with true flowers. Their ovules lie protected in an **ovary**. In the gymnosperms such as conifers, on the other hand, they lie exposed. With around **300,000** described species, the angiosperms are the most species-rich group of plants. They include grasses, herbs, broadleaved trees and almost all crop plants.

After **fertilisation**, the wall of the ovary becomes the **fruit wall**. This produces a fruit that encloses the seeds. In some fruits further parts of the flower grow into it as well. In the ovule lies a tiny, greatly reduced part, the **embryo sac**. It usually consists of seven cells with eight nuclei.

The oldest reliable pollen and flower fossils come from the **Early Cretaceous**, around 130 million years ago. After that the flowering plants spread astonishingly fast. **Charles Darwin** wrote in 1879 to his friend Joseph Hooker of an “abominable mystery”. The rapid diversity fitted badly with his idea of gradual change.

Plants conduct water upwards from the roots in fine cells. Many plants have only **tracheids** for this. Most angiosperms also have **vessels**. These are long tubes made of cells whose end walls have dissolved. They conduct water faster than tracheids.

The angiosperms are divided into several groups. One early-branching group is the **magnoliids**. They include magnolia, laurel, pepper, nutmeg and avocado. The largest group is the **eudicots**, to which for example roses, beans and oaks belong. A particularly impressive example is the **giant water lily** Victoria from South America. Its floating leaves reach a diameter of around three metres.

gewusst: Thanks to ribs on the underside, the leaves of the giant water lily are so sturdy that they can carry a small child.
Almost everything we eat in the way of cereals, fruit and vegetables comes from angiosperms.

teile.einleitung: The floodplains of national importance are the most valuable river landscapes in Switzerland. The Confederation has listed them in an inventory and placed them under protection. Many rare animals and plants live here.
wichtigste: Floodplains of national importance are listed in the federal inventory of floodplains.
Floodplains are very rich in species.
Typical of the softwood floodplain are willows and alders.
Floods create new gravel areas and pools in the floodplain.
The tree frog and the kingfisher are typical residents.
The Bolle di Magadino lie where the Ticino flows into Lake Maggiore.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland keeps a **federal inventory of floodplains of national importance**. It has existed since **1992** and has been added to several times since. The areas listed are to be **preserved undiminished**. The **cantons** are mainly responsible for protection. The inventory includes floodplains along rivers and lakes, but also glacier forelands and alpine alluvial plains.

In a near-natural floodplain, **floods are important**. They **create new gravel areas and pools** and sweep old plants away. This gives rise again and again to pioneer areas where new plants sprout. In the **softwood floodplain** close to the water, **willows** and **alders** grow. They cope well with flooding and grow back quickly.

Because there are so many different habitats, floodplains are **very rich in species**. The **tree frog** is a small green frog that is good at **climbing**. It spawns in warm, shallow floodplain pools. The **kingfisher** is a bright blue and orange bird. It hunts small fish and digs its nesting burrow into **steep banks** of earth or sand.

The **beaver** also changes the floodplain. It **fells trees** and **builds dams**, so that water is held back. This creates new ponds, dead wood and light gaps. Many insects, amphibians and birds benefit from this. In several Swiss floodplains the beaver lives again today.

Many rivers used to be straightened and squeezed into narrow beds. In a **restoration**, a canalised river gets **more room** and **natural banks** again. A well-known floodplain area is the **Bolle di Magadino** in Ticino. They lie at the **mouth of the Ticino into Lake Maggiore**. Many migratory birds rest there on their way across the Alps.

gewusst: Floodplains cover only a small part of Switzerland, but are home to a large share of the native plant and animal species.
The kingfisher dives headfirst into the water to catch a fish.

teile.einleitung: Many animals and plants have become rare, or had even disappeared completely from Switzerland. With species conservation, people try to help them in a targeted way. This ranges from the amphibian fence beside the road to the reintroduction of ibex, beaver and lynx.
wichtigste: Species conservation means targeted measures for rare or threatened species.
From 1906, the ibex was reintroduced with animals from the Gran Paradiso.
The beaver returned to Switzerland from 1956.
The lynx was reintroduced from 1971.
Amphibian fences help toads to cross the road safely in spring.
Zoos breed threatened species in conservation breeding programmes.

abschnitte.titel: The return of the big animals
abschnitte.text: In the 19th century, several wild animals had been **wiped out** in Switzerland. The **ibex** survived only in the **Gran Paradiso** area in Italy. From **1906**, animals from there were reintroduced in Switzerland, and today many ibex live in the Alps again. The **beaver** returned from **1956**, the **lynx** from **1971**. Since 1991 the **bearded vulture** has also been reintroduced, first in the Swiss National Park.

In spring, toads, frogs and newts migrate to their spawning waters. On the way they often have to cross **roads**, where many are run over. At such places volunteers put up **amphibian fences**. The animals walk along the fence and fall into buckets, from which they are carried safely to the other side. In some places, permanent tunnels are also built under the road.

abschnitte.titel: Living space in villages and towns
abschnitte.text: Many animals live in built-up areas, but hardly find shelter there any more. **Bats** and **swifts** need crevices and niches in buildings, which often disappear during renovations. **Nest boxes** and artificial **roosts** provide a substitute. **Hedges of native shrubs** offer many animals **food, shelter and nesting places**. Even a near-natural garden can achieve a lot.

The **lapwing** is a bird that builds its nest **on the ground**, often in the middle of fields and meadows. There the eggs are at risk from farm machinery and foxes. Nature conservationists on the Central Plateau **mark the nests** so that farmers can drive around them. With **protective fences** they keep predators away. Thanks to such measures, more young lapwings hatch again.

Often the greatest help is to improve whole habitats. To **restore** a river means to **make it near-natural again**, with gravel banks, shallow shores and more room. In **zoos** there are **conservation breeding programmes** in which threatened species are bred in a targeted way. Zoos from many countries work together on this. Some animals from such programmes are later released into the wild.

gewusst: Almost all ibex in the Swiss Alps descend from a few animals from the Gran Paradiso.
At some amphibian fences, volunteers carry several thousand animals across the road in a single spring.

teile.einleitung: In spring the bare trees turn green again. The new leaves come out of the buds that were already formed in autumn. This process is called **leaf emergence**.
wichtigste: The new leaves grow out of the buds in spring.
In the bud the young leaves lie tightly folded or rolled.
Warmth makes the buds swell and open.
Young leaves are delicate and shine light green.
The horse chestnut comes into leaf early, oak, ash and walnut later.
The larch, as a conifer, gets completely new needles every year.

abschnitte.titel: Leaves in their winter hiding place
abschnitte.text: Already in summer and autumn a tree forms its **buds**. In them the future leaves lie ready, tiny. Because there is little room, they are **tightly folded** or rolled. Hard **bud scales** protect them in winter from cold and drying out. The buds of the horse chestnut are also sticky.

When it has been **warm enough** for some time in spring, the buds begin to swell. In some trees the lengthening days also play a part. Then the scales open and the leaves unfold. Not all trees are equally fast. The **horse chestnut** in Switzerland often comes into leaf as early as April. **Oak**, **ash** and **walnut** take more time.

Very young leaves are soft and thin. They still contain little **chlorophyll** and so shine **light green**. With time they become firmer and darker. The plant needs the chlorophyll to make **sugar** with **sunlight**, water and air. The whole tree lives from this.

Most conifers keep their needles for several years. The **larch** is an exception. In autumn it loses all its needles, which turn golden yellow beforehand. In spring it forms completely **new, light green needles**. In the mountain valleys of Switzerland, for example in the Engadine or in Valais, larch forests are common.

gewusst: When the trees come into leaf has been observed in Switzerland for many years. This shows that spring today often begins earlier than it used to.
In Geneva, since 1818 a note has been made of when the first leaf appears on a particular horse chestnut.

teile.einleitung: Lake Baldegg lies in the Seetal in the canton of Lucerne. It is known because it belongs to a nature conservation organisation and is artificially aerated. It shows clearly how over-fertilisation harms a lake.
wichtigste: Lake Baldegg lies in the canton of Lucerne, in the Seetal.
Its water flows via the Aabach into Lake Hallwil.
The lake belongs to Pro Natura.
Phosphorus from farming has over-fertilised the lake.
Since the early 1980s the lake has been artificially aerated.
The aeration fights only the effects, not the cause.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Baldegg** lies in the north of the canton of **Lucerne**, in the Hochdorf area. It is one of the lakes of the Central Plateau. The landscape is called the **Seetal**, meaning lake valley, because several lakes lie there. The water of Lake Baldegg flows via the **Aabach** into the lower-lying **Lake Hallwil**. This lies for the most part in the canton of Aargau.

Lake Baldegg belongs to the nature conservation organisation **Pro Natura**. This makes it one of the few Swiss lakes owned by a nature conservation organisation. Around the lake there are reeds and wet meadows where many birds live. Strict rules therefore apply on the lake, for example for boats.

In the area around the lake there is a lot of **livestock farming**. With the slurry, **phosphorus** reaches the streams and the lake. Phosphorus is a nutrient and makes algae grow strongly. When the algae die, they sink to the bottom and are broken down there. This uses up oxygen, and in the end it was missing completely in the deep water. This is called **over-fertilisation**.

Since the early 1980s Lake Baldegg has been **artificially aerated**. Two methods are combined: in winter, air is blown in so that all the water mixes well. In summer, **oxygen** is added directly to the deep water, without disturbing the layers of water. Later Lake Sempach and Lake Hallwil also received similar installations.

The aeration counts as **treating the symptoms**. It does supply oxygen, but it does not lower the nutrients that flow into the lake from the catchment area. Only letting less phosphorus into the lake helps in the long term. That is why the canton and farmers work together, so that less fertiliser gets from the fields into the water.

gewusst: A lake without oxygen in its deep water no longer offers fish a habitat there.
The aeration installations in the Seetal were an early example of lake restoration in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Leaves are the mostly green, flat parts of a plant that grow on twigs and stems. With the help of sunlight they make food for the whole plant. In autumn many leaves turn colourful and then fall off.
wichtigste: Most leaves are green in summer.
Leaves need sunlight to make food for the plant.
The leaf hangs on the twig by its stalk.
In the leaf veins, water flows through the leaf.
If a plant gets too little water, its leaves hang limply.
In autumn many leaves turn yellow, orange or red and fall off.
Every tree species has its own leaf shape, by which you can recognise it.

abschnitte.text: A leaf usually consists of a flat **leaf blade** and a thin **leaf stalk**. With the stalk it hangs on the twig. Across the leaf blade run fine lines, the **leaf veins**. They bring water into the leaf and at the same time make it stable, like the spokes of an umbrella.

Leaves are like the plant’s little kitchens. They take sunlight, water and carbon dioxide from the air and make sugar from them. This process is called **photosynthesis**. In doing so they give off oxygen, which people and animals need for breathing.

The water comes from the roots up the stem into the leaves. On the underside of the leaves there are tiny openings through which water evaporates. If water is missing, the leaves lose their firmness and hang limply. If you water a wilted pot plant in time, the leaves often straighten up again after a few hours.

In summer leaves are green because they contain a lot of green pigment, **chlorophyll**. In autumn the tree breaks this pigment down and takes valuable substances back into the trunk and roots. Then yellow and orange colours become visible that were hidden before. After that a separating layer forms at the stalk, and the leaf falls off.

The leaf of the beech is oval, the leaf of the oak has wavy lobes. A maple leaf looks like an open hand. In the horse chestnut a leaf consists of five to seven fingers. The needles of firs and spruces are, by the way, also leaves, only very narrow and hard.

With autumn leaves you can make nice things, such as leaf wreaths or pictures. If you lay leaves between newspaper under heavy books, they become flat and dry, which makes a **herbarium**. Laid under paper and rubbed with a coloured pencil, leaves show their veins very clearly. In Switzerland many school classes collect leaves in autumn and identify the trees.

begriffe.erklaerung: The little stalk by which a leaf hangs on the twig.
Fine lines in the leaf in which water and nutrients flow.
The green pigment in the leaves that captures sunlight.
How plants make their food with light, water and air.
A collection of pressed and dried plants.

gewusst: A large beech has several hundred thousand leaves in summer.
The needles of a fir are also leaves, and they stay green on the tree in winter.
The yellow colours in autumn leaves are already in the leaf in summer, they are only covered by the lots of green.

teile.einleitung: In spring many trees turn into a sea of blossom. Tree blossom is important, because without flowers there is no fruit. Bees and the wind help with pollination.
wichtigste: Bees pollinate the blossoms of fruit trees most of all.
The hazel already flowers in February with yellow catkins.
Cherry trees mostly flower before apple trees.
Birches are pollinated by the wind, and their pollen triggers hay fever in some people.
Late frost can freeze the blossoms.
The lime tree flowers in June and July and smells sweet.
In Japan the cherry blossom is celebrated with the festival Hanami.

abschnitte.text: For a flower to become a fruit, it must be **pollinated**. In fruit trees this is done above all by **bees**. They fly from flower to flower, collect nectar and carry pollen with them. In this way the pollen gets from one flower to another. From the pollinated flower a cherry or an apple later grows.

Some trees do not need insects. **Birches** are pollinated by the **wind**. It carries the fine dust of the flowers, the **pollen**, to other birches. Some people get **hay fever** from it. The **hazel** is also pollinated by the wind. It flowers already in February, before the leaves, and lets its yellow catkins dangle in the wind.

Not all trees flower at the same time. In March the **goat willow** forms soft, silvery **pussy willow catkins**, an important first food for bees. **Cherry trees** here often flower as early as April, the **apple trees** a little later. In June and July the **lime tree** flowers. Its blossoms smell sweet, attract many bees, and are made into lime blossom tea.

A late **frost** during flowering can do a lot of damage. The delicate blossoms freeze and can no longer form fruit. Then there is less fruit in summer and autumn. Some fruit growers protect their trees on cold nights, for example by spraying the blossoms with water. The ice forms a protective shell.

When the flowering is over, the **petals** fall off. They then lie like snow under the tree. In **Japan** the cherry blossom is a big event. In spring many people sit under flowering cherry trees, eat and celebrate. This festival is called **Hanami**, which means roughly “looking at flowers”.

gewusst: On the hazel there are male catkins and tiny red female flowers on the same shrub.
A single bee colony can visit millions of flowers in one day.

teile.einleitung: The Amazon rainforest is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth and influences the climate far beyond South America. Researchers warn that deforestation, fires and climate change could push it to a tipping point. After that, parts of the forest could turn into a drier, savannah-like landscape.
wichtigste: Around 60 per cent of the Amazon rainforest lies in **Brazil**.
**Timothy Lenton** and colleagues counted the Amazon among the **tipping elements** of the climate system in 2008.
In 2018, Lovejoy and Nobre suspected a tipping point at **20 to 25 per cent** deforestation.
Through its evaporation, the forest forms **“flying rivers”**.
According to a study from 2021, the south-east of the Amazon releases more carbon than it absorbs.
In 2023 the Rio Negro at Manaus fell to its lowest level since measurements began.

abschnitte.text: The trees of the rainforest evaporate huge amounts of water. This rises, forms clouds and falls again as rain further inland. These streams of water vapour are called **“flying rivers”**. They even supply regions in the south of Brazil with rain. A large part of the rain in the Amazon region therefore comes from the **evaporation of the trees** themselves.

A **tipping point** is a threshold: when it is crossed, a system switches to a new state. In 2008, **Timothy Lenton** and colleagues described such **tipping elements** in the climate system, including the Amazon rainforest, the Greenland ice sheet and the Atlantic overturning circulation. Often there is **hysteresis**: after the tipping, it is not enough to ease the cause just slightly. The pressure would often have to fall well below the original threshold for the old state to return.

When forest is cleared, less water evaporates and less rain falls. The remaining forest becomes drier, which makes **fires** more likely and weakens even more forest. This favours open, drier vegetation, which is called **savannisation**. In 2018, **Thomas Lovejoy** and **Carlos Nobre** estimated that parts of the forest could tip at **20 to 25 per cent** deforestation. Climate change and fire lower this threshold even further.

A healthy rainforest absorbs carbon dioxide and stores carbon in its wood. In 2021, **Luciana Gatti** and colleagues published a study in the journal “Nature” based on measurement flights. It showed that above all the heavily deforested **south-east of the Amazon** now releases more carbon than it absorbs. Fires and drought are important causes of this.

In 2023 the Amazon region suffered a severe **drought**. In the port of **Manaus**, the **Rio Negro** fell in October to its lowest level since measurements began, which go back over 120 years. River villages were cut off, and river dolphins died in the overheated water. In 2024 this record low was broken again.

gewusst: The Amazon rainforest is spread across Brazil and eight other countries and territories, including Peru, Colombia and French Guiana.
A single large rainforest tree can evaporate hundreds of litres of water in one day.

teile.einleitung: Arbuscular mycorrhiza is a partnership between plant roots and certain soil fungi. The fungus helps the plant to take up nutrients and gets sugar in return. This cooperation is ancient and widespread on Earth.
wichtigste: The fungi of this mycorrhiza belong to the group Glomeromycota.
Arbuscules are finely branched little fungal trees inside the cortex cells of the root.
Around 70 to 80 per cent of land plant species form this mycorrhiza.
The fungus supplies the plant mainly with phosphate.
Crucifers such as rape and cabbage usually form no mycorrhiza.
The fungi are obligate symbionts and always need a host plant.

abschnitte.titel: Fungus and root as a team
abschnitte.text: The word **mycorrhiza** comes from Greek and means roughly “fungus root”. In **arbuscular mycorrhiza**, fungal threads, the **hyphae**, grow into the root. The fungi belong to the group **Glomeromycota**. Both partners benefit: this is called a **symbiosis**. The plant gives the fungus sugar from photosynthesis, and the fungus supplies it with water and nutrients.

This mycorrhiza gets its name from the **arbuscules**. These are finely branched **little hyphal trees** that the fungus forms in the **cortex cells** of the root. This is where the exchange of nutrients takes place. Many of these fungi also form **vesicles**. These are bubble-shaped storage organs in which the fungus keeps fat as a reserve.

The most important nutrient the fungus supplies is **phosphate**. Phosphate moves poorly in the soil, and the root alone often cannot reach enough of it. The fungal threads reach much further and are much finer than root hairs. This way they open up a large volume of soil. Around **70 to 80 per cent** of land plant species use this help, including many crops such as maize and wheat.

abschnitte.titel: How the partners find each other
abschnitte.text: Plant roots release signal substances into the soil, the **strigolactones**. They attract the fungal threads and encourage them to branch. The fungi are **obligate symbionts**: they cannot live without a host plant. That is why they cannot be grown alone on a culture medium in the laboratory. A few plants do not take part, for example the **crucifers** such as **rape** and **cabbage**.

Fossils show that this cooperation is very old. In the **Rhynie chert** in Scotland, a rock around **400 million years** old, arbuscules are found even in early land plants. Many researchers suspect that the fungi helped the first plants to settle on land. At that time there were no true roots yet and hardly any fertile soil.

gewusst: The hyphae of the fungi are so fine that they penetrate soil pores that are too narrow for root hairs.
Strigolactones are not only recognised by fungi: the seeds of some parasitic plants also germinate when they sense these substances.

teile.einleitung: Beard lichens hang like grey beards from the branches. They are found mainly in damp mountain forests. Where they grow, the air is especially clean.
wichtigste: Beard lichens hang in long, grey-green threads from branches.
They often grow on firs and spruces in mountain forest.
They do not harm the tree, they only use it for support.
They have no roots and get water from rain and fog.
They are very sensitive to air pollution.
When dry they become brittle, after rain they become soft again.

abschnitte.text: **Beard lichens** hang in long, fine threads from the branches. They are mostly **grey-green** or yellowish-green and are reminiscent of a beard. A lichen is a special partnership between a **fungus** and an alga. The fungus gives support and protection, and the alga makes food using sunlight. When damp, beard lichens look greener.

Beard lichens like **damp**, clean air. They hang especially often in **mountain forest** on firs and spruces. They do not harm the tree. They use the branch only as a place to hold on and take no food away from it. They make their food themselves.

Beard lichens have **no roots**. They soak up water directly from rain, dew and **fog**. If it stays dry for a long time, they dry out and become **brittle** and fragile. After the next rain they become soft again and carry on living. This is how they can survive long dry spells.

Beard lichens are very sensitive to **air pollution**. Because they take up everything from air and rain, they also take up pollutants. Where many beard lichens hang, the air is therefore very clean. Such living things are called **indicator organisms**. Some birds also use the soft, fibrous lichens to build their nests.

gewusst: Lichens grow very slowly, often only a few millimetres a year.
In towns with a lot of traffic, beard lichens are almost completely absent.

teile.einleitung: A tree is a large plant with a woody trunk, branches and a crown of leaves or needles. Trees are among the largest and oldest living things on Earth. They give us oxygen, wood, fruit and shade.
wichtigste: A tree consists of roots, trunk and crown.
The thick main part between roots and crown is called the trunk.
The bark protects the trunk from the outside.
From the annual rings you can estimate the age of a tree.
Trees give off oxygen, which we need for breathing.
A distinction is made between broadleaved trees and conifers.
About a third of Switzerland is covered with forest.

abschnitte.text: A tree has three main parts: the **roots** hold it firmly in the ground and take up water and nutrients. The **trunk** carries the tree and conducts the water upwards. At the top the **crown**, with branches, twigs and leaves, forms the roof of the tree. The **bark** wraps the trunk and protects it from heat, cold and pests.

**Broadleaved trees** such as beech, oak or maple have broad leaves, which most of them drop in autumn. **Conifers** such as spruce, fir or pine have narrow needles and usually stay green all year round. An exception is the **larch**: its needles turn golden yellow in autumn and fall. In the mountains, larch forests colour whole slopes a bright yellow.

In the leaves, the tree makes sugar using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, which is called **photosynthesis**. In doing so it gives off oxygen into the air. A large beech can evaporate hundreds of litres of water on a summer day. This is how trees cool their surroundings, especially in towns.

Every year a tree lays down a new layer of wood under the bark. In spring light, loose wood grows, in summer darker, firmer wood. This produces **annual rings**, which can be counted on a felled trunk. Wide rings show good years, narrow rings for example dry or cold years.

The tallest known tree is a coast redwood in California called Hyperion, which is over 115 metres tall. Some bristlecone pines in the USA are almost 5,000 years old. In Switzerland, old yews, limes and oaks are among the oldest trees, and some are many hundreds of years old. So trees can live much longer than humans.

About a third of the area of Switzerland is **forest**. The commonest tree is the spruce, followed by the beech. In the mountains, trees protect villages and roads from **avalanches**, rockfall and landslides. Since the 19th century the forest in Switzerland has been protected by law, and anyone who clears forest usually has to plant new forest elsewhere.

begriffe.erklaerung: The upper part of the tree with branches and leaves.
The layer of wood that a tree forms in one year.
The process in which plants make sugar using light and give off oxygen.
Forest that protects people from avalanches and rockfall.

gewusst: Most of a tree’s roots do not lie deep, but spread far to the side.
Trees can exchange substances with each other through fungal threads in the soil.
The science that determines the age of wood from annual rings is called dendrochronology.

teile.einleitung: Biomonitoring means watching over the environment for a long time with the help of living things. Plants, animals or their traces show how polluted air, water and soil are. In Switzerland there are several programmes for this.
wichtigste: Biomonitoring is the long-term monitoring of the environment with the help of living things.
In active biomonitoring, test organisms are deliberately placed at measuring points.
In moss monitoring, mainly heavy metals such as lead and cadmium are measured.
Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland has monitored species diversity since 2001.
The IBCH index uses small invertebrates of the stream bed.
The tobacco variety Bel W3 indicates ground-level ozone.
With environmental DNA, traces of genetic material are found in water or soil samples.

abschnitte.text: In **biomonitoring** you observe living things in order to judge the state of the environment. The advantage over a single chemical measurement: it shows the **overall effect** of many pollutants over a longer period. In **passive** biomonitoring you examine living things that already live on the spot. In **active** biomonitoring you deliberately place test organisms at measuring points.

Mosses take up substances directly from air and rain. In Europe-wide **moss monitoring**, mainly **heavy metals** such as lead and cadmium are measured in them. The tobacco variety **Bel W3** is very sensitive to ground-level **ozone**. At high levels it gets spots on its leaves. That is why it is used as an indicator.

**Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland** has systematically monitored species diversity since 2001. For streams and rivers there is the **IBCH** index. It assesses waters on the basis of **small invertebrates** of the stream bed, such as insect larvae, snails and worms. Which animals occur reveals a lot about the water quality.

In the **environmental DNA** method, **eDNA** for short, you examine traces of genetic material in water or soil samples. Every living thing leaves such traces. This way you can detect species without seeing them. **Honeybees** are also used. They collect over a large area and carry pollutants into honey, pollen and wax.

gewusst: With eDNA you can even detect rare fish in a river from a water sample.
A bee colony visits flowers within a radius of several kilometres.

teile.einleitung: An absorption spectrum shows which colours of light a substance absorbs. For plants this is important because their pigments use only certain colours for photosynthesis. This also explains why leaves look green.
wichtigste: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly blue and red light.
Green light is absorbed little, which is why leaves are green.
Plants use light of about 400 to 700 nanometres.
In chlorophyll there is a magnesium atom.
Carotenoids widen the spectrum and become visible in autumn.
In 1882 Theodor Wilhelm Engelmann showed which light drives photosynthesis.

abschnitte.text: White sunlight consists of many colours. Each colour has its own **wavelength**, measured in nanometres. An **absorption spectrum** is a diagram that shows how strongly a pigment absorbs each wavelength. Plants use almost only visible light from about **400 nanometres** (violet) to **700 nanometres** (red). This range is called **photosynthetically active radiation**. UV and infrared radiation contribute hardly anything to photosynthesis.

The most important pigment is **chlorophyll**. It absorbs mainly **blue** and **red** light. Green light, by contrast, is absorbed little. It is mostly reflected or let through and reaches our eye. That is why leaves look **green**. **Chlorophyll a** forms the reaction centres of the photosystems. **Chlorophyll b** helps in the antennae as an accessory pigment. In the centre of chlorophyll sits a **magnesium atom**, whereas in the similarly built red blood pigment there is iron.

**Carotenoids** are yellow to orange pigments. They absorb blue and blue-green light and pass the energy on to chlorophyll. In **autumn** the chlorophyll is broken down, and then the carotenoids come to the fore and colour the leaves yellow and orange. **Red algae** and **cyanobacteria** additionally have **phycobilins**. These absorb green and yellow light. In this way red algae can carry out photosynthesis even in deeper water.

The **action spectrum** shows how strongly photosynthesis actually takes place at each wavelength. In 1882 **Theodor Wilhelm Engelmann** fanned out light with a prism and shone it on a filamentous alga. Bacteria that love oxygen gathered where **blue and red light** fell. So the most oxygen arose there. **Robert Emerson** found that two wavelengths together work more strongly than each alone. This **Emerson effect** pointed to two **photosystems** working together.

gewusst: The yellow tones of autumn are in the leaf all summer; they are only covered by the green of the chlorophyll.
Engelmann’s experiment managed without modern measuring instruments: the bacteria themselves showed where oxygen arose.

teile.einleitung: The Convention on Biological Diversity is an international treaty for the protection of biological diversity. Almost all states in the world have joined it. It was presented in 1992 at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.
wichtigste: The convention entered into force in 1993.
It has three aims: conservation, sustainable use and fair sharing of benefits.
In 2025 it had 196 contracting parties.
The United States has not joined it (as of 2025).
The highest body is the Conference of the Parties (COP).
The Nagoya Protocol regulates access to genetic resources.
In 2010 the 20 Aichi Targets were adopted.

abschnitte.text: The **Convention on Biological Diversity** was opened for signature in 1992 at the Earth Summit in **Rio de Janeiro**. It entered into force in **1993**. In 2025 it had 196 contracting parties. The **United States** signed it, but never joined. Switzerland too is a member.

The convention pursues three main aims. First, biological diversity is to be **conserved**. Second, its components are to be **used sustainably**, that is, in such a way that later generations can also live from them. Third, the benefits from the use of **genetic resources** are to be shared fairly. This concerns, for example, plants from which medicines are developed.

The highest body is the **Conference of the Parties**, abbreviated **COP**. There the states meet regularly and make decisions. The convention includes additional treaties called protocols. The **Nagoya Protocol** regulates access to genetic resources and the fair sharing of benefits. The Cartagena Protocol deals with genetically modified organisms.

In 2010 the states adopted 20 targets for the year 2020, the **Aichi Targets**. Most of them were not met. In 2022 a new framework followed with targets up to 2030. At COP16 in Colombia in 2024 the states created the **Cali Fund**. Companies that make profits from digital sequence information, that is, stored genetic data, are to pay into it.

gewusst: The secretariat of the convention has its seat in Montreal in Canada.
The Aichi Targets are named after a prefecture in Japan where the conference took place in 2010.

teile.einleitung: The Asian tiger mosquito is a small mosquito with black and white stripes. It originally lived in South-East Asia, but today it occurs in many countries, including Switzerland. It bites during the day and can pass on disease-causing agents.
wichtigste: The tiger mosquito is black with white stripes and has a white lengthways stripe on its back.
It bites mainly during the day.
In Switzerland it was first detected in 2003, in Ticino.
In Europe it first appeared in Albania in 1979.
It can transmit dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses.
It lays its eggs in small collections of water.

abschnitte.text: The **Asian tiger mosquito** (Aedes albopictus) is smaller than most native mosquitoes. It is **black with white stripes** on its legs and body. A **white lengthways stripe** in the middle of the back is typical. Unlike many native mosquitoes, it bites mainly **during the day**. As with all mosquitoes, only the females bite.

The tiger mosquito comes from **South-East Asia**. With world trade it was carried to many countries, for example in used car tyres. In Europe it was first detected **in Albania in 1979**. In Switzerland it was found **in Ticino in 2003**. Since then it has also spread north of the Alps, for example in Basel and Zurich.

The tiger mosquito lays its eggs in **small collections of water**. These can be the **saucers** of flowerpots, **watering cans**, buckets or blocked gutters. The eggs are very tough and **survive dryness for months**. As soon as water flows over them again, the larvae hatch. This property makes it easier for the mosquito to be carried unnoticed into other countries.

In principle the tiger mosquito can transmit **dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses**. To do so, however, it must first bite a person who is ill. In Switzerland such viruses are hardly present in nature, so the risk has so far been low. In southern Europe, however, there have already been small outbreaks. The authorities therefore monitor its spread closely.

abschnitte.titel: What you can do about it
abschnitte.text: The most important thing is to **avoid standing water**: empty saucers, turn buckets over, cover rain barrels. Against the larvae, a biological agent is used, the bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis**, or **Bti** for short. It harms mainly mosquito larvae. In **Ticino** the **sterile insect technique** has also been tested. In it, many males that have been made infertile are released, so that fewer offspring are produced.

gewusst: A tiger mosquito usually flies only a few hundred metres. Over long distances it travels as a stowaway in cars and lorries.
In Switzerland you can report sightings of the tiger mosquito, so that experts can follow its spread.

teile.einleitung: The Atacama in the north of Chile is one of the driest deserts on Earth. In some places it does not rain for years. Even so, there is life there that gets its water from the fog.
wichtigste: The Atacama lies in the north of Chile on the Pacific coast.
The cold Humboldt Current contributes greatly to the dryness.
The coastal fog is called Camanchaca.
People collect water from the fog with fog nets.
A lot of lithium is obtained from the Atacama’s salt lakes.
Because of the dry, clear air, large observatories stand there.

abschnitte.text: The **Atacama** lies in the north of **Chile**, between the Pacific and the **Andes**. It is one of the **driest deserts on Earth**. One reason is the cold **Humboldt Current** off the coast. It cools the air above the sea, so that hardly any rain clouds form. In the east, the high Andes keep out damp air from the Amazon region.

On the coast a dense fog often forms, the **Camanchaca**. It drifts from the sea against the coastal mountains. People put up large **fog nets** there. Droplets of water stick to the fine mesh and drip into gutters and containers. In this way small villages get drinking water and water for gardens.

Where the fog comes regularly, green islands of plants grow. In Peru and northern Chile they are called **lomas**. Especially astonishing are some **tillandsias**, which lie in the sand **completely without roots**. They take water directly from the fog through fine **absorbing scales**. After **rare heavier rainfalls**, something special happens: the desert begins to bloom. This is called the **“blooming desert”**.

In the Atacama there are large **salt flats**, for example the Salar de Atacama. **Lithium** is obtained from their brine in large quantities. The metal is needed for the **batteries** in mobile phones and electric cars. A lot of **copper** is also mined in the region. Mining needs a lot of water, which leads to disputes in this dry area.

Because the **air is very dry and clear**, several large **astronomical observatories** stand in the Atacama. There are hardly any clouds and little light from cities. The European Southern Observatory, **ESO**, of which Switzerland is also a member, runs telescopes there, for example on Cerro Paranal.
